graphics.title: Seeing a result is not explaining it
graphics.alt: A bus has a red display showing a 12-minute delay. That is an observation. A supplied engineering note says past journeys fitted the delay model; that is evidence about its mechanism.

graphics.title: Who or what makes this decision?
graphics.alt: A remote-controlled car follows human commands, a motion lamp follows a written rule, and a trained photo sorter applies a learned model. A product can combine mechanisms. AI also includes symbolic reasoning.

graphics.title: One bus display. Three different decisions.
graphics.alt: Three separate rows trace the bus estimate, display colour and driver override. The fitted model estimates 12 minutes; the written greater-than-10 rule makes the display red; the driver can choose ROUTE CLOSED.

graphics.title: Learn first. Predict later.
graphics.alt: Earlier weather records are used to fit a model. Later, new measurements are passed to that fitted model to obtain a 70 percent rain forecast. It is an estimate, not a guarantee.

graphics.title: Change the rule. Keep the forecast.
graphics.alt: With a 70 percent rain forecast, a 60 percent-or-more rule displays TAKE ONE. An 80 percent-or-more rule does not trigger that message. Only the boundary changed; the fitted model and forecast did not.

graphics.title: “Not enough information” is a useful answer
graphics.alt: An unspecified smart robot vacuum moves and cleans, but its route mechanism is unknown. Ask for evidence of human commands, written rules or model fitting, and allow combinations. Apply this reasoning to a classroom sorter.

graphics.title: Input, Process, Output: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional classroom cupboard records coloured pencils, then reports just a total. Supplied facts: Box A has 2 red and 4 blue pencils. Box B has 5 red and 1 blue. The process adds colour counts and stores only the total, not the two counts.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Read colours: A: red 2, blue 4. B: red 5, blue 1. → Add counts: A: 2+4=6. B: 5+1=6. → Store total: Both records become total 6. → Ask a new question: The saved totals cannot tell which box has more red pencils.

graphics.title: Different pencil colours. The same total.
graphics.alt: Box A: 2 red pencils and 4 blue, total 6. Box B: 5 red pencils and 1 blue, total 6. The equal totals do not preserve the colour counts.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: The saved totals cannot tell which box has more red pencils. Changed condition: Store red count alongside total. Expected result: The records become (6,2) and (6,5). Reason: Blue count can now be recovered by total minus red, assuming these are the only colours.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Adding preserves the number of pencils but discards how that number was divided between colours. Both distinct inputs lead to the same stored output. Working backwards from 6 therefore has several possible answers; it is not an instruction to divide equally. Limit: The two-colour assumption matters. Extra colours would prevent inferring blue from total and red alone.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Choose sorter inputs that retain the clues needed for its decision; draw the transformation and identify discarded details. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Use the richer record to find blue pencils in Box B. Explain why total alone was insufficient.

graphics.title: Sensors Are Messengers: the case
graphics.alt: Two fictional light sensors disagree in a classroom. Compare them fairly rather than declaring one broken. Supplied facts: On the same shelf, simultaneous readings are A: 40,50,60 and B: 45,55,65 in declared toy light units. Neither device has been compared with a trusted reference.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Same shelf: Place both devices together and allow them to settle. → Paired readings: Record three matching times: (40,45), (50,55), (60,65). → Compare gaps: B minus A is 5, 5 and 5 units. → Check a reference: A trusted reference is needed to decide which reading is closer.

graphics.title: Simultaneous light readings
graphics.alt: Simultaneous light readings. Time 1: Sensor A = 40, Sensor B = 45, B minus A = 5. Time 2: Sensor A = 50, Sensor B = 55, B minus A = 5. Time 3: Sensor A = 60, Sensor B = 65, B minus A = 5.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: A trusted reference is needed to decide which reading is closer. Changed condition: Move only B into brighter light. Expected result: The next gap could change for reasons other than a difference in device accuracy. Reason: The comparison now changes location as well as device; there is no supplied reading from the new location.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A repeated difference of 5 supports investigating an offset between devices. Matching time and location removes two obvious comparison problems. It does not show which device is correct: both could have errors. Preserve paired readings instead of adjusting them silently. Limit: Three pairs do not prove an offset holds at every light level, nor identify the accurate device.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Save sorter measurements with device, location and time so unusual inputs can be checked before decisions. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why can we calculate the earlier gap but not predict an exact new B reading?

graphics.title: Rules or Learned Patterns?: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional paper sorter learns a size boundary for toy pebbles. Supplied facts: Training diameters are 1,3,5,7 cm with labels small,small,large,large. Compare large-at-least-3 with large-at-least-5; choose fewer errors.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Training examples: Diameters 1,3,5,7 have reference labels S,S,L,L. → Candidate 3: Predictions S,L,L,L: one disagreement at 3. → Candidate 5: Predictions S,S,L,L: zero disagreements. → New pebble: Selected boundary 5 predicts small for a new diameter 4.

graphics.title: Training errors by candidate boundary
graphics.alt: Training errors by candidate boundary. Units: disagreements. Boundary 3: 1. Boundary 5: 0.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Selected boundary 5 predicts small for a new diameter 4. Changed condition: Give a new pebble diameter 5 instead of 4. Expected result: The selected rule predicts large. Reason: At least includes equality, so 5 meets the boundary.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The learning procedure compares candidate rules against supplied examples and selects boundary 5. Applying that boundary to diameter 4 is a later prediction step. An explicit threshold can be selected from data; being easy to write does not make its origin unknowable. Limit: Zero training disagreements do not prove every future pebble receives the correct label.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Document whether the sorter’s rules were teacher-written or chosen from examples, retaining candidate errors. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Show which stage used labels and which stage used only the new measurement.

graphics.title: Pictures Become Numbers: the case
graphics.alt: Two fictional 2-by-3 pixel badges contain the same number of dark squares. Supplied facts: Dark=1, light=0; rows are read top to bottom, left to right. Badge A rows: 1,0,1 / 0,1,0. Badge B: 1,1,1 / 0,0,0.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Pixel convention: Each image has two rows and three columns; 1 means dark. → Badge A: Top 101, bottom 010: three dark pixels. → Badge B: Top 111, bottom 000: also three dark pixels. → Compare arrangements: The totals agree, but middle-top and middle-bottom positions differ.

graphics.title: Pixel positions: two badges, same dark count
graphics.alt: Pixel positions: two badges, same dark count. A top: Left = 1, Middle = 0, Right = 1. A bottom: Left = 0, Middle = 1, Right = 0. B top: Left = 1, Middle = 1, Right = 1. B bottom: Left = 0, Middle = 0, Right = 0.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: The totals agree, but middle-top and middle-bottom positions differ. Changed condition: Change A’s bottom-left pixel from 0 to 1. Expected result: A now has four dark pixels; its row encoding is 101 / 110. Reason: Exactly one light pixel becomes dark; the other five positions remain unchanged.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A grid preserves where each brightness belongs. Adding the six values preserves only the dark count, which is 3 in both images. The total therefore cannot distinguish these badges. Dimensions and reading order belong to the representation, not to an optional caption. Limit: This toy binary encoding does not include real photographs’ colour channels, compression or illumination effects.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: If the sorter uses images, retain dimensions and arrangement rather than assuming a dark-pixel count describes shape. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Find a position where the original badges differ, then read the changed A back as a picture.

graphics.title: Sound Becomes a Signal: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional microphone display records five samples during a short classroom tap. Supplied facts: Times are 0,1,2,3,4 ms in order. Signal A: 0,3,0,1,0. Signal B: 0,1,0,3,0. Toy values are signed measurement units; these happen to be nonnegative.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Timed sampling: Associate every measurement with its sampling time. → Signal A: Its largest sample 3 occurs at 1 ms. → Signal B: Its largest sample 3 occurs at 3 ms. → Maximum summary: Both maxima are 3, but the strongest recorded tap arrives at different times.

graphics.title: Same peak, different sample timing
graphics.alt: Same peak, different sample timing. Signal A: 0 ms = 0, 1 ms = 3, 2 ms = 0, 3 ms = 1, 4 ms = 0. Signal B: 0 ms = 0, 1 ms = 1, 2 ms = 0, 3 ms = 3, 4 ms = 0.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Both maxima are 3, but the strongest recorded tap arrives at different times. Changed condition: Retain only samples at 0,2,4 ms. Expected result: Both retained sequences are 0,0,0. Reason: The selected times omit both nonzero samples from each signal.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The sequences contain the same values in different orders. Keeping the maximum preserves peak recorded value while losing its timing. A graph should keep time on the horizontal axis; shuffling samples changes the recorded signal even if its maximum stays fixed. Limit: These sparse toy values cannot establish perceived loudness, pitch or what happened between sampling times.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Record the sorter’s sampling interval and retain relevant sequences when a decision depends on changes over time. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Does the all-zero retained record prove the full signal was silent? Use the picture.

graphics.title: Categories and Labels: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional craft club labels cardboard-order cards ready, review or revise. Supplied facts: Allowed quantity: whole number 1–4. Required colour: red or blue. If any known field fails, revise; otherwise if a required field is blank, review; otherwise ready. Cards A=(4,red), B=(5,blank), C=(2,blank).

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Read policy: Check known invalid fields before checking missing ones. → Card A: 4 is allowed and red is allowed: ready. → Card B: 5 is outside 1–4: revise, even though colour is missing. → Card C: 2 is valid but colour is blank: review.

graphics.title: Three ordered checks for a calendar card
graphics.alt: Three ordered checks for a calendar card. First check known values | Any known field fails its criterion | Revise even if another field is unknown. Then check missing information | No known failure but a field is blank or unreadable | Review because evidence is incomplete. Otherwise all checks have passed | Day is 1 through 30 and room is A or B | Ready under this record policy
source: sections.diagram:Three ordered checks for a calendar card

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: 2 is valid but colour is blank: review. Changed condition: Change B’s quantity from 5 to 4; leave colour blank. Expected result: B becomes review. Reason: The known failure is removed, but a required field is still missing.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Operational labels specify what a word means for this task. Two labellers using the same priority should agree on these cards. Review describes missing evidence, not a hidden assumption that the card is wrong. Revise is supported by a known failure. Limit: Agreement between labellers does not prove this policy is suitable for every school or that labels are objective truths.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Write a sorter label guide with examples of complete, invalid and unresolved inputs before comparing labels. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Explain why B originally was revise rather than review, then label its changed version.

graphics.title: Features: Useful Clues: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional shelf accepts a craft box only if width is at most 6 cm and height at most 4 cm. Supplied facts: Boxes P=(6,4,stripes), Q=(7,4,stripes), R=(6,5,dots), S=(6,4,dots). A green acceptance sticker is attached only after the shelf check.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Width check: P,Q,R,S have widths 6,7,6,6. → Height check: Their heights are 4,4,5,4. → Apply both limits: P and S fit; Q fails width; R fails height. → Reject a shortcut: The later sticker cannot be an input available before checking.

graphics.title: Dimensions determine shelf acceptance
graphics.alt: Dimensions determine shelf acceptance. P stripes: Width cm = 6, Height cm = 4, Outcome = fits. Q stripes: Width cm = 7, Height cm = 4, Outcome = width fails. R dots: Width cm = 6, Height cm = 5, Outcome = height fails. S dots: Width cm = 6, Height cm = 4, Outcome = fits.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: The later sticker cannot be an input available before checking. Changed condition: Change Q’s width to 6 without changing its height. Expected result: Q fits the shelf. Reason: Both dimensions now meet their including equality limits; stripe pattern does not change the rule.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Comparing P with Q isolates width; comparing P with R isolates height. Comparing P with S changes pattern while both remain accepted. Under this declared policy, pattern is not a deciding feature. A later acceptance sticker leaks the very answer the system should produce. Limit: These comparisons establish the written shelf rule, not the importance of pattern for unrelated tasks.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Choose sorter features that exist at decision time and actually connect to the stated classroom requirement. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Point to the pair that tests pattern, then explain why the sticker is a bad early input.

graphics.title: Algorithms as Recipes: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional paper badge machine transforms an initial score using an ordered recipe. Supplied facts: Start score=3. Recipe A: double, add 4, subtract 1, report. Recipe B swaps the first two operations but keeps the same starting score.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Start: Both runs begin at 3. → Recipe A: 3 → 6 after doubling → 10 after adding 4 → 9 after subtracting 1. → Recipe B: 3 → 7 after adding 4 → 14 after doubling → 13 after subtracting 1. → Compare outputs: Same operations, different order: outputs 9 and 13.

graphics.title: Changing instruction order
graphics.alt: Changing instruction order. Recipe A: Start = 3, After step 1 = 6, After step 2 = 10, Report = 9. Recipe B: Start = 3, After step 1 = 7, After step 2 = 14, Report = 13.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Same operations, different order: outputs 9 and 13. Changed condition: Change the starting score to 0 for both recipes. Expected result: A reports 3 and B reports 7. Reason: A: 0→0→4→3. B: 0→4→8→7.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Every instruction reads the current score, not the original one unless explicitly told to. In B, doubling also doubles the added 4. In A, the extra 4 is added after doubling. The final difference of 4 follows from that order, not from different starting data. Limit: One traced input checks one run; it does not establish every recipe is equivalent or validate an entire program.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Write the sorter’s steps in order, showing which values each step updates so a partner can reproduce the result. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Use the arrows to explain where the two zero-start runs first differ.

graphics.title: If/Then Decisions: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional counter begins with a number, adds 2, then chooses one branch. Supplied facts: If the updated value is at least 6, subtract 1; otherwise double it. Report once and stop. Use separate starting values 3,4,5.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Update first: Starts 3,4,5 become 5,6,7. → Test current value: 5≥6 is false; 6≥6 and 7≥6 are true. → Choose one branch: Double 5 to 10; subtract 1 from 6 to 5; subtract 1 from 7 to 6. → Report: The three independent runs report 10,5,6.

graphics.title: Inclusive branching trace
graphics.alt: Inclusive branching trace. Run 1: Start = 3, After +2 = 5, At least 6? = false, Report = 10. Run 2: Start = 4, After +2 = 6, At least 6? = true, Report = 5. Run 3: Start = 5, After +2 = 7, At least 6? = true, Report = 6.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: The three independent runs report 10,5,6. Changed condition: Replace at least 6 with above 6. Expected result: Only the run starting at 4 changes: it reports 12. Reason: Updated value 6 fails a strict above comparison and is doubled.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The condition is evaluated after adding 2. Equality belongs to the at-least branch, so starting at 4 checks the boundary. Once a branch finishes, the program reports; it does not reconsider the condition just because doubling 5 produced 10. Limit: A large reported value need not mean the true branch ran; branch choice depends on the earlier value.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Include equality examples when reviewing sorter conditions, and trace from original input through output. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which input detects the difference between the two written conditions? Explain its entire run.

graphics.title: Repeating Efficiently: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional paper counter advances through a display until its condition becomes false. Supplied facts: Start at 2. While the current counter is below 10, add 3. Test before each addition; report when the condition is false.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: First test: 2<10 is true: update to 5. → Repeat: 5<10: update to 8. 8<10: update to 11. → Stop test: 11<10 is false; do not add again. → Report: Final counter 11 after three additions.

graphics.title: Condition checks before additions
graphics.alt: Condition checks before additions. Check 1: Current = 2, Below 10? = true, Next = 5. Check 2: Current = 5, Below 10? = true, Next = 8. Check 3: Current = 8, Below 10? = true, Next = 11. Check 4: Current = 11, Below 10? = false, Next = stop.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Final counter 11 after three additions. Changed condition: Start at 10 instead of 2. Expected result: The loop runs zero times and reports 10. Reason: Its first condition is already false, so no addition happens.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The condition checks whether to do the next update; it does not constrain every resulting value to stay below 10. The final 11 is therefore allowed by this procedure. Record both the condition and counter to distinguish a correct stop from an assumed endpoint. Limit: This loop stops because positive increments eventually cross the limit. Other updates can fail to make progress.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Give any repeated sorter step an explicit stopping condition and trace a zero-iteration example. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Trace a fresh start of 9. How many additions occur, and must the report equal 10?

graphics.title: Debug the Cause: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional paper calculator should double the current value, but a copied instruction behaves strangely. Supplied facts: After input 6, the faulty step reports 12. Hypothesis A: add 6. Hypothesis B: double. Both hypotheses fit this first observation. A new input may be chosen.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Observe: Input 6 produced 12; that fact fits two explanations. → Predict alternatives: For input 2, adding 6 predicts 8; doubling predicts 4. → Run revealing test: The fictional new record is input 2 → output 8. → Locate cause: This record supports add-6 over doubling for this comparison.

graphics.title: A revealing test separates explanations
graphics.alt: A revealing test separates explanations. Original input: Input = 6, Add 6 predicts = 12, Double predicts = 12. Recorded new input: Input = 2, Add 6 predicts = 8, Double predicts = 4. Proposed input: Input = 0, Add 6 predicts = 6, Double predicts = 0.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: This record supports add-6 over doubling for this comparison. Changed condition: Use input 6 again instead of 2. Expected result: Both hypotheses predict 12; the test remains inconclusive. Reason: A revealing test requires different predicted outputs, not merely another recorded run.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Repeating input 6 would not separate the two hypotheses because both again predict 12. Input 2 makes their predictions different before the test is run. The second record supports investigating an added constant, but inspecting the instruction is still needed to confirm the implementation. Limit: Two toy hypotheses do not exhaust every possible bug; a matching output alone cannot identify arbitrary hidden code.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: When the sorter fails, write competing explanations and predicted traces before changing code or instructions. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Propose input 0 and give both predicted outputs without inventing an observed result.

graphics.title: Learning from Examples: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional classifier learns whether measured sticks are short or long. Supplied facts: Training lengths 2,4,8,10 cm have labels short,short,long,long. Candidate boundaries: long at least 5 or at least 7. Lowest errors wins; tie chooses smaller boundary.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Training rows: 2 and 4 are short; 8 and 10 are long. → Candidate checks: Boundaries 5 and 7 both predict S,S,L,L: zero errors each. → Tie policy: Choose boundary 5 because the declared tie rule prefers the smaller value. → New prediction: Length 6 is predicted long by the selected rule.

graphics.title: Same training errors, different new prediction
graphics.alt: Same training errors, different new prediction. Candidate 5: Boundary = 5, Training errors = 0, Prediction at 6 = long. Candidate 7: Boundary = 7, Training errors = 0, Prediction at 6 = short.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Length 6 is predicted long by the selected rule. Changed condition: Reverse the tie policy to prefer the larger boundary. Expected result: Boundary 7 is selected and predicts short at 6. Reason: The training fit is unchanged; only the explicit choice between tied candidates changes.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: There is no training stick between 4 and 8 to distinguish these candidates. The tie policy chooses one consistently; it is not additional evidence that its prediction at 6 is true. Label-free prediction applies the selected boundary, while evaluation would require an appropriate new reference label. Limit: Zero training errors for both rules cannot determine the correct label of every unobserved stick.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Save candidate definitions, training errors and tie policy with any sorter model version. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which new measured length would reveal disagreement between the candidates?

graphics.title: Build a Human Classifier: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional ribbon sorter uses a fixed instruction card called RibbonR. Supplied facts: Valid input: whole-number length from 0 to 15 with unit cm. Predict long at least 9 cm; otherwise short. Missing, wrong-unit or out-of-range values request clarification.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Input contract: Check that length is present, whole, within 0–15, and in cm. → Valid cases: 8 cm → short; 9 cm → long. → Invalid cases: 16 cm and blank length → clarification, not a forced label. → Keep records: Store input, contract result, rule version and prediction.

graphics.title: Three records through the Tower1 classifier
graphics.alt: Three records through the Tower1 classifier. 5 cm | Accepted; 5 is below 6 | Tower1 predicts short. 6 cm | Accepted; 6 is at least 6 | Tower1 predicts tall. Height blank | Missing height; stop before rule | Tower1; no prediction
source: sections.diagram:Three records through the Tower1 classifier

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Store input, contract result, rule version and prediction. Changed condition: Provide length 9 with unit mm. Expected result: Request clarification rather than predicting long. Reason: RibbonR requires cm; the unit mismatch fails its declared input contract.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A prediction boundary answers a different question from input validation. Length 9 passes the contract and meets the long boundary. Length 16 must not receive long merely because it exceeds 9: it violates the allowed range first. Zero is permitted and receives short. Limit: Contract validity does not prove the predicted category agrees with a checked reference label.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Create a sorter instruction card covering valid values, equality, missing fields and who can resolve clarification requests. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Trace 0 cm and explain why clarification is different from predicting short.

graphics.title: Save New Examples for Testing: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional envelope exercise evaluates a fixed pencil-length sorter. Supplied facts: Freeze PencilP: long at least 6 cm; short below 6. Reserved valid lengths are 3,5,6,9 cm. Teacher envelope labels, revealed only after predictions, are short,long,long,long.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Freeze: Write PencilP and its boundary before opening the label envelope. → Predict: For 3,5,6,9 cm predict short,short,long,long. → Reveal references: Envelope labels are short,long,long,long. → Compare: Three of four agree; the disagreement is at 5 cm.

graphics.title: Frozen predictions versus reserved labels
graphics.alt: Frozen predictions versus reserved labels. Test 1: Length cm = 3, PencilP = short, Reference = short, Result = agree. Test 2: Length cm = 5, PencilP = short, Reference = long, Result = disagree. Test 3: Length cm = 6, PencilP = long, Reference = long, Result = agree. Test 4: Length cm = 9, PencilP = long, Reference = long, Result = agree.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Three of four agree; the disagreement is at 5 cm. Changed condition: After feedback, change the boundary to 5. Expected result: The revised rule matches all four known labels but needs a different final test. Reason: These labels influenced the revision, so replaying them is evidence of repair rather than unseen performance.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The prediction record must exist before the labels are seen. PencilP scores 3/4=75% agreement on these four selected cases. Moving the boundary after inspecting the envelope makes this a development exercise; the same four cases can no longer serve as untouched final evaluation. Limit: Four selected cases cannot establish a reliable accuracy rate for every future pencil or classroom.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Maintain dated sorter versions and separate development examples from reserved project-evaluation cases. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Does 4/4 on the replay replace the original 3/4 result? Explain.

graphics.title: Boundaries and 'Not Sure': the case
graphics.alt: A fictional cubby selector accepts a block if width is at most 5 cm. Supplied facts: An unclear measurement means Block A is either 4 or 5 cm; Block B is either 5 or 6 cm. These complete possibility sets contain all widths under consideration. Other dimensions are known to fit.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Block A possibilities: 4 and 5 both satisfy the including equality width limit. → Block B possibilities: 5 fits; 6 does not. → Compare decisions: A has one supported decision; B’s possible decisions disagree. → Review B: Ask a named reviewer to remeasure B using the specified width unit.

graphics.title: Possibilities and decisions
graphics.alt: Possibilities and decisions. Block A: Width 1 cm = 4, Decision 1 = fits, Width 2 cm = 5, Decision 2 = fits. Block B: Width 1 cm = 5, Decision 1 = fits, Width 2 cm = 6, Decision 2 = fails.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Ask a named reviewer to remeasure B using the specified width unit. Changed condition: Narrow B’s possibilities to 6 or 7 cm. Expected result: Both fail the width limit; rejection no longer depends on resolving their difference. Reason: All remaining possibilities lead to the same decision.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Uncertainty about a number need not always create uncertainty about the decision. Every allowed width for A fits, so its width uncertainty does not affect acceptance. B straddles the boundary. Record both possibilities and request a better measurement instead of selecting the one that makes a preferred outcome. Limit: A review path is not automatically accurate; its conclusion depends on relevant, better evidence.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Add explicit review paths to the sorter, including unresolved input, responsible person and evidence needed. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which original block needs a better width before accepting or rejecting it? What should the reviewer do?

graphics.title: Prediction Is Not Fact: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional drying trial uses a fixed rule and later measures what actually happened. Supplied facts: Model D predicts slow when moisture score is at least 5; quick otherwise. Observation policy: slow if drying takes above 8 minutes; quick otherwise. Trial T has score 4 and measured time 9 minutes.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Prediction input: T has moisture score 4. → Predict: 4 is below 5, so D predicts quick. → Observe later: Measured time is 9 minutes; above 8 means observed slow. → Compare evidence: Prediction quick disagrees with observation slow.

graphics.title: Two records meet at a comparison
graphics.alt: Two records meet at a comparison. A: height 4 cm | Distance 3 units | Near matches near. B: height 6 cm | Distance 3 units | Far differs from near. C: height 8 cm | Distance 5 units | Far matches far
source: sections.diagram:Two records meet at a comparison

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Prediction quick disagrees with observation slow. Changed condition: Keep score 4 but measure exactly 8 minutes. Expected result: The observed label becomes quick and agrees with the prediction. Reason: Above 8 is strict: equality is quick under this policy.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The moisture score generates a prediction; it is not the observed drying time. The later measurement supplies separate evidence under the stated observation policy. Save both values and their units. Altering the recorded time to match D would destroy the evaluation rather than repair the model. Limit: One failure does not prove every prediction is wrong; one agreement does not establish reliability on future trials.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: In sorter trials, record predicted categories before collecting reference evidence, then retain disagreements for investigation. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which field changes the observation label, and which field changes the model prediction?

graphics.title: Confidence Is Not Correctness: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional card classifier reports a claimed 80% chance that each chosen label is correct. Supplied facts: Ten predictions all have score 80%. Later checks find 7 correct, 2 incorrect and 1 outcome unavailable. The selected cards were not a representative survey.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Keep scores: Ten chosen labels each carry 80%; this is a claim about uncertainty. → Checked outcomes: Seven correct plus two wrong gives nine known outcomes. → Report coverage: Observed agreement is 7/9 among checked cards; outcome coverage is 9/10. → Retain unknown: The missing result could change the all-ten correct count to 7 or 8.

graphics.title: Known outcomes and missing evidence
graphics.alt: Known outcomes and missing evidence. Units: predictions. Correct: 7. Incorrect: 2. Unknown: 1.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: The missing result could change the all-ten correct count to 7 or 8. Changed condition: The missing outcome is checked and found incorrect. Expected result: All-ten agreement is 7/10=70%. Reason: There are now three wrong labels and no unknown outcomes.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Do not count the missing outcome as correct or silently remove it from the coverage report. These records allow an all-ten agreement range from 70% to 80%. They do not show that claimed probabilities match checked correctness over many comparable predictions; that requires much more suitable evidence. Limit: This small selected set cannot establish that the claimed probabilities match actual correctness or show performance for all future cards.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Keep sorter scores, reference outcomes and missingness separately; use review policies instead of treating high scores as facts. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Was the unknown label guaranteed correct because its confidence was 80%?

graphics.title: Similarity: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional craft-card matcher compares each candidate with a target. Supplied facts: Target: red, round, smooth. A: red,square,smooth. B: blue,round,smooth. C: red,round,rough. Initially each exact feature match scores 1; return all highest scorers. For the second comparison only, colour and shape matches score 1 each and a texture match scores 3.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Target features: Compare colour, shape and texture separately. → Equal weights: A matches colour+texture=2; B shape+texture=2; C colour+shape=2. → Initial result: All three tie at 2. → Texture weight 3: New scores A=4, B=4, C=2; A and B remain tied.

graphics.title: Declared weights change similarity
graphics.alt: Declared weights change similarity. A: All weights 1 = 2, Texture weight 3 = 4. B: All weights 1 = 2, Texture weight 3 = 4. C: All weights 1 = 2, Texture weight 3 = 2.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: New scores A=4, B=4, C=2; A and B remain tied. Changed condition: Keep original weights but change the target texture to rough. Expected result: C scores 3; A and B each score 1. Reason: C now matches all three target features; the others lose their smooth-texture match.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Similarity is defined by the chosen representation and weights. The cards did not change when texture gained weight; the comparison rule did. Two high scores need not mean two identical cards. A complete rule also says what to do with tied scores, rather than choosing whichever appears first by accident. Limit: A high feature-match score does not establish usefulness or suitability beyond the features represented.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Declare sorter similarity features, weights and tie behavior before using scores to explain recommendations. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Point to the matches supporting C’s new score and explain why there is no tie.

graphics.title: Recommendations: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional classroom break chooser recommends a suitable paper activity. Supplied facts: Must be quiet and take at most 12 minutes. Score 2 for puzzles and 1 for solo. A puzzle,solo,noisy,8 min; B puzzle,group,quiet,12 min; C drawing,solo,quiet,10 min.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Requirements: Reject A because it is noisy despite a preference score of 3. → Eligible candidates: B and C both satisfy time and quiet requirements. → Preference scores: B scores 2; C scores 1. → Recommend: Choose B; preserve the reasons and any later feedback.

graphics.title: Requirements before preferences
graphics.alt: Requirements before preferences. A: Quiet = No, Minutes = 8, Score = 3, Status = excluded. B: Quiet = Yes, Minutes = 12, Score = 2, Status = eligible. C: Quiet = Yes, Minutes = 10, Score = 1, Status = eligible.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Choose B; preserve the reasons and any later feedback. Changed condition: Change the maximum time to 10 minutes. Expected result: Only C remains eligible and is recommended. Reason: B takes 12 minutes; A is still noisy.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A hard requirement determines whether an option can be chosen at all. Preferences rank the eligible options. The apparent best preference match, A, is not suitable under the quiet requirement. If a learner clicks C instead, the event alone does not tell us whether they disliked B, misclicked or wanted variety. Limit: One click is an observed event, not proof of satisfaction or a stable personal preference.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Separate sorter requirements, preferences and observed feedback; document why a suggestion was eligible. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why does the recommendation change without changing anyone’s preferences?

graphics.title: Good Data, Bad Data: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional toy-car distance table needs cleaning before use. Supplied facts: Contract: unique run ID; whole distance 0–30 cm. Raw rows: A=0 cm, B=200 mm, C=blank, another A=0 cm. Source log confirms one A run and B’s original measurement of 200 mm; C has no measurement.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Validate rows: A’s zero is valid; B has wrong unit; C is missing; A is duplicated. → Evidence repair: 200 mm ÷10 =20 cm; source log supports retaining one A. → Keep unknown: C stays unresolved; do not replace it with 0. → Clean record: Usable unique rows: A=0 cm, B=20 cm; retain a separate change log.

graphics.title: Preserve the original and explain each decision
graphics.alt: Preserve the original and explain each decision. T2 height 60 cm | Card C2 says 6 cm | Correct to 6; log C2. T3 travel blank | Card C3 also blank | Keep missing; flag. T4 travel 0 cm | Card C4 confirms zero | Keep measured zero
source: sections.diagram:Preserve the original and explain each decision

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Usable unique rows: A=0 cm, B=20 cm; retain a separate change log. Changed condition: The source log gives B only as bare 200 with no unit. Expected result: B remains unresolved rather than becoming 20 cm. Reason: Without a confirmed unit, division by 10 would be an unsupported assumption.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Cleaning is not permission to make inconvenient values plausible. The source log supports a unit conversion and removal of a duplicate copy. Zero means a measured zero distance; blank means no supplied measurement. Keep the raw table and explain every change so someone can reconstruct what happened. Limit: A clean table can still contain measurement or labelling errors that these checks do not detect.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Keep raw sorter inputs, validated records and an evidence-linked repair log as different artifacts. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which repairs are evidence-backed in the original case, and which row must remain unknown?

graphics.title: Missing and Unbalanced Examples: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional badge reader will be used in both bright and dim rooms. Supplied facts: Intended target has 8 bright plain,8 bright patterned,8 dim plain,8 dim patterned cards. A development sample contains 6 bright plain cards and 2 bright patterned cards; no dim cards.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Target conditions: Four lighting-by-pattern groups, eight target cards each. → Current sample: Eight bright cards only; dim groups have zero coverage. → Coverage gap: Current results cannot describe dim-room reading. → Targeted follow-up: Select and record new cases from both dim groups before claiming coverage.

graphics.title: Target groups and development coverage
graphics.alt: Target groups and development coverage. Bright plain: Target cards = 8, Sample cards = 6. Bright patterned: Target cards = 8, Sample cards = 2. Dim plain: Target cards = 8, Sample cards = 0. Dim patterned: Target cards = 8, Sample cards = 0.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Select and record new cases from both dim groups before claiming coverage. Changed condition: Add eight more bright plain cards and no dim cards. Expected result: The sample becomes larger but still has no dim coverage. Reason: The missing lighting condition remains untested.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Adding more bright cards can increase sample size without addressing the missing condition. A coverage check asks which relevant situations are absent, not merely how many rows exist. Deliberately selecting dim cases helps investigate those conditions, but the resulting test should not be advertised as a random survey unless its selection really was random. Limit: Coverage does not guarantee accuracy, and targeted cases alone do not supply a population-wide success estimate.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Create a sorter coverage table crossing important classroom conditions, then state which groups each test actually represents. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Would testing only dim plain cards close every current gap? Point to the target groups.

graphics.title: Fair for Whom?: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional badge reader is evaluated on bright and dim cards with known reference labels. Supplied facts: Version M is correct on 9 of 10 bright cards and 3 of 6 dim cards. Version N uses the same cards: 8 of 10 bright and 5 of 6 dim correct.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Bright group: M:9/10=90%; N:8/10=80%. → Dim group: M:3/6=50%; N:5/6≈83.3%. → Combined counts: M:(9+3)/16=75%; N:(8+5)/16=81.25%. → Discuss trade-off: N improves total and dim results but loses one bright success.

graphics.title: Group rates compared on the same cards
graphics.alt: Group rates compared on the same cards. Units: percent correct. M bright: 90. M dim: 50. N bright: 80. N dim: 83.33333333333333.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: N improves total and dim results but loses one bright success. Changed condition: Give bright and dim groups equal weight as an explicitly different metric. Expected result: M scores 70%; N scores about 81.7%. Reason: This averages group rates and is not the original 16-card agreement rate.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Adding correct counts and denominators weights each tested card once. Averaging 90% and 50% would incorrectly give unequal groups equal size in the all-card rate. The group breakdown reveals a trade-off hidden by the total. Decide what matters with the relevant users rather than announcing that one number proves fairness. Limit: Six dim cards supply limited evidence; these descriptive rates do not prove a system is fair for all users.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Report sorter outcomes by relevant conditions and record whose failures matter when choosing a revision. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which group loses performance under N, and can total improvement erase that fact?

graphics.title: Privacy by Choosing Less: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional teacher wants to count broken craft tools by type, without contacting borrowers. Supplied facts: Needed output: totals for scissors, ruler and hole-punch repairs. Draft form requests pupil name, birthday, tool type and repair-needed Yes/No. No borrower follow-up is required.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: State purpose: Count repairs by tool type, not by person. → Choose fields: Retain tool type and repair-needed status. → Remove excess: Name and birthday are unnecessary for this stated task. → Report totals: Aggregate each tool type’s Yes count; record the authorised retention plan.

graphics.title: A small information plan for a fictional vote
graphics.alt: A small information plan for a fictional vote. Collect | One topic per slip | No name or address. Count | Teacher totals choices | Keep slips restricted. Share | Three topic totals | No individual choices. Delete | After totals checked | Follow agreed plan
source: sections.diagram:A small information plan for a fictional vote

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Aggregate each tool type’s Yes count; record the authorised retention plan. Changed condition: The teacher adds an authorised task to return one repaired tool to its borrower. Expected result: A minimal contact mechanism may now be needed for that tool. Reason: The purpose changed; reassess necessity rather than restoring every old field.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A field is justified by what the task needs to do, not by whether it might become useful someday. Names and birthdays do not help these repair totals. Replacing names with codes still leaves linked personal records if someone keeps a name-code key; collecting less can remove the need for that link entirely. Limit: Removing these fields is not a universal guarantee of anonymity or permission to collect other identifying combinations.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Write the sorter’s purpose, necessary fields, access rules and deletion point before collecting any real classroom information. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: For the original task, does adding an anonymous-looking pupil code improve the repair count?

graphics.title: Generate, Retrieve, or Calculate?: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional craft invitation combines three different operations. Supplied facts: Approved record C: Tuesday, Hall 4, three tables with four learner places each. Two places are reserved for helpers; no snack information is supplied.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Retrieve facts: Read Tuesday, Hall 4 and 3×4 places from approved C. → Calculate: 12 total places minus 2 reserved =10 learner places. → Generate wording: Draft a friendly invitation using only those supported details. → Check claims: A sentence promising snacks has no supporting record.

graphics.title: One club task with three kinds of work
graphics.alt: One club task with three kinds of work. Retrieve N2 | Room 4 on Wednesday | Right event and version. Calculate | 6 × 4 − 3 = 21 | Inputs and operations. Generate wording | Try a making activity | Facts and constraints
source: sections.diagram:One club task with three kinds of work

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: A sentence promising snacks has no supporting record. Changed condition: Reserve four places instead of two, keeping the room and day unchanged. Expected result: Eight learner places remain. Reason: 3×4−4=8; this changes capacity for learners, not the retrieved date or location.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Retrieval copies relevant source information; calculation follows arithmetic; generation proposes wording. These jobs can cooperate, but one does not validate the others. A friendly generated sentence can still contain an invented detail. Keep the approved source beside the draft and check each factual claim separately. Limit: The fictional source must itself be current and authoritative; retrieval alone does not ensure a record is correct.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Use the sorter’s approved catalogue for facts, explicit calculations for scores and checked prose for explanations. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Label each arrow with its operation. Can the system add snacks because invitations often mention them?

graphics.title: Prompts Are Design Instructions: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional club needs a short exhibit card, without guesses. Supplied facts: Source A: exhibit Paper Birds, location Shelf 2. No duration appears. Required output: two labelled lines, Exhibit and Duration; missing values must say not supplied.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: State task: Produce exactly two labelled lines using source A only. → Find evidence: A supplies Paper Birds but no duration. → Follow missing rule: Exhibit: Paper Birds. Duration: not supplied. → Check contract: Check labels, two-line format and each factual claim.

graphics.title: From prompt requirement to evidence of success
graphics.alt: From prompt requirement to evidence of success. Use source C only | Monday and Room 7 | Compare with C. Mark missing values | Time: not stated | Check absent time. Four labelled lines | Day Time Place Bring | Count and inspect. No added details | No invented promises | Check every claim
source: sections.diagram:From prompt requirement to evidence of success

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Check labels, two-line format and each factual claim. Changed condition: Add source B naming the same exhibit duration 20 minutes, with B declared current and authoritative. Expected result: Duration becomes 20 minutes. Reason: There is now an authorised source for the previously missing field.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A useful prompt describes both the wanted answer and what to do when evidence is insufficient. Asking for a duration does not create one. Examples can demonstrate the format, but they must not become sources of event facts. Check content support separately from whether the answer looks tidy. Limit: Even a complete prompt does not guarantee an AI system follows it; test returned outputs against the contract.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Specify sorter input, output fields, evidence limits and missing/conflict behavior before improving its wording. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: What must happen if B instead conflicts with another equally authoritative duration record?

graphics.title: Verify Important Outputs: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional craft sheet calculates ribbon left after making bookmarks. Supplied facts: Four rolls each contain exactly 150 cm. Eight bookmarks use exactly 50 cm each. No other ribbon loss is assumed; no competition result is recorded.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Available ribbon: 4×150=600 cm. → Ribbon used: 8×50=400 cm. → Remainder: 600−400=200 cm=2 m. → Audit draft: “200 m remains and everyone wins” fails unit and evidence checks.

graphics.title: Ribbon quantities in one consistent unit
graphics.alt: Ribbon quantities in one consistent unit. Units: centimetres. Available: 600. Used: 400. Remaining: 200.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: “200 m remains and everyone wins” fails unit and evidence checks. Changed condition: Make ten bookmarks instead of eight. Expected result: 100 cm, or 1 m, remains. Reason: 600−10×50=100 cm.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: All arithmetic first uses centimetres. Converting only after subtraction avoids mixing units. The record supports available, used and remaining lengths under its no-loss assumption. It does not support a promise about winning. A numerically correct total elsewhere in a draft cannot rescue a wrong unit or an invented claim. Limit: Real cutting losses or inaccurate roll lengths would change this toy calculation; the assumption must be declared.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Check sorter calculations with explicit units and verify explanation claims against their actual catalogue evidence. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Correct the draft and identify which part needs another source rather than a calculation.

graphics.title: Humans Set Boundaries: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional teacher approves one checked classroom poster for internal display. Supplied facts: Approval: publish exactly poster P2 on the classroom noticeboard today, once. Assistant proposes P2 there; P3 there after an edit; P2 on a public website.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Read authority: The teacher approved P2, one internal noticeboard and one publication. → Allowed action: Publishing unchanged P2 there today matches the approval. → Changed version: P3 requires new review; P2 approval does not automatically cover edits. → Changed audience: Public-web publication exceeds the approved destination.

graphics.title: Match the proposed action to its permission
graphics.alt: Match the proposed action to its permission. Version A on class board | Today, once, by editor | Within scope. Version A on public site | Public posting excluded | Outside scope. Changed version B | Only A was approved | Review changed version. Post A a second time | Once has been used | Outside scope
source: sections.diagram:Match the proposed action to its permission

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Public-web publication exceeds the approved destination. Changed condition: P2 has already been published once under this approval. Expected result: A second publication is not covered. Reason: The instruction allowed a single use, not repeated actions.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A general intention to help the class does not grant every action that might help. Check the version, destination and time explicitly. An edit may improve accuracy while still changing the approved artifact. The assistant should hold the changed poster for review rather than treating its own confidence as permission. Limit: Permission does not prove content accuracy; factual checks and action authority are separate requirements.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Record sorter actions allowed automatically and actions requiring the classroom owner’s explicit review. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which original proposal is authorised? Why do the other two need separate approval?

graphics.title: Find a Real Problem: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional class loses time finding the correct craft tray. Supplied facts: In eight recorded requests, three selected trays lack a required tool; five match. The teacher permits a paper finder using fictional requests and an approved tray list, with no pupil names.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Observe problem: Three mismatches are recorded out of eight requests. → Define need: Help users choose a tray containing every requested tool. → Set success test: Compare selected tray against the approved inventory for each new case. → Bound the project: Use fictional tool requests; do not collect identity or purchase equipment.

graphics.title: From an observed difficulty to a testable goal
graphics.alt: From an observed difficulty to a testable goal. 4 of 10 choices mismatch | Some re-selection occurred | Cause is not established. Need a compatible choice | Check time and conditions | User can still decline. Paper suggestion process | Small permitted prototype | Benefit needs a comparison. Measure fit and coverage | Observe useful outcomes | Do not hide no-result cases
source: sections.diagram:From an observed difficulty to a testable goal

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Use fictional tool requests; do not collect identity or purchase equipment. Changed condition: The approved list contains no tray with every requested tool. Expected result: The finder should report no suitable tray rather than guess. Reason: Success includes honestly identifying unsatisfied requirements.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The mismatch record describes a concrete need. A measurable goal checks whether the chosen tray satisfies the request; calling the system smart would not tell us how to evaluate it. Start with a transparent paper baseline, and keep unsatisfied requests visible instead of selecting a near match without warning. Limit: Eight requests do not show the problem’s frequency across the entire school or prove AI is necessary.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Helpful Classroom Sorter, retain the problem record, permitted scope, baseline and observable acceptance criteria. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Write a one-sentence project goal and say what evidence would count as a failure.

graphics.title: Choose Inputs and Outputs: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional classroom chooses a storage bin for model parts. Supplied facts: Catalogue order: B1 capacity 5, B2 capacity 9. Valid request is a whole part count 1–12. Return first bin with capacity at least the count; none if neither fits; clarify invalid input.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Validate request: Count 6 is whole and within 1–12. → Check first bin: B1 capacity 5 is below 6; reject it. → Check second bin: B2 capacity 9 is at least 6; accept it. → Baseline output: Report B2 and stop; save the comparison evidence.

graphics.title: The manual checklist baseline
graphics.alt: The manual checklist baseline. Validate the request | Check minutes and Yes or No | Clarify invalid input. Inspect catalogue in order | Check time and quiet for each | Mark compatible rows. Choose or explain absence | First compatible row or none | Suggestion or no match. Keep the evidence | Record input, result, reason | Comparable baseline record

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Report B2 and stop; save the comparison evidence. Changed condition: Change request 6 to 5. Expected result: The baseline returns B1. Reason: Its capacity equals the request, and at least includes equality.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The baseline is an ordered catalogue scan, not a preference ranking. It makes expectations testable before a prototype is built. Count 10 is valid but has no matching bin; that differs from a blank count, which fails the input contract. Both situations need explicit output behavior. Limit: Bin capacity is the only supplied fitting criterion; weight or shape suitability cannot be inferred.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Document sorter schema, catalogue order, acceptance rule and all output types; use a manual trace as the comparison baseline. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Trace requests 10 and blank. Why should they not receive the same explanation?

graphics.title: Design the Decision Process: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional worksheet routes craft kits by required glue and number of scissors. Supplied facts: K1: glue No, scissors 2. K2: glue Yes, scissors 2. K3: glue Yes, scissors 4. Request: glue required Yes, scissors needed 2. Return first kit meeting both requirements.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Validate fields: Require Yes/No glue input and whole scissors count 0–4. → Evaluate K1: Scissors fit, but required glue is absent: continue. → Evaluate K2: Glue is present and 2 scissors meet the request: accept. → Stop: Return K2 without replacing it with later K3.

graphics.title: Four paths through the recommender
graphics.alt: Four paths through the recommender. Input missing or invalid | Ask for corrected input | Stop this run. Candidate fails a check | Move to the next row | Continue search. Candidate passes both | Suggest it with a reason | Stop this run. All rows checked and failed | Report no match | Stop this run

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Return K2 without replacing it with later K3. Changed condition: Increase scissors needed to 3. Expected result: K3 is selected. Reason: K1 lacks glue; K2 has only 2 scissors; K3 has glue and 4.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A complete decision process specifies what to do after each result. One passing requirement is insufficient. After a kit passes both, stopping preserves the first-match contract; automatically choosing the largest later kit would implement a different rule. A full scan with no accepted kit returns no match. Limit: A correct flow depends on accurate catalogue entries and the declared requirements; the picture does not verify inventory.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Draw the sorter’s decision branches, loop-back arrows, final outputs and invalid-input path so every valid case can terminate. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Where does the first original rejection occur, and why is K3 not originally selected?

graphics.title: Build a Paper Prototype: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional team turns a storage-bin specification into movable instruction cards. Supplied facts: Bins X capacity 3 then Y capacity 7; valid count 1–9. Select first capacity at least count. For request 4, write baseline Y before operating cards. Prototype cards mistakenly stop with X immediately.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Expected result: Baseline checks X then Y and expects Y for count 4. → Operate literally: Follow the current prototype cards without secretly repairing them. → Actual trace: Prototype stops at X; it never performs the capacity comparison. → Record mismatch: Expected Y, actual X: locate the missing check.

graphics.title: A paper run that can be checked
graphics.alt: A paper run that can be checked. Request and version labels | Validate the two fields | Record pass or clarification. Marker at current row | Check time AND quiet | Record checks and next step. First fit or end of list | Suggest or report no match | Record output and stop
source: sections.diagram:A paper run that can be checked

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Expected Y, actual X: locate the missing check. Changed condition: Insert “if capacity is below count, continue” before accepting a bin. Expected result: The revised trace rejects X and accepts Y for 4. Reason: 3<4 is true; 7<4 is false, so Y fits.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A paper prototype is executable when another person can follow its instructions without guessing your intention. Record the actual wrong result separately from the expected one. Discovering a missing comparison is useful evidence for repair; pretending the operator followed the intended rule would hide the defect. Limit: One repaired paper case does not establish usability, correctness on every input or performance of a later software implementation.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Save sorter instruction cards, dated versions and operator traces alongside the manual expected outputs. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: What should appear in the test log before and after the repair?

graphics.title: Test Normal Cases: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional pencil-pouch finder has been run on four ordinary requests. Supplied facts: Catalogue: P1 capacity 3, P2 capacity 7; first fitting pouch. Valid whole counts 1–9. Requests 2,4,6,8; recorded outputs P1,P2,P1,none. These are invented records, not class results.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Write expectations: For 2,4,6,8 expect P1,P2,P2,none. → Compare outputs: Runs at 2,4 and 8 agree; run at 6 disagrees. → Trace failure: P1 holds only 3, so it cannot satisfy request 6. → Report: Three of four routine cases pass; retain the failure.

graphics.title: Expected versus recorded routine outputs
graphics.alt: Expected versus recorded routine outputs. Test 1: Request = 2, Expected = P1, Recorded = P1, Result = pass. Test 2: Request = 4, Expected = P2, Recorded = P2, Result = pass. Test 3: Request = 6, Expected = P2, Recorded = P1, Result = fail. Test 4: Request = 8, Expected = none, Recorded = none, Result = pass.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Three of four routine cases pass; retain the failure. Changed condition: Prototype reports none for request 6 instead of P1. Expected result: That run still fails. Reason: P2 can hold 6, so none is also wrong under the first-fit rule.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: An ordinary case is not automatically correct. Define expected outputs from the contract before reading prototype outputs. Checking both selected ID and eligibility catches the wrong P1 suggestion. A no-match output can be a full pass when that is exactly what the valid request requires. Limit: Four routine tests do not cover equality, invalid inputs or every relevant classroom condition.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Maintain sorter tests with input, independently derived expectation, actual output, version and full-pass judgment. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why is none correct for 8 but incorrect for 6? Use both capacity cards.

graphics.title: Test Edge Cases and Fairness: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional craft-book chooser accepts requests for whole available minutes from 0 to 20. Supplied facts: Booklet A takes 6 minutes; B takes 12. Return first duration at most available time. Check 5,6,7; also 0,20,21 and blank. Same catalogue applies to every user.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Near a boundary: At 5: none. At 6 and 7: A. → Valid extremes: 0: none. 20: A, because first-fit order remains fixed. → Invalid inputs: 21 and blank require clarification, not ordinary search. → Coverage record: Record each user condition tested; do not invent unrun outcomes.

graphics.title: Three requests around ten minutes
graphics.alt: Three requests around ten minutes. 9 minutes | 10 is too long | No match in catalogue B. 10 minutes | 10 fits exactly | Suggest B1. 11 minutes | 10 fits with time left | Suggest B1

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Record each user condition tested; do not invent unrun outcomes. Changed condition: Faulty code uses duration strictly below available time. Expected result: Request 6 now wrongly returns none. Reason: A’s duration equals the available time and should be eligible under at most.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Adjacent values below, at and above 6 expose an accidental strict inequality. Zero is valid even though no activity fits. The top valid input does not require selecting the longest activity: catalogue order still controls selection. Coverage also asks whose conditions were tested, which cannot be inferred from these numbers alone. Limit: Equal written rules do not prove equally good outcomes for every group; actual condition-specific evidence is still needed.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Add sorter boundary cases, missing fields and relevant user conditions to the test plan before making fairness claims. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which single boundary run most directly detects the strict-comparison bug, and why?

graphics.title: Improve One Cause: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional quiet-activity chooser has a boundary bug and a proposed repair. Supplied facts: A: quiet Yes, 8 minutes; B: quiet No, 5 minutes. Request quiet required Yes. U0 accepts only duration<available time. U1 fixes ≤ but accidentally removes the quiet requirement.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Boundary failure: At 8 minutes, U0 rejects A and rejects noisy B: none. → Expected repair: Correct logic must allow A when time equals 8. → Regression case: At 6 quiet-required minutes, correct output is none. → Bad revision: U1 selects noisy B at 6; fixing equality introduced a new failure.

graphics.title: A repair with evidence
graphics.alt: A repair with evidence. Keep the failing trace | Save a new version | Rerun the revealing case. Name the broken requirement | Correct the faulty step | Rerun earlier passing cases. Keep input and catalogue labels | Record what changed | Keep every result and limit

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: U1 selects noisy B at 6; fixing equality introduced a new failure. Changed condition: Use U2, which changes < to ≤ and keeps the quiet check. Expected result: At 8 return A; at 6 return none. Reason: Equality is repaired while B remains ineligible because it is noisy.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A repair must preserve the full contract, not just make one failing example pass. The quiet condition and duration comparison are separate requirements. Changing only the inequality targets the recorded cause; removing the quiet check changes another behavior. Save previously passing cases to reveal such regressions. Limit: Two examples establish only these outcomes; further cases are needed before generalising the repair.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Maintain sorter regression tests and compare complete version traces, retaining new failures rather than hiding them. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Explain why “our repaired version now picks something” is not enough to show success at 6.

graphics.title: Expo and Defense: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional paper sorter team prepares an exhibition evidence board. Supplied facts: Both prototype and manual baseline attempt the same 10 reserved cases. Prototype passes 8; baseline passes 9. Two additional planned cases are unrun. No timing or pupil-satisfaction measures were collected.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Describe contract: Show the task, inputs, rule and reserved case selection. → Show results: Prototype 8/10=80%; baseline 9/10=90% on attempted cases. → Keep incomplete work: Two unrun cases remain visible, without pass/fail labels. → Defend conclusion: Prototype did not beat baseline on this measured outcome; explain its failures.

graphics.title: Shared reserved-case comparison
graphics.alt: Shared reserved-case comparison. Units: passes out of 10 attempted. Prototype: 8. Manual baseline: 9.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Prototype did not beat baseline on this measured outcome; explain its failures. Changed condition: Someone adds the two unrun cases to the denominator as failures. Expected result: That reports a different measure, 8/12 completed successes out of planned cases. Reason: It cannot be called the original attempted-case pass rate; distinguish completion from evaluated correctness.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: An exhibition should make the evidence inspectable. A polished demonstration is not a substitute for the reserved-case record. The shared cases allow a direct descriptive comparison of pass rates; missing timing data prevents a claim that the prototype is faster. Unrun cases must not be treated as successes. Limit: This fictional evaluation does not demonstrate classroom learning impact or performance on every future request.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Present the Helpful Classroom Sorter’s versions, test records, baseline, failures and next investigation as an evidence portfolio. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Write one defensible success statement and one claim the evidence cannot support.

graphics.title: Precision in Algorithms: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional book-box counter has three boxes with five books each and two loose books. Supplied facts: Python instructions: boxes=3; total=boxes*5; total=total+2; print(total). Run the instructions in this order with ordinary integer arithmetic.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Read input: boxes is assigned 3. → Multiply: total becomes 3×5=15. → Update total: total becomes its current value 15 plus 2: 17. → Print: The program prints 17 once.

graphics.title: A calculation from paper to output
graphics.alt: A calculation from paper to output. Record pack count | packs = 4 | Name holds 4. Multiply two quantities | total = packs * per_pack | Name holds product. Show the answer | print(total) | Displays the value
source: sections.diagram:A calculation from paper to output

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: The program prints 17 once. Changed condition: Set boxes=0, keeping the two loose books. Expected result: The printed result is 2. Reason: 0×5+2=2; there is no rule saying zero boxes means zero loose books.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Assignment replaces a variable’s stored value. In total=total+2, Python first reads the current total on the right, calculates 17, then assigns that result to total on the left. The equal sign is an instruction here, not a claim that 15 and 17 are mathematically equal. Predict output before running. Limit: These statements count supplied books; they do not validate input types or infer stock from measurements.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Use small predicted traces when translating the Transparent Book Recommender’s paper logic into code. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: If print(total) moves before total=total+2, what gets printed for the original input?

graphics.title: Decompose a Goal: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional library computes total spine labels needed for several equal shelves. Supplied facts: Define labels(shelves,per_shelf): return shelves*per_shelf. Call needed=labels(4,6), then print(needed). No other side effects are defined.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Call with arguments: The call supplies shelves=4 and per_shelf=6 locally. → Function body: Multiply 4×6 to calculate 24. → Return value: return sends 24 back to the caller; it does not print. → Caller prints: needed receives 24; print(needed) displays 24.

graphics.title: Arguments matched in order
graphics.alt: Arguments matched in order. show_remaining(12, 4) | capacity 12; used 4 | 8. show_remaining(10, 7) | capacity 10; used 7 | 3

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: needed receives 24; print(needed) displays 24. Changed condition: Call labels(4,0) instead. Expected result: The returned result is 0, and the caller prints 0. Reason: Four shelves times zero labels per shelf is zero.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A function separates one named job from the surrounding program. Arguments supply data for this call; return supplies its result. A print statement in the caller is a different action. Clear parameter names help detect swapping or misusing inputs without assuming every function prints automatically. Limit: This function assumes compatible numeric inputs; it does not reject negative shelves or verify real shelf contents.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Give the recommender separate validation, eligibility and scoring functions whose inputs and results can be tested independently. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: What happens visibly if the caller stores needed but omits print(needed)?
