graphics.title: Branching Logic: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional reading-time labeler uses one Python if/elif/else chain. Supplied facts: Whole minutes below 0: Invalid; 0: Empty; 1–10: Short; above 10: Long. Order checks as minutes<0, minutes==0, minutes<=10, otherwise. Print the assigned label once.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Negative check: −1 takes Invalid and skips later branches. → Zero check: 0 takes Empty, not Short. → Inclusive short range: 1 and 10 take Short. → Remaining inputs: 11 takes Long; only the selected branch assigns the label.

graphics.title: One chain chooses one label
graphics.alt: One chain chooses one label. -1 | Below zero is True | Invalid. 12 | Below zero False; <= 12 True | Short. 13 | Both checks False | Long

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: 11 takes Long; only the selected branch assigns the label. Changed condition: Move minutes<=10 to the first branch. Expected result: −1 and 0 wrongly receive Short. Reason: Both satisfy the earlier comparison before their intended checks are reached.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The third comparison alone would include negative values and zero, but earlier branches already handle them. An elif chain selects its first true branch. Multiple independent if statements would have different behavior and could overwrite an earlier label. Boundary traces show why order belongs to the specification. Limit: The example assumes whole numeric minutes; strings, missing values and fractional values need a separate declared input contract.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Validate recommender requests before ranking items, retaining explicit labels for missing or invalid cases. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Give expected labels for −1,0,10,11 and identify the equality boundary for Short.

graphics.title: Trace Tables: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional reading-token jar starts with one token and gains three per round. Supplied facts: Python: total=1; for turn in range(4): total=total+3; after the loop print(total). The update is inside the loop; print is outside.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Initial state: Before the loop, total=1. → Iteration values: range(4) supplies turn values 0,1,2,3. → Updated totals: After each turn total is 4,7,10,13. → After the loop: Print 13 once, after all four updates.

graphics.title: Loop totals after each iteration
graphics.alt: Loop totals after each iteration. First: turn = 0, total after update = 4. Second: turn = 1, total after update = 7. Third: turn = 2, total after update = 10. Fourth: turn = 3, total after update = 13.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Print 13 once, after all four updates. Changed condition: Use range(0) instead of range(4). Expected result: The loop body never runs and the printed total is 1. Reason: The iterable contains no turn values; the initial assignment still happened.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The turn value labels an iteration; it is not the number added. The fixed update adds three each time. Four iterations take the total from 1 to 13. Keeping print outside the loop produces one final display rather than four intermediate displays. Initialise total before the loop so a zero-iteration run still has a defined value. Limit: This finite loop does not establish behavior of a while-loop with a different update or stopping condition.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Trace recommender loops with current item, eligibility, score and current best so each update can be explained. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Move print inside the original loop. What sequence is displayed?

graphics.title: Loops and Stopping: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional counter starts at 12 and decreases while above a boundary. Supplied facts: Python: count=12; while count>3: count=count-4; print after the loop. The condition is checked before each subtraction.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Initial check: 12>3: true; subtract 4 to get 8. → Next check: 8>3: true; subtract 4 to get 4. → Final update: 4>3: true; subtract 4 to get 0. → Stop: 0>3 is false; report 0 after three updates.

graphics.title: State after each addition
graphics.alt: State after each addition. 1 | 0 | 1. 2 | 1 | 3. 3 | 3 | 6

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: 0>3 is false; report 0 after three updates. Changed condition: Replace count>3 with count!=3. Expected result: From 12, the loop never reaches 3 and does not terminate in this toy model. Reason: 12,8,4,0,−4,… are multiples of 4; none equals 3.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The condition does not promise the counter ends exactly at 3. Subtractions can cross the boundary. The count strictly decreases, so the below-or-equal stopping region is eventually reached from this start. A condition requiring exact equality can be unsafe when repeated updates skip that value. Limit: Do not run an intentionally unbounded loop in class; trace a finite prefix to inspect the defect safely.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Use progress and stopping arguments for any repeated recommender process; test inputs that require zero, one and several updates. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why is report 0 correct for the original loop, and why is equality-only stopping risky here?

graphics.title: Debugging Strategies: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional shelf function should count books in complete bundles plus loose books. Supplied facts: Correct definition: shelf(bundle_count,loose) returns bundle_count*6+loose. Faulty copied body returns (bundle_count+loose)*6. Predict tests before running.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Expected normal test: For (2,1), correct result is 2×6+1=13. → Faulty trace: Copied code gives (2+1)×6=18. → Zero-bundle test: For (0,3), correct 3; copied code 18. → Nonrevealing test: For (2,0), both return 12; a pass does not locate every bug.

graphics.title: Expected outputs versus a specific bug
graphics.alt: Expected outputs versus a specific bug. Test 1: Bundles = 2, Loose = 1, Correct = 13, Faulty = 18. Test 2: Bundles = 0, Loose = 3, Correct = 3, Faulty = 18. Test 3: Bundles = 2, Loose = 0, Correct = 12, Faulty = 12.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: For (2,0), both return 12; a pass does not locate every bug. Changed condition: Repair the body to bundle_count*6+loose. Expected result: Expected results for (2,1),(0,3),(2,0) are 13,3,12. Reason: Only bundles are groups of six; loose books are counted individually.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Test cases need not all expose the same error. Here loose books must be added after multiplying bundles. A zero-loose case cannot distinguish the two formulas because multiplying zero loose books changes nothing. Keep expected and actual columns so an observed output does not quietly become its own expected answer. Limit: These three tests check a specified formula and bug; they do not prove correct handling of every type or invalid request.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Test the recommender’s helper functions with normal, zero and boundary inputs before debugging the whole application. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which test most directly isolates the handling of loose books, and what should it produce?

graphics.title: Rows Columns and Data Types: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional approved book catalogue has three fields per row. Supplied facts: Schema: id is nonempty text; pages is an integer 1–300; illustrated is Boolean True or False. Rows A={id:"B7",pages:90,illustrated:True}; B={id:"B8",pages:"90",illustrated:False}; C={id:"",pages:80,illustrated:True}.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Column contract: Field names identify values; order is not the only guide. → Validate A: B7 is text, 90 is allowed integer, True is Boolean: valid. → Validate B: Quoted "90" is text, so pages fails the integer contract. → Validate C: Empty id fails even though its other two values have allowed types.

graphics.title: Follow the evidence
graphics.alt: Follow the evidence. activity | Nonempty text | Names the session activity. minutes | Integer 0 through 60 | Duration in minutes

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Empty id fails even though its other two values have allowed types. Changed condition: Change B’s pages from "90" to integer 90 using an approved repair. Expected result: B now satisfies the declared schema. Reason: Its id is nonempty and illustrated is Boolean; the page-type defect is removed.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A schema makes row meanings and expected types explicit. The string "90" looks like a number when printed but does not meet this strict integer schema. A repair can be authorised later, but must not be assumed silently. Missing or empty identifiers also prevent tracing an item back to its source. Limit: Schema validity does not confirm that the book really has 90 pages or that its metadata is accurate.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Publish the recommender’s row schema and validation results before ranking books, preserving repair provenance. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which two rows originally fail, and do they fail for the same reason?

graphics.title: Operational Labels: the case
graphics.alt: Two fictional catalogue reviewers label books compact or extended. Supplied facts: Agreed policy: compact means at most 80 pages; extended means more than 80. Reviewer A uses pages<80; reviewer B uses pages<=80. Inspect books of 79,80,81 pages.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Shared definition: At most 80 includes a book with exactly 80 pages. → Reviewer A: 79 compact; 80 and 81 extended. → Reviewer B: 79 and 80 compact; 81 extended. → Repair boundary: A must use <=80; retain the disagreement and changed policy implementation.

graphics.title: Operational label boundary
graphics.alt: Operational label boundary. Book 1: Pages = 79, A labels = compact, B labels = compact. Book 2: Pages = 80, A labels = extended, B labels = compact. Book 3: Pages = 81, A labels = extended, B labels = extended.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: A must use <=80; retain the disagreement and changed policy implementation. Changed condition: Change the documented policy to fewer than 80 instead. Expected result: A’s original labels now match; B must change its equality behavior. Reason: The authoritative definition changed, not the physical books.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The reviewers agree on two of three examples, but that fraction does not decide which definition to keep. The documented policy decides the equality case. Repairing A’s implementation aligns its labels with the agreed meaning. Rechecking 79 and 81 ensures the boundary fix preserves adjacent decisions. Limit: A shared definition improves consistency but does not prove the category captures every learner’s needs.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Give Transparent Book Recommender metadata labels explicit definitions and boundary examples for reviewers. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why can we not resolve the disagreement merely by taking a majority of reviewers?

graphics.title: Features and Distractors: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional book-topic classifier sees mystery books with triangular logos and science books with circular logos. Supplied facts: Training contains no mystery-circle or science-triangle covers. Goal is to identify topic from actual subject information, not publisher logo. New controlled test outputs have not been supplied.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Spot confounding: Topic and logo always move together in the training set. → Hold topic fixed: Compare the same mystery description with triangle versus circle logo. → Hold logo fixed: Compare mystery versus science descriptions with identical triangle logo. → Observe separately: Record predictions before concluding which clue the classifier uses.

graphics.title: The same cards under two feature choices
graphics.alt: The same cards under two feature choices. A is 10 by 7 cm and fits | Keep length only | 10 cm. B is 10 by 9 cm and is too large | Keep length only | 10 cm. A is 10 by 7 cm and fits | Keep length and width | 10 cm and 7 cm. B is 10 by 9 cm and is too large | Keep length and width | 10 cm and 9 cm
source: sections.diagram:The same cards under two feature choices

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Record predictions before concluding which clue the classifier uses. Changed condition: The first controlled pair yields mystery for triangle and science for circle. Expected result: That pair is evidence of unwanted logo sensitivity. Reason: The subject description stayed mystery; only the irrelevant logo changed.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Either subject information or logo could explain success on the old combinations. Controlled pairs separate their predictions by changing one aspect at a time. Designing the pair is not equivalent to observing the model’s response. Keep the descriptions identical when testing logo so differences do not have two possible causes. Limit: Controlled observations support specific sensitivity claims; they do not reveal every internal feature a learned model uses.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Test recommender features for shortcuts, keeping relevant subject information separate from superficial catalogue styling. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Does this one pair prove the classifier always ignores subject? Explain a narrower claim.

graphics.title: Human Classifier Simulation: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional librarian wants illustrated mystery books with at most 100 pages. Supplied facts: Written rule: choose only genre mystery AND illustrated True AND pages<=100. Rows J=(mystery,True,100), K=(mystery,False,90), L=(science,True,80), M=(mystery,True,blank). Missing required fields request review.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Read all conditions: Three requirements must pass, not just a high preference score. → Trace J: Mystery, illustrated and exactly 100 pages: choose. → Trace K and L: K fails illustration; L fails genre: do not choose. → Trace M: Missing pages means review rather than assuming it is short.

graphics.title: Three records through the Tower1 classifier
graphics.alt: Three records through the Tower1 classifier. 5 cm | Accepted; 5 is below 6 | Tower1 predicts short. 6 cm | Accepted; 6 is at least 6 | Tower1 predicts tall. Height blank | Missing height; stop before rule | Tower1; no prediction
source: sections.diagram:Three records through the Tower1 classifier

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Missing pages means review rather than assuming it is short. Changed condition: Supply M’s pages as 101. Expected result: M is now rejected rather than awaiting page review. Reason: The required field is known but fails the maximum-length condition.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: This human simulation lets students inspect every decision without needing a trained model. Equality matters at 100. Known failures give reasons for rejection; M lacks enough information for the page check. The order should not turn blank into zero or quietly ignore a required field. Limit: This declared rule checks eligibility, not whether an eligible book will actually be enjoyed.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Build a transparent filtering stage for the recommender, storing each failed or unresolved requirement in its explanation. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why are J and M initially treated differently even though both are illustrated mysteries?

graphics.title: Training and Testing: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional catalogue model learns from scans of book covers and will face previously unseen books. Supplied facts: Book A has scans A1,A2; B has B1,B2; C has C1,C2; D has D1,D2. Proposed training A1,B1,C1; validation A2,D1; test B2,C2,D2.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Choose unit: The intended kind of new example being evaluated is a new book, not merely a new scan. → Find leakage: A crosses train/validation; B,C cross train/test; D crosses validation/test. → Group repair: Training all A,B scans; validation all C scans; test all D scans. → Freeze assignment: Keep every scan from one book in exactly one role before fitting.

graphics.title: Keep each trip in one role
graphics.alt: Keep each trip in one role. A B C with all frames | Training | Fit from examples. D with all frames | Validation | Compare choices. E F with all frames | Test | Final check after choices
source: sections.diagram:Keep each trip in one role

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Keep every scan from one book in exactly one role before fitting. Changed condition: Give A2 a new filename without changing the book it depicts. Expected result: Its group is still A; the original related examples still cross the split. Reason: Renaming a row does not remove the relationship between scans.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Different scan IDs do not make examples independent books. A model may recognise repeated cover details from another view. Grouping by book matches the intended claim about new books and makes the split inspectable. The repaired split has four training, two validation and two test scans, but only two, one and one books respectively. Limit: One validation book and one test book provide very limited diversity even though no groups overlap.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Group the recommender’s related reviews, editions or repeated-user examples according to its intended evaluation claim. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: How many distinct books are in each repaired role, and why report that as well as scan counts?

graphics.title: Accuracy as a Fraction: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional shelf classifier predicts repair needed or not needed. Supplied facts: Evaluation reference labels: 16 not-needed and 4 needed. Positive class is needed. Always-not-needed baseline is correct on 16. Candidate has TP=3,FN=1,FP=2,TN=14.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Reference population: 20 labelled cases, including four repair-needed books. → Baseline: 16/20=80% accuracy; catches 0/4 needed cases. → Candidate: (3+14)/20=85% accuracy; catches 3/4=75% needed cases. → Compare costs: Candidate also raises two false alarms; discuss both missed repairs and extra checks.

graphics.title: Accuracy can hide missed repair cases
graphics.alt: Accuracy can hide missed repair cases. Units: percent. Baseline accuracy: 80. Baseline repair recall: 0. Candidate accuracy: 85. Candidate repair recall: 75.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Candidate also raises two false alarms; discuss both missed repairs and extra checks. Changed condition: A candidate instead marks every book repair needed. Expected result: Recall is 4/4=100%, but accuracy is only 4/20=20%. Reason: All 16 not-needed books become false alarms.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A majority-class baseline can look accurate while missing every positive case. The candidate improves overall agreement and repair detection in this table, but false alarms still matter. Use the same cases, denominators and positive-class definition for both. Do not infer that a single metric identifies the best policy for every library. Limit: These selected cases do not establish future rates or specify the real cost of each error.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Compare recommender choices with a simple baseline and report relevant rare-category failures, not only aggregate accuracy. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why is 100% repair detection not sufficient to declare the changed classifier best?

graphics.title: Types of Classification Error: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional book-condition checker predicts repair or sound. Supplied facts: Use reference rows and prediction columns in order sound,repair. Repair is positive. Six reference/prediction pairs: sound/sound twice; sound/repair once; repair/sound once; repair/repair twice.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Declare axes: Rows: reference sound,repair. Columns: predicted sound,repair. → Fill sound row: Two true negatives and one false positive: [2,1]. → Fill repair row: One false negative and two true positives: [1,2]. → Read result: Matrix [[2,1],[1,2]]: agreement 4/6, repair recall 2/3.

graphics.title: Reference rows, prediction columns
graphics.alt: Reference rows, prediction columns. Reference sound: Predicted sound = 2, Predicted repair = 1. Reference repair: Predicted sound = 1, Predicted repair = 2.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Matrix [[2,1],[1,2]]: agreement 4/6, repair recall 2/3. Changed condition: Change one repair/sound prediction to repair/repair after a real model revision. Expected result: Repair row becomes [0,3]; agreement becomes 5/6. Reason: One false negative moves to true positive; the sound row stays [2,1].

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Each case enters one cell according to its reference and predicted label. The off-diagonal cells represent different mistakes: a false alarm on a sound book versus a missed repair. Trace the cell definitions before naming rates; swapping axes changes the table’s interpretation even if its diagonal sum remains unchanged. Limit: Reference labels can themselves be disputed; a true-positive name does not guarantee the annotation is infallible.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Use a confusion table when evaluating recommender category predictions and attach concrete consequences to each error. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which error causes a sound book to be sent for unnecessary repair review?

graphics.title: Decision Trees: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional toy classifier predicts whether a book needs an illustration label. Supplied facts: Training rows (colour_cover,diagram_inside,label): (1,1,Yes),(1,0,No),(0,1,Yes),(0,0,No). Candidates ask colour_cover or diagram_inside; each leaf uses its training majority. A leaf tie chooses No. Select fewer training errors.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Colour candidate: Both colour leaves tie Yes/No, choose No: two training errors. → Diagram candidate: Diagram 1 leaf predicts Yes; diagram 0 leaf predicts No: zero errors. → Select tree: Choose the diagram question using the training comparison. → Apply new input: A new (1,0) row follows diagram=0 and predicts No.

graphics.title: Two paths through the learned tree
graphics.alt: Two paths through the learned tree. Is near equal to 1 | No near is 0 | Predict clear. Is near equal to 1 | Yes near is 1 | Predict blocked
source: sections.diagram:Two paths through the learned tree

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: A new (1,0) row follows diagram=0 and predicts No. Changed condition: New input becomes (0,1). Expected result: The fitted tree predicts Yes. Reason: It follows diagram=1; cover colour is not the selected question.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A question becomes a fitted tree only after its leaves and selection procedure are specified. The training comparison prefers the feature that separates these labels. Prediction follows the selected question; it does not reselect the tree using a new case’s answer. Save candidate leaves and errors so the choice can be repeated. Limit: Zero errors on four toy examples do not establish that diagrams always determine a real book’s classification.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Fit or hand-specify recommender classification rules transparently, retaining candidate definitions and training-only selection evidence. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why does changing colour alone not change this tree’s prediction?

graphics.title: Choose Informative Questions: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional guessing game has eight catalogue cards and asks yes/no questions to narrow the target. Supplied facts: Cards: four mystery, four science; six paperback, two hardback; all English. Compare worst-case remaining group size after asking mystery?, paperback? or English?. No claim about unequal target probabilities is made.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: List possibilities: There are eight possible target cards initially. → Mystery question: Yes group 4; No group 4; largest remaining group 4. → Paperback question: Yes 6; No 2; largest remaining group 6. → English question: Yes 8; No 0; largest remaining group 8.

graphics.title: Worst-case remaining candidates
graphics.alt: Worst-case remaining candidates. Units: cards remaining. Mystery?: 4. Paperback?: 6. English?: 8.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Yes 8; No 0; largest remaining group 8. Changed condition: The current possibility set contains only the four mystery cards. Expected result: Asking mystery now leaves all four; it no longer narrows the set. Reason: Question value depends on the remaining candidates, not just on its wording.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Under the stated worst-case criterion, mystery is the most useful of these questions because it leaves at most four cards. The constant language clue never narrows the set. This is an identification-game criterion; a classifier fitting labels may instead compare prediction errors or another declared training measure. Limit: Balanced groups do not guarantee a truthful user answer or optimal choices under every probability or cost model.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Choose recommender questions that distinguish feasible options, documenting the decision criterion rather than asking unnecessary personal details. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Choose the best original question and explain why its more balanced split matters here.

graphics.title: Overfitting Intuition: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional project compares three book-length prediction models on the same development sets. Supplied facts: Mean absolute errors in pages: Simple training 5, validation 6; Medium training 2, validation 3; Complex training 0, validation 7. Select lowest validation error; untouched final tests are not used for selection.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Training comparison: Complex fits training perfectly with zero error. → Validation comparison: Medium has error 3, versus Simple 6 and Complex 7. → Choose for development: Select Medium under the declared lowest-validation-error rule. → Final evaluation: Freeze the selection, then evaluate new reserved cases.

graphics.title: Training and validation errors
graphics.alt: Training and validation errors. Simple: Training MAE pages = 5, Validation MAE pages = 6. Medium: Training MAE pages = 2, Validation MAE pages = 3. Complex: Training MAE pages = 0, Validation MAE pages = 7.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Freeze the selection, then evaluate new reserved cases. Changed condition: Complex’s validation error becomes 2 on a newly documented, fair development comparison. Expected result: The stated rule now selects Complex. Reason: The rule compares validation errors; it does not ban complex models.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A flexible model can fit quirks of its training set without predicting new examples well. Here Complex’s training success occur togethers with the worst validation error. The numbers are invented comparisons, not a claim that complexity always hurts. Choosing Medium uses development evidence; its validation score must not be advertised as an untouched final-test result. Limit: A single small validation set may be noisy; selection evidence does not prove future population performance.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Compare recommender revisions on fixed development cases, reserving new cases for the final presentation. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Does zero training error justify choosing Complex in the original record?

graphics.title: Noise and Outliers: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional library records five book-processing times in minutes. Supplied facts: Sorted times: 2,3,3,4,18. All are recorded measurements; no evidence yet shows 18 is a mistake.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Mean: Sum 30; divide by 5: mean 6 minutes. → Median: The middle of five sorted values is 3 minutes. → Investigate 18: Check the source record and whether an unusually slow task occurred. → Document repair: Change a value only if evidence supports a correction; preserve the raw record.

graphics.title: Retain unusual recorded measurements
graphics.alt: Retain unusual recorded measurements. Units: minutes. Task 1: 2. Task 2: 3. Task 3: 3. Task 4: 4. Task 5: 18.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Change a value only if evidence supports a correction; preserve the raw record. Changed condition: An authorised log confirms 18 was a transcription error for 3. Expected result: Corrected mean is 3 minutes and median is 3. Reason: Values become 2,3,3,4,3 with sum 15; sorted middle remains 3.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The mean uses every value and is pulled upward by 18. The median identifies the middle recorded time and stays at 3. Neither statistic declares the unusual observation invalid. Deleting it simply because it changes the mean would hide potentially real slow work and change the question being answered. Limit: Five task times do not estimate all library processing times reliably or prove which summary suits every decision.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Investigate unusual recommender features and show evidence-backed repairs instead of removing inconvenient records. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: If 18 was genuine, which summary better describes the middle observed task, and what extra fact should be shown?

graphics.title: Missing Data: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional catalogue records counts of available copies under a strict input contract. Supplied facts: Accept count only if type(value) is int and 0<=value<=8. Missing fields are invalid, and Booleans are not counts. Rows have count 0, count 4, absent count, count "4", count True and count 9.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Retrieve carefully: Use row.get("count"); absent field gives None, distinct from 0. → Check exact type: Integers 0,4 pass; text "4", Boolean True and None fail. → Check range: Integer 9 fails maximum 8. → Report validation: Accepted counts [0,4]; four rows rejected with recorded reasons.

graphics.title: Follow the evidence
graphics.alt: Follow the evidence. Recorded zero | 0 | Accept as a measurement. Absent or None | Unknown | Hold for review. Negative integer | Outside range | Reject under this schema

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Accepted counts [0,4]; four rows rejected with recorded reasons. Changed condition: Replace text "4" with integer 4 through an authorised conversion. Expected result: Accepted values become [0,4,4]; three rows remain rejected. Reason: The converted value now satisfies both type and range checks.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Testing if value would wrongly discard zero, which is a real valid count. Python’s isinstance(True,int) is true, so the stated exact-integer contract uses type(value) is int to reject Boolean input. Keep missing, type-invalid and range-invalid reasons separate rather than turning every rejected value into zero. Limit: Type and range checks cannot confirm whether the real shelf count was measured accurately.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Validate recommender stock and numeric features explicitly, recording zero stock as measured zero rather than missing. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why is the Boolean True rejected even though arithmetic can treat it like 1 in Python?

graphics.title: Sampling and Representation: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional Grade 7 class wants to understand book-format preferences across its whole grade. Supplied facts: Population: all 60 Grade 7 learners. Frame: current school-approved list of those 60, used only by the teacher. Teacher randomly invites 15; 12 answer the same neutral comic/prose/either question. No names enter the analysis table.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Define target: The question concerns all Grade 7, not only library-club members. → Select invitations: Teacher uses the complete approved list and documented random selection. → Record responses: 12 replies from 15 invited; three nonresponses remain visible. → Report scope: Invitation response rate 12/15=80%; preference counts describe respondents.

graphics.title: Follow the evidence
graphics.alt: Follow the evidence. Target | All Grade 7 students | Population. Available data | Three club responses | Sample. Observed result | 2 of 3 choose Code | Describes respondents

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Invitation response rate 12/15=80%; preference counts describe respondents. Changed condition: Invite only the 15 library-club members instead. Expected result: The invitation process no longer covers the whole grade through this frame. Reason: Club members may differ in reading interests; selection is now limited to one group.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A sample plan states who could be selected, how selection happens and what happens after invitation. Random invitations do not guarantee that respondents resemble those who declined. Use a neutral question and preserve nonresponse coverage. Learners can discuss aggregate counts without receiving the identifiable selection frame. Limit: Even the random-invitation plan does not remove nonresponse bias or justify revealing identifiable school lists.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Document whose requests inform the recommender and avoid treating an easily reached group as all intended users. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Can 80% response be reported as 80% of the whole grade responding?

graphics.title: Repair Bias in Data: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional school polls learners about adding comic recommendations. Supplied facts: Library-club respondents: 12 Yes out of 15. Other respondents: 3 Yes out of 15. The full grade has 30 club members and 90 others. These respondents were volunteers, not random selections.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Group rates: Club:12/15=80%; others:3/15=20%. → Respondent total: 15 Yes out of 30 respondents =50%. → Check representation: Respondents split 50/50, but the grade is 25% club and 75% other. → Repair collection: Plan including equality, documented invitations and report nonresponse by group.

graphics.title: Volunteer group comparison
graphics.alt: Volunteer group comparison. Club: Yes responses = 12, Respondents = 15, Grade members = 30. Others: Yes responses = 3, Respondents = 15, Grade members = 90.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Plan including equality, documented invitations and report nonresponse by group. Changed condition: Recruit more club volunteers only. Expected result: Sample size increases without fixing missing representation of other learners. Reason: The added respondents come from the already overrepresented group.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The combined respondent result gives club members more influence than their share of the grade. A weighted illustration using 25% and 75% gives 0.25×80%+0.75×20%=35%, but volunteers may differ within each group, so weighting alone does not establish the true grade preference. Improve the collection process rather than announcing the weighted number as fact. Limit: Neither raw nor weighted volunteer rates prove the whole grade’s opinion; privacy and consent rules still apply.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Broaden recommender feedback collection and show respondent group coverage before making user-preference claims. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why must 35% be labelled an illustration rather than the measured grade-wide Yes rate?

graphics.title: Similarity by Selected Traits: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional toy book matcher represents two preferences with numeric features. Supplied facts: Target vector [2,5]. Candidate A=[2,2], B=[4,5], C=[3,4]. Use Manhattan distance: add absolute coordinate differences; return all smallest-distance candidates.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Distance A: |2−2|+|5−2|=0+3=3. → Distance B: |2−4|+|5−5|=2+0=2. → Distance C: |2−3|+|5−4|=1+1=2. → Choose closest: B and C tie at distance 2; keep the tie visible.

graphics.title: Toy feature positions
graphics.alt: Toy feature positions. A: (2, 2). B: (4, 5). C: (3, 4). Query Target: (2, 5). Axes: first toy feature; second toy feature. Distance: Manhattan distance; horizontal=first feature, vertical=second feature.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: B and C tie at distance 2; keep the tie visible. Changed condition: Give the first-coordinate difference weight 2 while the second keeps weight 1. Expected result: Distances become A=3, B=4, C=3; A and C tie. Reason: The representation’s comparison rule changes; the supplied vectors stay the same.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Each coordinate contributes according to the declared distance rule. Smaller distance means closer in this representation, not automatically a better reading experience. If one coordinate uses a much larger numerical scale, it can dominate the sum even when it is not more important. Feature units and scaling belong in the method record. Limit: A toy numeric encoding does not establish meaningful interpersonal distances or suitability of a recommendation.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Specify recommender feature meanings, units, scaling and tie policy before explaining nearest matches. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Explain why B ceases to be a closest option without any candidate data changing.

graphics.title: Nearest Neighbor Reasoning: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional one-feature classifier predicts compact or extended book format. Supplied facts: Stored training rows: A at 2 units compact, B at 6 extended, C at 8 compact, D at 12 extended. Query is 7. Distance is absolute difference; ties sort by ID; tied category vote chooses compact.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Measure distances: From 7: A=5, B=1, C=1, D=5. → Order neighbours: Distance then ID gives B,C,A,D. → k=1 prediction: First neighbour B is extended: predict extended. → k=3 prediction: B,C,A vote extended,compact,compact: predict compact.

graphics.title: Distances from query 7
graphics.alt: Distances from query 7. Units: absolute distance units. A at 2: 5. B at 6: 1. C at 8: 1. D at 12: 5.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: B,C,A vote extended,compact,compact: predict compact. Changed condition: Move query from 7 to 9 while keeping training fixed. Expected result: Order becomes C,B,D,A; k=1 predicts compact and k=3 predicts extended. Reason: Distances are C=1,B=3,D=3,A=7; B beats D by the ID tie rule.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Changing k changes how many training neighbours vote, even though all distances remain fixed. The query’s reference label must not enter the stored pool before predicting. Tie policies make ordering reproducible; without them, list order could unexpectedly determine the single-neighbour result. Limit: Nearest-neighbour votes depend on feature representation; they are not calibrated probabilities or guaranteed correct labels.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Retain recommender neighbour IDs, distances, k and tie decisions so similar-book explanations can be audited. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why do k=1 and k=3 disagree for the original query?

graphics.title: Recommendation Scores: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional book-activity chooser has a 14-minute limit. Supplied facts: Score=2×interest+practice. A=(interest3,practice2,time14); B=(4,3,15); C=(2,5,12). Require whole nonnegative feature values; time must be at most the limit. Highest score wins; tie by ID.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Eligibility first: A and C fit time; B takes 15 and is excluded. → Scores: A:2×3+2=8. C:2×2+5=9. → Choose: C wins at score 9 among eligible activities. → Explain exclusion: B’s score 11 cannot override its failed time requirement.

graphics.title: Time filtering and scores
graphics.alt: Time filtering and scores. A: Minutes = 14, Score = 8, Status = eligible. B: Minutes = 15, Score = 11, Status = excluded. C: Minutes = 12, Score = 9, Status = eligible.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: B’s score 11 cannot override its failed time requirement. Changed condition: Change interest weight from 2 to 3, keeping time limit 14. Expected result: A scores 11; C also scores 11; tie-by-ID chooses A. Reason: B remains too long; changing preferences changes only ranking of A and C.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A score combines preferences according to explicitly chosen weights; it does not erase hard constraints. Computing a high score for an excluded item can be useful in an audit, but it must not allow that item back into the candidate set. Store both eligibility reasons and score components for explanations. Limit: Toy interest scores are supplied inputs, not measured enjoyment or a universal definition of a good activity.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Publish the recommender’s constraints, score formula and tie rule; include component-level reasons in each suggestion. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why does B not become the winner when its score is largest?

graphics.title: Feedback Loops: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional catalogue repeatedly recommends two books using observed clicks. Supplied facts: Initially each click count is 0. Equal counts choose earlier ID A over B. Only the recommended book is shown. In an invented three-round record, A is shown and clicked each round; B is never shown.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Initial tie: Counts A=0,B=0; ID rule shows A. → Record event: A receives a click, so its count becomes 1; B stays 0. → Repeat selection: Higher A count causes A to be shown again; after three clicks A=3,B=0. → Interpret carefully: B’s zero may mean no exposure, not dislike.

graphics.title: Exposure and clicks after the invented three rounds
graphics.alt: Exposure and clicks after the invented three rounds. A: Shown = 3, Clicked = 3. B: Shown = 0, Clicked = 0.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: B’s zero may mean no exposure, not dislike. Changed condition: On a planned trial, show B once and record no click. Expected result: B gains one exposure but still zero clicks. Reason: The observation now supports a nonclick on that display, not a permanent dislike.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The selection policy changes which evidence is available. A accumulates clicks partly because the system gives it every opportunity, while B has none. These records cannot compare enjoyment of two equally exposed books. Keep display counts separate from click counts; investigate alternatives with a teacher-approved exposure plan rather than treating zero as negative feedback. Limit: A click can reflect curiosity or a mistake; even equal exposure does not reveal every reason for selection.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Log recommender exposure, choice and explicit feedback separately; consider whether its own policy narrows future evidence. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: What extra field would reveal why comparing raw clicks is misleading?

graphics.title: Text as Pieces: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional tokenizer converts a short catalogue phrase into tokens. Supplied facts: Vocabulary entries: book, books and the space character. At each position choose the longest matching entry; preserve the actual space. Text is “books book”. Exclamation marks have no token; zero-based character positions are used.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Read prefix: At position 0, longest matching entry is books, not book. → Encode phrase: Tokens: books, space-character, book; three tokens. → Decode: Joining token text returns exactly books book. → Unknown character: For books book!, the ! at position 10 has no token: stop with error.

graphics.title: Keep the evidence roles separate
graphics.alt: Keep the evidence roles separate. Exact text: cats sat | Longest-match encoding | IDs 1, 5, 6, 7. IDs 1, 5, 6, 7 | Concatenate token strings | Exact text: cats sat. Exact text: Cat | No match for uppercase C | Report unsupported input

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: For books book!, the ! at position 10 has no token: stop with error. Changed condition: Use a character vocabulary covering b,o,k,s and space instead. Expected result: The same phrase uses ten character tokens. Reason: There are five letters, one space and four letters; its decoded text remains unchanged.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A token is defined by the vocabulary and encoding rule; it need not be one word or one character. Longest matching matters where vocabulary entries overlap. Counting text tokens here does not count letters. Preserve spaces during decoding so the reconstructed text matches the original exactly. Limit: This deterministic toy tokenizer omits real subword training, Unicode handling and model-specific special tokens.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Document the recommender’s text representation and unknown-token behavior rather than assuming every model counts words identically. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why is the unknown ! at position 10 rather than position 9?

graphics.title: Image and Voice Pipelines: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional librarian dictates a shelf note that passes through transcription and catalogue lookup. Supplied facts: Teacher-supplied ground truth audio phrase is “shelf fourteen”. Transcript says “shelf forty”. A current signed inventory is declared authoritative and lists the requested book on shelf 14. The original audio recording remains available.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Audio input: Known phrase names fourteen, not forty. → Transcription: Text output changes the shelf number to forty. → Cross-check: The authoritative inventory gives shelf 14. → Review and correct: Replay the audio, preserve the faulty transcript and use confirmed shelf 14.

graphics.title: Speech pipelines and multimodal evidence — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Speech pipelines and multimodal evidence — evidence trace. Audio transcript reads fifteen boxes; a clear written inventory says fifty boxes. The original audio is unavailable and the assistant reports fifteen as certain. | Track source modality, segment/time references, transcription, interpretation and final claims separately. Compare conflicting evidence without assuming one modality always wins. Ask for clarification when the task needs unresolved information. | There is an unresolved quantity conflict and no audio replay. Preserve both sources and ask the responsible person; certainty is unsupported.
source: sections.diagram:Speech pipelines and multimodal evidence — evidence trace

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Replay the audio, preserve the faulty transcript and use confirmed shelf 14. Changed condition: Remove access to the audio, while keeping the authoritative inventory. Expected result: Shelf 14 remains supported for the lookup, but transcription accuracy cannot be replay-checked. Reason: The inventory resolves the shelf task; it does not recreate unavailable audio.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A correct later lookup cannot repair an earlier wrong input by magic. Locate the first difference between known audio and transcript, then compare the stated source authority. Keeping both records makes the correction auditable. A confident spoken answer for shelf 40 would remain wrong despite fluent synthesis. Limit: Declared authority resolves this task’s source choice; it does not make every inventory entry universally accurate.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For voice-driven recommendations, confirm important recognised fields before searching or acting and retain source provenance. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which stage first fails, and why should the faulty transcript not be silently overwritten?

graphics.title: Predictive vs Generative: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional toy generator predicts the next word after “The box is”. Supplied facts: Observed training continuations: full 6, empty 3, unknown 1. Use counts divided by total 10. The current physical box is separately checked and found empty.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Count table: Continuation counts are 6,3,1; total 10. → Probabilities: full=0.6; empty=0.3; unknown=0.1. → Greedy continuation: Largest probability chooses full for this toy prefix. → Check reality: Current observation says empty; frequent wording is not a present inventory reading.

graphics.title: Toy next-word distribution
graphics.alt: Toy next-word distribution. Units: probability. full: 0.6. empty: 0.3. unknown: 0.1.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Current observation says empty; frequent wording is not a present inventory reading. Changed condition: Change the training table to full 2, empty 7, unknown 1. Expected result: Greedy output becomes empty with probability 0.7. Reason: The continuation distribution changed; the independently observed box has not changed.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The table predicts a continuation in a text exercise, not the contents of the current box. Generating the most frequent token is a model-defined decision. A factual inventory statement needs current evidence. The numerical table is intentionally small; real generative systems condition on richer context and do not simply consult these three counts. Limit: A one-step toy distribution does not describe every predictive or generative model or validate factual accuracy.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Use approved book facts for recommender explanations; generated fluency is not a replacement for catalogue evidence. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Does matching the physical box in the changed table prove the generator measures boxes?

graphics.title: Prompt Experiments: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional book-help project tests two prompt versions on seven shared development cases. Supplied facts: P passes cases 1,2,3,4. Q passes 1,2,3,5,6. Cases 4 and 7 involve missing sources. Same inputs, system configuration and rubric; only the prompt changes. These are invented records.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Paired setup: Use the same seven cases and pass criteria for both prompts. → Overall rates: P=4/7; Q=5/7. → Missing-source slice: P passes 1/2; Q passes 0/2 in cases 4 and 7. → Decide explicitly: Q improves overall count but worsens missing-source behavior; use the declared priorities.

graphics.title: Paired overall and missing-source passes
graphics.alt: Paired overall and missing-source passes. P: Overall passes /7 = 4, Missing-source passes /2 = 1. Q: Overall passes /7 = 5, Missing-source passes /2 = 0.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Q improves overall count but worsens missing-source behavior; use the declared priorities. Changed condition: Make missing-source correctness a required selection gate. Expected result: Neither prompt clears a 2/2 gate on these records. Reason: P fails 7 and Q fails both 4 and 7; both need revision.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A larger total can conceal a more serious failure category. Paired records show which cases changed, not just how many passed. If refusing unsupported claims is mandatory, Q’s overall advantage may not justify selection. Keep the failing examples for development and obtain fresh cases after choosing a final version. Limit: Seven development cases cannot establish causal learning benefits or untouched final performance; repeated generation may also vary.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Run controlled recommender explanation experiments with paired cases and report important failure conditions separately. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Name the case P passes and Q fails, and explain why it matters.

graphics.title: Evidence and Sources: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional catalogue answer contains three factual statements and cites existing records. Supplied facts: Record R: book Ocean Maps has 80 pages and is available on shelf 2. Claims: 80 pages [R]; shelf 2 [R]; suitable for every child [R]. All three citations resolve to R.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Break into claims: Count three factual claims rather than treating the answer as one blob. → Check links: All three citation links resolve to the intended R. → Check exact source support: R supports page count and shelf, not universal suitability. → Report separately: Citation presence 3/3; link validity 3/3; supported claims 2/3.

graphics.title: Different citation checks
graphics.alt: Different citation checks. Units: percent. Citation presence: 100. Link validity: 100. Claim support: 66.66666666666667.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Citation presence 3/3; link validity 3/3; supported claims 2/3. Changed condition: Change the third claim to “the record does not assess suitability”. Expected result: That statement accurately describes the supplied record’s limits. Reason: R gives pages and shelf only; it contains no suitability assessment.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: An existing citation is not automatically evidence for every nearby sentence. Read the cited passage and compare its exact scope with the claim. The universal suitability statement extends beyond what R says. Remove or qualify unsupported content; adding more copies of the same link does not create the missing evidence. Limit: Source support is relative to supplied records; those records can themselves be incomplete, outdated or incorrect.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Attach source IDs to recommender explanation facts and separately audit whether each source supports its precise statement. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why is the original answer not fully supported despite having citations on every claim?

graphics.title: Agents and Tools: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional read-only catalogue assistant follows a fixed state machine. Supplied facts: Allowed edges: ready→searching; searching→checking; checking→done. done has no outgoing edge. Trace A: ready→searching→checking→done. Trace B: ready→searching→done.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Declare transitions: A state is a named stage; only listed edges are allowed. → Trace A: Every adjacent edge is listed: valid. → Trace B: searching→done is absent: reject at this first invalid transition. → Terminal check: After done, another search requires a separately defined new run.

graphics.title: State machines for bounded agents — evidence trace
graphics.alt: State machines for bounded agents — evidence trace. Trace ready -> looking_up -> review -> looking_up -> done. | States are ready, looking_up, review, done. ready may start lookup; lookup may finish done or request review; review may finish done after authorised evidence. done is terminal. Maximum two lookup attempts. | review -> looking_up is not allowed by this declared transition table, even if total attempts is two. Reject the transition or explicitly redesign and retest the table.
source: sections.diagram:State machines for bounded agents — evidence trace

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: After done, another search requires a separately defined new run. Changed condition: Add a review state between checking and done, without updating Trace A. Expected result: Trace A becomes invalid at checking→done under the revised table. Reason: A required new transition changes what constitutes a complete run.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Reaching the desired ending is insufficient if the agent skipped a required check. Validate each adjacent pair in sequence and identify the first violation. A state machine governs control flow; it does not by itself grant permission to call tools or prove retrieved facts correct. Those are separate checks inside the relevant stages. Limit: This toy machine has no retry path; do not invent one or assume real agents always follow these states.

graphics.alt: Make recommender tool workflows explicit, with bounded retries, validation stages and terminal behavior. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Can the assistant accept Trace B because its final state is done?

graphics.title: Permissions and Human Review: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional catalogue helper receives a narrowly scoped tool token. Supplied facts: Token allows read on catalogue records R2 and R5 only. No write permission is granted. Proposals: read R2; read R8; write R5. Generated text claims all are helpful.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Read token: Authorised operation is read; authorised objects are R2,R5. → Allowed call: read R2 matches both operation and object: allow. → Wrong object: read R8 fails object scope: deny. → Wrong operation: write R5 fails operation scope: deny even for an allowed record.

graphics.title: Least privilege and tool scopes — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Least privilege and tool scopes — evidence trace. Tool token permits lookup(public-room). A proposed call writes teacher notes. | A reporting assistant may lookup public rooms but may not write records, send messages or read teacher notes. Check actor, operation and resource before executing a proposed call. | Both operation and resource exceed scope; deny before execution, regardless of generated confidence.
source: sections.diagram:Least privilege and tool scopes — evidence trace

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: write R5 fails operation scope: deny even for an allowed record. Changed condition: The helper says it needs write R5 to correct an apparent typo. Expected result: The write remains denied under the existing token. Reason: A useful purpose does not create an authorised operation; an authorised owner must review any scope change.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Permissions are concrete restrictions, not a confidence score or a general instruction to be useful. Each proposed call must match both dimensions before it happens. A request written inside catalogue text cannot enlarge the token’s authority. Denial should preserve the proposed action and reason without executing the disallowed mutation. Limit: Permission checks do not establish that a read result is trustworthy or that an allowed action is factually correct.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Give the recommender read-only access wherever sufficient, and require explicit owner review for catalogue edits or publication. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which proposal is allowed, and why is an authorised object alone insufficient?

graphics.title: Project Problem and Success Test: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional reading-break chooser needs a transparent contract. Supplied facts: Items have id text, minutes integer 0–30, interest integer 0–5. Request limit is integer 0–30. Eligible if minutes<=limit; score=interest; highest wins; ties choose alphabetically smaller ID; invalid rows excluded and counted.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Specify inputs: Validate each row and request; keep rejected-row reasons. → Filter and rank: At limit 8: A(time8,interest3), B(9,5), C(6,3). B is ineligible. → Expected output: A beats tied C by ID; report A and its score 3. → Acceptance cases: Also plan invalid request, no eligible item and equal-score cases.

graphics.title: Follow the evidence
graphics.alt: Follow the evidence. Input | Local fictional records | Validate schema. Decision | Filter then score then tie rule | Explain selected item. Output | Suggestion or no eligible item | Teacher reviews

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Also plan invalid request, no eligible item and equal-score cases. Changed condition: Reduce the limit from 8 to 5. Expected result: Return no eligible item. Reason: All three valid rows take more than five minutes.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Planning fixes what success means before code returns an answer. The duration boundary is including equality, and the tie policy prevents accidental list-order dependence. A complete output may include why other rows were excluded. Test expectations should come from the contract rather than copying the first program result. Limit: The supplied interest scores are fictional; the specification does not establish genuine learner preferences.

graphics.alt: Retain the Transparent Book Recommender’s schema, constraints, score, tie rule and acceptance table as its build specification. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Write an equality test and explain which requirement it checks.

graphics.title: Build the Recommender: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional book chooser filters a request before comparing preference scores. Supplied facts: Request: animal subject, at most 90 pages. Score 2 for illustrated and 1 for comic. Tie chooses smaller ID. A animal90 illustrated prose; B animal70 plain comic; C space60 illustrated comic; D animal80 illustrated comic.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Filter: A,B,D meet subject and page requirements; C fails subject. → Compute scores: A=2; B=1; D=3. → Choose best: Return D with both preference matches recorded. → Deterministic output: Reordering the input rows must not change D’s unique winning score.

graphics.title: Filtering before scoring
graphics.alt: Filtering before scoring. A: Pages = 90, Preference score = 2, Status = eligible. B: Pages = 70, Preference score = 1, Status = eligible. C: Pages = 60, Preference score = 3, Status = subject fails. D: Pages = 80, Preference score = 3, Status = eligible.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Reordering the input rows must not change D’s unique winning score. Changed condition: Change D’s pages to 91, leaving every other field unchanged. Expected result: D becomes ineligible, so A wins with score 2. Reason: The strict excess over the 90-page maximum changes filtering before ranking.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Eligibility and ranking answer different questions. C has a high preference score but is not an animal book, so it must stay excluded. The implementation needs a no-match result and explicit tie policy even when this example has a unique winner. Save rejected reasons for an explanation, not just the final ID. Limit: Toy preference weights do not imply shorter or illustrated books are universally better for all learners.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Save the recommender code, contract and this full trace; test the same records in different input orders. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Explain why B does not win after D is excluded even though it has fewer pages.

graphics.title: Test Diverse Users: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional recommender is tested on distinct ordinary, equality, invalid-input and tie cases. Supplied facts: Recorded full passes: ordinary 4/4; equality 1/3; invalid 2/3; ties 1/2. Categories are disjoint and every case was run on the same frozen version with the same contract.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Total count: Passes 4+1+2+1=8; cases 4+3+3+2=12. → Overall rate: 8/12≈66.7% full passes. → Find weak slices: Equality 1/3; invalid 2/3; ties 1/2; ordinary 4/4. → Prioritise repair: Inspect failed equality traces and any invalid-input safety consequence, not only the total.

graphics.title: Disjoint evaluation categories
graphics.alt: Disjoint evaluation categories. Ordinary: Full passes = 4, Cases run = 4. Equality: Full passes = 1, Cases run = 3. Invalid: Full passes = 2, Cases run = 3. Ties: Full passes = 1, Cases run = 2.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Inspect failed equality traces and any invalid-input safety consequence, not only the total. Changed condition: Someone reports only the ordinary slice. Expected result: The claim becomes 4/4 on ordinary cases, not 100% across all tests. Reason: Eight nonordinary cases and their failures have been omitted.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Varied tests expose behavior an ordinary demonstration misses. The overall result combines disjoint cases once each; overlapping labels would require unique-case accounting. Prioritisation also depends on consequences: a malformed input that triggers an unauthorised action can be more serious than a harmless tie-order failure. Retain each failed case and its expected output. Limit: Twelve designed cases describe this test suite, not an unbiased estimate of future usage accuracy.

graphics.alt: Build a recommender evaluation matrix with routine, boundary, missing, invalid and tie cases, then add separately planned user-condition coverage. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Can these records establish performance for different user groups?

graphics.title: Improve and Challenge: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional recommender excludes books at an intended including equality page limit. Supplied facts: Contract: pages<=100; highest interest; ties choose smaller ID. Old code uses pages<100. Rows A pages100 interest5; B pages90 interest3; C pages101 interest5.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Identify cause: A wrongly excluded at equality, so old code selects B. → Focused repair: Replace <100 with <=100 without changing ranking or type checks. → Expected revised result: A becomes eligible and wins; C remains excluded. → Challenge repair: Rerun 99,100,101; invalid pages; tied scores; reversed row order.

graphics.title: Follow the evidence
graphics.alt: Follow the evidence. Before fix | 10 < 10 is False | Violates at most rule. After fix | 10 <= 10 is True | Boundary accepted. Neighbor check | 11 <= 10 is False | Over-limit still excluded

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Rerun 99,100,101; invalid pages; tied scores; reversed row order. Changed condition: An alternative patch simply increases the limit to 101. Expected result: C is wrongly admitted as well as A. Reason: Changing the maximum alters the contract instead of repairing its comparison.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A focused change makes the claim about what caused the error testable: the equality comparison rule caused this specific failure. Regression tests check surrounding behavior that should remain unchanged. A tie case and reversed input order are necessary because a correct boundary does not ensure deterministic selection. Log the old failure and revised replay separately. Limit: Passing a small regression suite does not prove all behavior unchanged; record the suite’s actual coverage.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For each recommender revision, retain cause, code change, targeted test, regression results and unresolved issues. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why are tests at both 100 and 101 needed?

graphics.title: Capstone Expo: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional team presents its transparent book recommender on a reserved catalogue. Supplied facts: Request maximum 120 pages; score=2×interest+illustrated, where illustrated is 1 for True and 0 for False; tie by ID. A pages120 interest3 True; B pages100 interest4 False; C pages121 interest5 True; D pages90 interest"4" True. Numeric fields require exact integers.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Validate: D has text interest and is rejected; A,B,C have valid fields. → Filter: A and B meet the page limit; C exceeds it. → Rank: A scores 7; B scores 8, so B wins. → Defend evidence: Explain two eligible items, one page-limit exclusion and one type rejection.

graphics.title: Follow the evidence
graphics.alt: Follow the evidence. Claim | A selected by stated policy | Show trace and inputs. Quality | Tested cases and failures | Show full denominators. Handover | Versions and run steps | Peer can reproduce

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Explain two eligible items, one page-limit exclusion and one type rejection. Changed condition: An authorised repair converts D’s interest to integer 4. Expected result: D becomes eligible and scores 9, so it wins. Reason: The evidence-backed input repair changes validation and then ranking; record this as a new case/version.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A presentation should let someone rebuild the result from the stated contract. A’s equality is accepted; D is not silently converted; C’s high preference score cannot override the page requirement. Reversing rows must preserve B because it has the unique highest eligible score. Keep the reserved case distinct from practice demonstrations. Limit: A defensible algorithmic trace does not prove B will be liked or that classroom learning improved.
