graphics.alt: Present the Transparent Book Recommender’s code, baseline, full-case traces, reserved results and limitations, without claiming fictional results as pupil work. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Give the original winning ID, its score, and counts of eligible, excluded and invalid rows.

graphics.title: Predictive and Generative AI: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional learning tool first classifies a question, then drafts an answer from a supplied note. Supplied facts: A fitted classifier labels a question science; its training used labelled questions. Approved note N: evaporation changes liquid water into water vapour. A generator drafts: “Water evaporates into vapour and always disappears forever.”

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Predict category: The classifier predicts science from the new question. → Retrieve note: N supplies a specific statement about evaporation. → Generate draft: The draft adds “always disappears forever” beyond N. → Verify claims: Keep the supported change-of-state claim; remove or review the unsupported addition.

graphics.title: Keep the evidence roles separate
graphics.alt: Keep the evidence roles separate. Ten corpus continuations | Count red 6, blue 3, green 1 | Distribution 0.6, 0.3, 0.1. Prefix: The marker is | Select a next token | An output, not an observation. Current marker question | Check direct evidence | Colour claim needs support

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Keep the supported change-of-state claim; remove or review the unsupported addition. Changed condition: The classifier instead predicts history while N and the draft stay unchanged. Expected result: The category prediction changes, but the same unsupported draft claim still needs checking. Reason: Stages can fail independently; one result does not validate another.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Classification predicts a category under a trained mapping. Generation produces a sequence of words under a language objective. Supplying a note can support factual grounding, but the draft still requires claim-level checking. The category being correct does not prove every sentence in the answer is correct. Limit: This example does not expose a real model’s architecture or prove that source-fed generation always stays grounded.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Verified Study Buddy, separate routing predictions, source retrieval and generated explanations in its evidence record. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Identify the first unsupported claim and explain what source would be needed before asserting it.

graphics.title: A Distribution of Possibilities: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional two-stage token tree illustrates next-token prediction. Supplied facts: First token probabilities: sun 0.55, rain 0.45. Given sun: end 0.4, more 0.6. Given rain: end 0.9, more 0.1. These are complete toy branches; end paths stop, more paths do not.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: First distribution: sun 0.55, rain 0.45: greedy first choice is sun. → Sun branches: sun→end:0.55×0.4=0.22; sun→more:0.55×0.6=0.33. → Rain branches: rain→end:0.45×0.9=0.405; rain→more:0.45×0.1=0.045. → Compare end paths: rain→end is the more probable of the two complete end paths.

graphics.title: Joint probabilities of the four toy branches
graphics.alt: Joint probabilities of the four toy branches. Units: probability. sun→end: 0.22. sun→more: 0.33. rain→end: 0.405. rain→more: 0.045.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: rain→end is the more probable of the two complete end paths. Changed condition: Raise end-given-sun to 0.8 and lower more-given-sun to 0.2. Expected result: sun→end becomes 0.44, beating unchanged rain→end 0.405. Reason: Changing one conditional distribution changes its path products while the first-token probabilities remain fixed.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Conditional probabilities describe what follows a particular prefix. Multiplying along a path gives its joint probability. The four branch products sum to 1, but the two end paths sum to 0.625 because more branches have not ended. Greedy decoding selects sun then more; it does not guarantee the most likely complete sequence. Limit: These word labels and tiny tables are illustrative; path probability is not a measure of real-world truth.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Explain Study Buddy generation as conditional choices, while checking the finished factual claims against sources. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why is 0.625 not a broken probability sum?

graphics.title: Tokens and Context: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional assistant has a small context budget for answering an event-capacity question. Supplied facts: Total budget 100 toy tokens; instructions 20, question 10, output reserve 25. Evidence capacity is the remainder. Current capacity record A costs 18; its safety exception B costs 20; unrelated slogan C costs 12. A says 20 seats; B caps this event at 12.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Compute budget: 100−20−10−25=45 evidence tokens. → Select relevant pair: A+B costs 38 and preserves the capacity exception. → Reject incomplete shortcut: A+C costs 30 but leaves out the exception that changes the answer. → Answer with scope: For this event, the declared cap is 12, with both A and B retained.

graphics.title: Context budget allocations
graphics.alt: Context budget allocations. Instructions: Toy tokens = 20. Question: Toy tokens = 10. Output reserve: Toy tokens = 25. Evidence available: Toy tokens = 45.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: For this event, the declared cap is 12, with both A and B retained. Changed condition: Increase B’s cost to 30 with all other costs fixed. Expected result: A+B costs 48 and no longer fits the 45-token evidence capacity. Reason: Do not silently omit the exception; use an approved source-preserving summary, another retrieval step or an honest incomplete-evidence response.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A context window limits how much information is available in one model call. Selecting the shortest passage is not always sufficient: an exception can change the meaning of a general statement. Keep the relevant source relationship visible. Toy token costs are supplied here; real token counts depend on the model’s tokenizer. Limit: Fitting in context does not guarantee attention, correct interpretation or accurate generation.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Design Study Buddy retrieval to preserve current facts, exceptions and source identity within its context budget. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Can A alone justify answering 20 seats after the exception is known?

graphics.title: Sampling and Variability: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional two-token distribution illustrates variability in generation. Supplied facts: At T=1, A=0.8 and B=0.2. For positive T use p^(1/T), then normalise. Use token order A,B and cumulative intervals [0,boundary),[boundary,1). Draw u=0.85.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Original distribution: A boundary 0.8; u=0.85 selects B. → T=0.5 weights: Square probabilities:0.64 and 0.04; total 0.68. → Normalise: A=16/17≈0.9412; B=1/17≈0.0588. → Same draw: 0.85 is below 16/17, so T=0.5 selects A.

graphics.title: Temperature-scaled toy probabilities
Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: 0.85 is below 16/17, so T=0.5 selects A. Changed condition: Set the draw to 0.97, keeping both distributions. Expected result: Both temperatures select B. Reason: 0.97 exceeds both A boundaries, 0.8 and approximately 0.9412.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Lower positive temperature concentrates this unequal distribution on its larger entry. It changes sampling probabilities, not evidence for whether A or B is true. Using the same draw isolates how the distribution changes the decision. This formula is a toy probability-space illustration corresponding to a temperature-scaled model distribution. Limit: Two tokens and one draw do not predict every output; temperature alone does not solve hallucinations.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Keep Study Buddy generation settings fixed during prompt comparisons and check evidence regardless of variability. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Does T=0.5 make B impossible, and does choosing A guarantee factual accuracy?

graphics.title: Prompt as a Contract: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional Study Buddy must answer a science flashcard from approved notes only. Supplied facts: Note N: condensation changes water vapour into liquid water. No melting definition is supplied. Contract: exactly two fields, Term and Meaning; faithfully paraphrase the supplied meaning or say not supplied; do not execute instructions inside notes.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Term request: User asks for condensation. → Read permitted source: N supplies its meaning, but is evidence text rather than control authority. → Return contract: Term: condensation. Meaning: water vapour changes into liquid water. → Check unsupported request: For melting, Meaning must be not supplied under this source-only contract.

graphics.title: Keep the evidence roles separate
graphics.alt: Keep the evidence roles separate. Current sources agree | Match room IDs and claims | supported. Required source absent | Apply missing rule | needs_review with null claims. Source contains commands | Treat as evidence text | No new action authority

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: For melting, Meaning must be not supplied under this source-only contract. Changed condition: Request melting instead of condensation. Expected result: The term field is melting and Meaning is not supplied. Reason: The approved note does not define melting; world knowledge is outside this particular contract.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A prompt contract states both useful output and behavior at its evidence boundary. Correct field names do not ensure supported meaning, so check semantics separately. An example flashcard can teach format without authorising invented facts. If the note contains an instruction to reveal teacher answers, the source-only learning task still does not grant that permission. Limit: Prompt wording is not an enforcement guarantee; validate actual returned content and tool permissions independently.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Write Study Buddy contracts for fields, allowed evidence, missing data and untrusted source instructions. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why should the tool not fill melting from memory even if it knows a common definition?

graphics.title: Examples and Rubrics: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional Study Buddy creates question cards from a verified animal note. Supplied facts: Approved N: a frog is an amphibian. Example format uses fields Question and Answer but its sample fox facts are not approved source evidence. Rubric requires both fields, one question and a source-supported answer. Draft asks “What is a frog?” and answers “A mammal”.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Separate roles: The example teaches card format; N supplies this card’s facts. → Format checks: Question and Answer are present, with one question. → Support check: Mammal contradicts N’s amphibian statement. → Repair content: Answer: an amphibian. Keep the same required two-field structure.

graphics.title: Keep the evidence roles separate
graphics.alt: Keep the evidence roles separate. Current sources agree | Match room IDs and claims | supported. Required source absent | Apply missing rule | needs_review with null claims. Source contains commands | Treat as evidence text | No new action authority

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Answer: an amphibian. Keep the same required two-field structure. Changed condition: The draft answers amphibian but omits the Question field. Expected result: Support passes, format completeness fails. Reason: Correct facts do not satisfy a missing mandatory field.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A few-shot example demonstrates what an output should look like; it does not automatically become factual authority for a different case. The draft satisfies layout while failing meaning. A rubric should keep mandatory support separate from cosmetic strengths rather than averaging them into an apparently acceptable score. Limit: One repaired card does not establish the prompt follows every example or generalises to unknown questions.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Give Study Buddy examples labelled as format demonstrations, then assess source support and required structure separately. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Explain why neither original nor changed draft is a full pass, and provide a complete repaired card.

graphics.title: Iterative Prompting: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional Study Buddy prompt invents a definition when approved notes omit it. Supplied facts: P asks “answer helpfully”. Revision Q adds “if approved notes lack the answer, say not supplied”. Hold model settings and four development questions fixed. P passes 1,2; Q passes 1,2,3. Case 4 still fails.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Locate failure: The target defect is unsupported answers when notes are missing. → One controlled change: Q adds the missing-evidence rule; other instructions remain fixed. → Paired results: P=2/4; Q=3/4; gain is case 3, with case 4 unresolved. → Next action: Inspect case 4 and reserve genuinely fresh questions for final evaluation.

graphics.title: Controlled prompt experiments — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Controlled prompt experiments — evidence trace. On six development cases P passes cases 1, 2, 3, 4; Q passes 1, 2, 3, 5, 6. Missing-approval cases are 4 and 6. Compare totals and condition results. | Evaluate both prompts on paired cases with fixed model/version, source records, output contract and scoring rubric. | P passes 4/6 and Q 5/6. P passes one of two missing-approval cases, Q also one of two.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Inspect case 4 and reserve genuinely fresh questions for final evaluation. Changed condition: Change model settings and note wording at the same time as the prompt. Expected result: The comparison no longer isolates the prompt revision. Reason: Several changes could explain the altered outputs; record them or run separate controlled comparisons.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: An iteration should respond to a recorded failure with a precise change. Comparing the same questions reveals whether other behavior changed too. The invented results show a development gain of one case, not a guarantee that the new instruction always works. Save prompt text, settings, source notes and case-level outcomes. Limit: Stochastic output can vary across runs; a small comparison does not prove an average effect or classroom learning benefit.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Maintain a Study Buddy experiment log linking failure, single revision and paired rubric results. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: What evidence supports improvement here, and what remains unproven?

graphics.title: Structured Output and Schemas: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional Study Buddy returns a machine-readable book fact. Supplied facts: Schema: exactly title text, pages integer, source_id text. Approved record R: River Notes, 64 pages. X={"title":"River Notes","pages":64,"source_id":"R"}; Y uses pages:"64"; Z uses pages:46 with otherwise identical fields.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Parse: Each shown object is valid JSON syntax. → Schema check: Y fails because its pages value is text, not an integer. → Meaning check: Z fits field types but contradicts R’s page count. → Accept X: X passes syntax, declared schema and source comparison.

graphics.title: Keep the evidence roles separate
graphics.alt: Keep the evidence roles separate. Generated text | JSON parse | A value or syntax error. Parsed value | Closed-schema check | Contract match or schema error. Contract-valid object | Match claims to current sources | Supported or semantic error

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: X passes syntax, declared schema and source comparison. Changed condition: Add an extra field "rating":5 to X under the exactly-fields schema. Expected result: The changed object fails schema despite keeping the correct page count. Reason: Exactly means additional fields are not allowed in this contract.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Parsing establishes that text forms a structured object. Schema checks establish required fields and types. Semantic validation compares their meaning with the approved source. These are different layers: a parseable, well-shaped object can still contain a false fact. Report the first failing layer without treating format success as factual success. Limit: Source agreement does not establish that the approved catalogue itself is correct or complete.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Validate Study Buddy outputs before another program consumes them; retain source IDs and separate syntax/type/support failures. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which object demonstrates that valid JSON and valid types are insufficient for truth?

graphics.title: Prompt Evaluation: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional Study Buddy compares two prompts across six development questions. Supplied facts: A passes cases 1,2,3,4. B passes 1,2,5,6. Cases 5 and 6 require refusing unsupported claims. Mandatory selection gate: pass both refusal cases. All cases use fixed sources and one common rubric.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Paired total: A and B both pass 4/6. → Different failures: A alone passes 3,4; B alone passes 5,6. → Mandatory slice: A passes 0/2 refusal cases; B passes 2/2. → Selection: B clears the declared gate, but its failures 3,4 remain visible.

graphics.title: Same total, different mandatory-case results
graphics.alt: Same total, different mandatory-case results. Prompt A: Total passes /6 = 4, Refusal passes /2 = 0. Prompt B: Total passes /6 = 4, Refusal passes /2 = 2.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: B clears the declared gate, but its failures 3,4 remain visible. Changed condition: Remove the gate and retain total passes as the only criterion. Expected result: The record is a tie; another predeclared tie policy or further development evidence is needed. Reason: Both prompts have four passes on six questions.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Equal totals do not imply equal behavior. The predeclared gate expresses an important requirement instead of choosing a criterion after seeing the result. Selecting B is justified under that rule, not by claiming it is best on every question. After development, freeze the chosen prompt and test new questions, including both ordinary and unsupported cases. Limit: Six invented development outcomes do not measure real model performance or prove a gain in student understanding.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Use Study Buddy case matrices with explicit priorities, source support gates and fresh final questions. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why is B’s selection defensible here without calling it universally superior?

graphics.title: Image Generation Models: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional lesson poster illustrates one family of image-generation approaches. Supplied facts: Toy 2×2 noisy numerical grid: [[0.2,0.8],[0.6,0.3]]. A specified illustrative denoising step gives [[0.1,0.9],[0.4,0.2]]. These supplied arrays illustrate steps only; they are not outputs from a real trained diffusion model.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Noisy representation: Four toy numerical cells form the starting grid. → Condition on request: A text request guides the imagined learned denoising process. → Illustrative update: Use the supplied second grid to show one change in representation. → Check provenance: Caption it as a generated-process illustration, not a photographed experiment.

graphics.title: Illustrative grids, not executed model outputs
graphics.alt: Illustrative grids, not executed model outputs. Before top: Left = 0.2, Right = 0.8. Before bottom: Left = 0.6, Right = 0.3. After top: Left = 0.1, Right = 0.9. After bottom: Left = 0.4, Right = 0.2.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Caption it as a generated-process illustration, not a photographed experiment. Changed condition: Relabel the illustration as a photograph of an actual laboratory measurement. Expected result: That caption is unsupported. Reason: Its provenance is an invented diagram of a process, not a camera record of an event.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Diffusion-style generators learn to remove noise in stages, often guided by text, but a real implementation can operate in a latent representation rather than direct pixels. The toy values let us inspect an update without pretending to simulate that trained process. An attractive final image still needs checks for labels, requested relations and factual claims. Limit: Not all image generators use diffusion; this toy step is neither a complete algorithm nor an executed model.

graphics.title: Visual Composition: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional Study Buddy requests a science-poster layout, then audits a supplied drawing description. Supplied facts: Brief: exactly two labelled bottles left of one beaker; one arrow from bottles toward beaker. Supplied drawing description: two labelled bottles are right of a beaker; an arrow points from beaker toward bottles.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Count objects: Two bottles and one beaker satisfy the count requirement. → Check position: Bottles on the right fail the required left-of relation. → Check direction: Arrow from beaker to bottles reverses the required flow. → Repair brief: Specify bottles-left, beaker-right, arrow left-to-right; verify the revised output.

graphics.title: Image generation and provenance — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Image generation and provenance — evidence trace. A fictional poster requires exactly three labelled circles. Generated image shows four circles and one unreadable label. A caption calls it a photograph of a real lesson. | Keep a provenance record containing specification, tool/version when known, generation date, edits, permissions and intended use. | It fails count and label criteria; the photograph claim is unsupported. Record it as a generated fictional illustration and revise or reject before use.
source: sections.diagram:Image generation and provenance — evidence trace

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Specify bottles-left, beaker-right, arrow left-to-right; verify the revised output. Changed condition: Move bottles left of the beaker but keep the arrow pointing from beaker toward bottles. Expected result: Position now passes; arrow direction still fails. Reason: Changing object placement does not automatically reverse an arrow’s semantic source and destination.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Having every requested object is not the same as conveying the requested relationship. Position and arrow direction can change a scientific explanation while object counts remain correct. Audit the provided description honestly: no actual image was supplied, so this evaluation concerns its stated layout rather than a claimed visual inspection. Limit: A compliant layout does not by itself verify the chemistry or procedure represented; content needs source checking.

graphics.alt: Create Study Buddy diagram rubrics covering counts, readable labels, containment, order and meaningful arrow direction. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which checks pass after that single change, and what still needs repair?

graphics.title: Speech and Audio Systems: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional learner dictates a calculation to a voice assistant. Supplied facts: Known audio phrase: “thirteen plus seven”. Transcript: “thirty plus seven”. Calculator returns 37. Synthetic voice says “thirty-seven”. The example supplies ground truth; no real audio was analysed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Recognise speech: Transcription changes thirteen into thirty. → Calculate text: 30+7=37 is correct for the mistaken transcript. → Speak result: Speech synthesis repeats 37; fluent voice does not validate the input. → Confirm intended input: Read back the recognised expression; intended 13+7=20.

graphics.title: Speech pipelines and multimodal evidence — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Speech pipelines and multimodal evidence — evidence trace. Audio transcript reads fifteen boxes; a clear written inventory says fifty boxes. The original audio is unavailable and the assistant reports fifteen as certain. | Track source modality, segment/time references, transcription, interpretation and final claims separately. Compare conflicting evidence without assuming one modality always wins. Ask for clarification when the task needs unresolved information. | There is an unresolved quantity conflict and no audio replay. Preserve both sources and ask the responsible person; certainty is unsupported.
source: sections.diagram:Speech pipelines and multimodal evidence — evidence trace

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Read back the recognised expression; intended 13+7=20. Changed condition: Correct the transcript to “thirteen plus seven” with all later stages unchanged. Expected result: The calculator and spoken result should become 20 under the declared pipeline. Reason: 13+7=20; the changed input removes the earlier recognition error.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The first error occurs before arithmetic. Blaming the calculator would target a stage that correctly processed its supplied text. Read-back or on-screen confirmation lets the user catch a number misunderstanding before action. Retain the original audio and transcript, where permitted, to separate recognition defects from later processing errors. Limit: These supplied transcript facts do not establish how an actual recogniser performs for accents, noise or different speakers.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Show Study Buddy recognised questions before calculating or retrieving important answers, especially numbers and dates. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which stage was initially wrong, and which stage was correctly operating on a wrong input?

graphics.title: Multimodal Evidence: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional Study Buddy audits a desk description and a separate caption. Supplied facts: Description: one open transparent box visibly contains three pencils; one closed opaque box hides its contents. Caption: “There are five pencils on this desk.” No other evidence reveals the closed box.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Visible evidence: Three pencils are explicitly visible in the open box. → Hidden region: The closed box’s pencil count is unknown. → Caption claim: Five total requires two additional pencils if these are the only relevant locations. → Supported response: At least three are supported; total five is not established by the description.

graphics.title: Speech pipelines and multimodal evidence — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Speech pipelines and multimodal evidence — evidence trace. Audio transcript reads fifteen boxes; a clear written inventory says fifty boxes. The original audio is unavailable and the assistant reports fifteen as certain. | Track source modality, segment/time references, transcription, interpretation and final claims separately. Compare conflicting evidence without assuming one modality always wins. Ask for clarification when the task needs unresolved information. | There is an unresolved quantity conflict and no audio replay. Preserve both sources and ask the responsible person; certainty is unsupported.
source: sections.diagram:Speech pipelines and multimodal evidence — evidence trace

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: At least three are supported; total five is not established by the description. Changed condition: Open the closed box and a verified observation shows two pencils inside, with no other desk locations. Expected result: The total is now supported as five. Reason: 3 visible initially plus 2 newly observed gives 5 under the complete-location assumption.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A caption is another claim, not a way of seeing through an opaque object. Keep observable information separate from inferences. The visible three give a lower bound under the stated desk scope; there is no supplied maximum for the closed box. Do not replace unknown contents with zero merely because none are visible. Limit: The conclusion depends on the supplied description’s accuracy; no actual image inspection or exhaustive room inventory was performed.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Label Study Buddy claims by their visual, audio or text evidence and retain uncertainty when modalities omit information. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Why were both “exactly three” and “exactly five” unsupported before opening the box?

graphics.title: Hallucination Failure Types: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional Study Buddy drafts a field-trip summary from one approved record. Supplied facts: Source S: trail length 12 km; planned constant speed 4 km/h, excluding stops; departure 09:00. Draft: “The walk takes two hours, starts at 09:00 and includes free lunch.” No lunch record is supplied.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Compute duration: 12÷4=3 hours, excluding stops. → Contradicted claim: Two-hour duration disagrees with the calculation from S. → Supported claim: Departure 09:00 is stated in S. → Unsupported claim: Free lunch has no source; missing evidence is not a confirmed no-lunch fact.

graphics.title: Generation failures and verification — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Generation failures and verification — evidence trace. Source R says room B seats 12 and the meeting starts at 15:00. Generated answer says B seats 20, starts at 15:00 and includes free lunch. | Split an answer into atomic claims. For each, record the exact source passage, support status and any needed calculation. Mark unsupported and contradicted claims separately; do not repair them by inventing sources. | Capacity 20 is contradicted; 15:00 is supported; free lunch is unsupported. One of three claims has support. The missing lunch fact is not evidence of no lunch.
source: sections.diagram:Generation failures and verification — evidence trace

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Free lunch has no source; missing evidence is not a confirmed no-lunch fact. Changed condition: Add a planned 30-minute stop while preserving speed and distance. Expected result: Planned total elapsed time becomes 3.5 hours. Reason: Three moving hours plus half an hour stopped; walking-time calculation itself stays three.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Different errors need different repairs. Recalculate the duration; keep the supported departure; remove or seek evidence for lunch. These categories are more informative than calling the whole answer wrong. Arithmetic inherits assumptions such as constant speed and no stops, so avoid turning the three-hour walking calculation into a guaranteed arrival time. Limit: The fictional plan does not establish actual speed, delays or what eventually occurred on a real trip.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Audit Study Buddy outputs claim by claim, recording contradiction, missing support and correct calculations separately. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Can we conclude there will definitely be no lunch from S alone?

graphics.title: Source Quality: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional Study Buddy answers which room a club is authorised to use. Supplied facts: Signed notice A: Hall 1 from day 1. Signed amendment B references A and changes to Hall 3 effective day 8. An old copy of A is reuploaded on day 10. B remains the authoritative amendment. Queries concern day 6 and day 9.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Check authority: B is a signed amendment to A, not an unrelated comment. → Day 6: Before effective day 8, authorised room is Hall 1. → Day 9: From day 8 onward, authorised room is Hall 3. → Ignore upload shortcut: Reuploading old A on day 10 does not revoke B.

graphics.title: Conflicting and time-sensitive sources — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Conflicting and time-sensitive sources — evidence trace. Notice N says room A from Monday. Signed amendment M references N and changes to B effective Wednesday. Query asks Tuesday, then Thursday. | For this toy task a signed amendment supersedes the referenced original from its effective time. Keep both records. A newer timestamp alone has no authority unless the policy grants it. | Tuesday uses A; Thursday uses B. The amendment effective time, not merely upload order, determines the change.
source: sections.diagram:Conflicting and time-sensitive sources — evidence trace

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Reuploading old A on day 10 does not revoke B. Changed condition: A signed amendment C explicitly revokes B effective day 12 and restores Hall 1. Expected result: Day 9 stays Hall 3; day 13 becomes Hall 1. Reason: The new authoritative change applies from its stated effective date, not retroactively.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A source’s upload time and the time its rule takes effect answer different questions. Preserve version relationships and the query’s intended date. The current authoritative chain gives a consistent answer to both queries. A later filename or timestamp alone cannot establish that an old record supersedes a signed amendment. Limit: Authority is declared in this fictional case; real conflicting sources may require the responsible owner’s review.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: Store Study Buddy source identity, version, authority and effective date, especially for schedules or changing classroom rules. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which source fields must be checked before answering day 9?

graphics.title: Verify Numbers and Dates: the case
graphics.alt: A fictional Study Buddy checks a science-club summary against supplied counts and calendar facts. Supplied facts: Record: 15 of 20 fictional model trials passed. Draft: “70% passed; the meeting is on June 31.” June has 30 days. No authoritative record gives the intended meeting date.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Check denominator: There are 15 passes out of 20 total trials. → Calculate percentage: 15÷20×100=75%, not 70%. → Validate date: June 31 is invalid because June has 30 days. → Resolve missing intent: Ask the event owner for the correct date; do not assume June 30 or July 1.

graphics.title: Claim support and citation evaluation — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Claim support and citation evaluation — evidence trace. An answer has four factual claims. Three have citations, but only two are supported by their cited passages. All links exist. | For this classroom rubric count a claim as supported only when its cited passage entails it. | Claim support is 2/4=50%; citation presence is 3/4=75%; link existence among three citations is 3/3. These measure different failures.
source: sections.diagram:Claim support and citation evaluation — evidence trace

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Ask the event owner for the correct date; do not assume June 30 or July 1. Changed condition: The count is revised to 14 passes out of 20, but no date record is added. Expected result: 70% now matches the count; June 31 remains invalid and unresolved. Reason: 14÷20×100=70%; changing a count provides no new calendar evidence.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A percentage requires the correct numerator and denominator. Calendar validation identifies an impossible date, but it cannot discover what date the author intended. These checks use different evidence: arithmetic repairs the percentage from the supplied counts, while the date needs another authoritative source before publication. Limit: This check confirms internal arithmetic and date validity, not whether the fictional trial measurements themselves were reliable.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project

Supported question: Which part can be corrected immediately from existing evidence, and which needs follow-up?

graphics.title: Model Memory vs Retrieval: the case
graphics.alt: The library assistant remembers an old opening time, but a current notice can be retrieved. Supplied facts: Approved notice LIB-v = 2 says Wednesday closes at 16: 00; the model previously produced 15: 00. The question asks the current Wednesday closing time. All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Old guess: A remembered-looking answer says 15: 00; no current notice is attached. → Find notice: Retrieve authorised LIB-v = 2, which explicitly says Wednesday closes at 16: 00. → Ground answer: Answer 16: 00 and attach LIB-v = 2. Its words, rather than the earlier guess, support this claim.

graphics.title: Retrieval and indexing — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Retrieval and indexing — evidence trace. Index v1 contains notice N1 for room A. Corpus v2 supersedes it with N2 for room B, but the query still returns N1. What can be reported? | Assign stable document IDs, versions and permitted access before indexing. Retrieve only authorised records. Preserve source references and define behaviour when a document is missing, outdated or access-restricted. | The stale index returns old evidence. It cannot establish current room approval; refresh against authorised corpus v2 or report unresolved freshness.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Answer 16: 00 and attach LIB-v = 2. Its words, rather than the earlier guess, support this claim. Changed condition: LIB-v = 2 is unavailable. Expected result: Report that the current time cannot be verified. Reason: The unsupported old guess does not become current evidence when retrieval fails.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Read the picture in order. Answer 16: 00 and attach LIB-v = 2. Its words, rather than the earlier guess, support this claim. The arrows show which recorded input or intermediate result each decision uses. Explain the deciding step aloud before checking the changed case; pointing to the final answer alone does not show how it follows. Limit: A retrieved document can itself be wrong or outdated; source approval, date and scope still need checking.

graphics.title: Retrieval Augmented Generation: the case
graphics.alt: Turn a short science source into an answer with a visible claim-to-source map. Supplied facts: Approved note S4 says: ice is solid water; warming can melt ice into liquid water. No temperature or speed is supplied. All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Read source: S4 supports the material identity and the solid-to-liquid change. → Draft two claims: Draft: ice is solid water; warming can turn it into liquid water. → Check each claim: Both claims match S4. A claim that melting takes exactly two minutes would not match.

graphics.title: Building a grounded answer — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Building a grounded answer — evidence trace. Current source P approves room C; Q lists C capacity 10. Draft says room C is approved, seats 10 and offers lunch. | Build a claim-evidence table before final wording. Preserve source versions and qualifiers, omit unsupported claims or explicitly state the gap, then validate the answer against the table. | Approval and capacity are supported by P and Q; lunch lacks evidence. A grounded answer reports the first two claims and does not invent lunch.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Both claims match S4. A claim that melting takes exactly two minutes would not match. Changed condition: The question asks exactly how long this ice takes to melt. Expected result: Say that S4 does not provide a time. Reason: A general change of state does not determine a duration for an unspecified sample.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Read the picture in order. Both claims match S4. A claim that melting takes exactly two minutes would not match. The arrows show which recorded input or intermediate result each decision uses. Explain the deciding step aloud before checking the changed case; pointing to the final answer alone does not show how it follows. Limit: This source-grounding exercise does not establish that every source is complete or scientifically authoritative.

graphics.title: User Need and AI Contribution: the case
graphics.alt: Define a useful reading helper before choosing its AI features. Supplied facts: A pupil needs the meaning of unfamiliar words in an approved glossary. graphics.title: Prototype a Grounded Assistant: the case
graphics.alt: Build a minimal grounded study answer with checks between retrieval and display. Supplied facts: Source PL2: seedlings need water. Source PL3: this activity checks soil daily. graphics.alt: Retrieve evidence: PL3 directly supports the daily soil-check claim; PL2 supplies a different fact. → Match question: Choose the activity’s soil check, not a general watering recommendation. → Validate draft: Display “This activity checks soil daily [PL3]”; reject an invented twice-daily watering schedule.

graphics.title: Representing inputs as vectors: the case
graphics.alt: Encode the same pixel measurements in a fixed vector order. Supplied facts: Toy image features are [left_brightness, right_brightness], each = 0..10. ImageA has left2, right7; imageB has left7, right2. All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Declare coordinate order: Coordinate0 is left brightness; coordinate1 is right brightness. → Encode both images: A becomes [2, 7]; B becomes [7, 2]. Their sums match but their spatial patterns differ. → Check input contract: Use the same order when training and predicting; record missing measurements rather than guessing.

graphics.title: An input vector keeps an agreed order
graphics.alt: An input vector keeps an agreed order. D width 50 mm | Divide width by 10 | First component 5. D height 30 mm | Divide height by 10 | Second component 3. Schema width then height | Keep named positions | Vector [5, 3] in cm
source: sections.diagram:An input vector keeps an agreed order

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Use the same order when training and predicting; record missing measurements rather than guessing. Changed condition: Swap only A’s vector order before prediction. Expected result: The encoded input becomes [7, 2], numerically identical to B’s original input. Reason: Changing coordinate order changes feature meaning even if the numbers are unchanged.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A vector is an ordered list, so the position of a number carries meaning. Here the first number always means left brightness. Adding the two measurements keeps total brightness but discards which side is brighter. A network receives the representation we give it; it cannot recover a lost distinction just because it has more layers. Limit: These two features are simplified measurements, not a complete image representation or evidence of learned vision.

graphics.title: Dot products and weighted sums: the case
graphics.alt: Draw each input’s contribution to a toy weighted brightness score. Supplied facts: Inputs [2, 5]; weights [3,-1]; no bias. Score is 2×3+5×(-1). All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Multiply first input: Left contribution=2×3=6. → Multiply second input: Right contribution=5×(-1)=-5. → Add contributions: Weighted sum=6-5=1; this is a score, not a probability.

graphics.title: Weighted brightness score
graphics.alt: Weighted brightness score. Inputs: [2, 5]; weights: [3, -1]; bias: 0; activation: identity; output: 1.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Weighted sum=6-5=1; this is a score, not a probability. Changed condition: Increase only the right input from 5 to6. Expected result: The score becomes6-6=0. Reason: The right weight is-1, so adding1 to that input lowers the score by1.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A weight controls how strongly an input contributes to the score. The left connection adds three times its measurement; the negative right connection subtracts its measurement. Calculate each contribution before adding them. This dot product is a signed score; it becomes a probability only if a separate, justified transformation and interpretation are supplied. Limit: These declared weights are hand-chosen toy parameters; no network training or calibrated probability is claimed.

graphics.title: Bias terms and decision boundaries: the case
graphics.alt: Move a toy boundary with a bias while keeping its input weights fixed. Supplied facts: Score z=2u-v-3; predict class 1 when z>=0. InputsA=[2, 1], B=[1, 1]. All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Trace input A: A score=4-1-3=0, so class 1 at the declared inclusive boundary. → Trace input B: B score=2-1-3=-2, so class 0. → Read boundary: The boundary is v=2u-3; the bias sets its position.

graphics.title: Input A reaches the inclusive boundary
graphics.alt: Input A reaches the inclusive boundary. Inputs: [2, 1]; weights: [2, -1]; bias: -3; activation: identity; output: 0.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: The boundary is v=2u-3; the bias sets its position. Changed condition: Change bias from-3 to-1. Expected result: A score becomes2 and B score 0; both predict class 1. Reason: Increasing bias by2 adds2 to every score without changing the weights.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The bias adds the same offset after the input contributions. It moves the dividing line without changing the weights that set the line’s orientation. Class 1 includes score zero under our stated rule. That is why B changes class when the bias rises by two: its score moves from minus two onto the included boundary. Limit: A linear boundary is a toy classifier rule. Raw score size does not automatically describe confidence or probability.

graphics.title: Activation functions: the case
graphics.alt: See what ReLU removes before the next weighted step. Supplied facts: Toy network z=x-3; h=max(0, z); y=3h+2. Inputs x=1, 3, 4. All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Compute preactivation: z values are-2, 0, 1. → Apply ReLU: h values are 0, 0, 1; the negative value is replaced by0. → Compute output: y values are2, 2, 5; x = 1 and x = 3 collapse to the same output.

graphics.title: ReLU hidden computation at x=1
graphics.alt: ReLU hidden computation at x=1. Inputs: [1]; weights: [1]; bias: -3; activation: relu; output: 0.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: y values are2, 2, 5; x = 1 and x = 3 collapse to the same output. Changed condition: Replace ReLU with identity. Expected result: h becomes-2, 0, 1 and outputs become-4, 2, 5. Reason: Identity retains the negative intermediate value instead of clipping it.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: ReLU means keep a positive value and replace a negative one with zero. The output layer receives that transformed value, not the original input. Inputs one and three therefore both deliver zero to the final layer and produce two. Replacing ReLU with identity changes the procedure: negative intermediate values now remain available to the next layer. Limit: ReLU is one activation choice. Clipping negatives does not itself train the network or prove useful representation.

graphics.alt: First hidden unit: u-2=2, so h1=2. → Second hidden unit: v-1=2, so h2=2. → Compose output: y=2-2=0; the output uses activated hidden values, not raw inputs.

graphics.title: Complete each stage before using its output

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Composition means one layer’s result becomes the next layer’s input. Compute both hidden units before combining them. At [4,3], their equal outputs cancel. Lowering only the second input removes its positive hidden contribution, so subtracting it no longer reduces the output. The final subtraction must use activated hidden values rather than the raw measurements. Limit: Hand-composed detectors illustrate layer order; they are not evidence of a learned or biologically realistic neural mechanism.

graphics.title: Trainable parameter count
graphics.alt: Trainable parameter count. input to hidden: weights = 6, biases = 3, total = 9. hidden to output: weights = 3, biases = 1, total = 4.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.

The three hidden outputs connect to one output unit through three more weights. ReLU applies a fixed function and adds no adjustable parameter here. Architecture determines the connection pattern; learned values occupy those connections. Limit: Parameter count describes capacity and storage structure, not accuracy, intelligence or guaranteed generalisation.

graphics.alt: Compare candidate losses with the same targets and denominator. Supplied facts: Targets [1, 3]; A predicts [0, 4]; B predicts [1, 5]. Use MSE over both cases. All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: MSE comparison on shared targets
graphics.alt: MSE comparison on shared targets. Units: squared target units. model A: 1. model B: 2.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: A wins under MSE; both MAEs equal1. Changed condition: Choose MAE instead of MSE as the sole criterion. Expected result: A and B tie at MAE1. Reason: Squared error penalises B’s concentrated error more, while absolute errors both sum 2.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: For this loss calculation, the signed error is prediction minus target. MSE squares each error before averaging; MAE takes its absolute value. A spreads its error equally across both cases, while B concentrates it in one case. Squaring makes the larger individual error count more. State the objective before selecting a model, because these two objectives give different comparisons. Limit: Training loss is not automatically a held-out performance estimate or a complete measure of use consequences.

graphics.title: Slopes and local change: the case
graphics.alt: Use a local slope to propose a small move rather than claiming every move helps. Supplied facts: Toy loss J(a)=(a-2)². At a = 0, use symmetric step 0.5. All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps

graphics.title: Compare slope clues on the same loss curve
graphics.alt: Compare slope clues on the same loss curve. 1 | -2 | Increase w a little. 2 | 0 | No first order direction. 3 | 2 | Decrease w a little
source: sections.diagram:Compare slope clues on the same loss curve

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Move to a = 0.25: loss 3.0625, below starting loss 4. Changed condition: Move from 0 all the way to5. Expected result: Loss becomes9, exceeding the starting4. Reason: A negative local slope suggests increasing a locally, not that every positive jump decreases loss.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A slope describes how the loss changes near the current parameter. The symmetric calculation compares equal small moves on either side. Its negative result suggests a small increase may help at zero. It does not promise every increase helps: jumping to five passes the optimum at two and produces a larger loss. Check the new loss after each proposed step. Limit: A finite difference approximates local change; numerical precision and nonsmooth points need care in more complex objectives.

graphics.alt: Check each coordinate of a gradient while holding the other parameter fixed. Supplied facts: Model y=2w+b, target 3. At [w, b]=[1, 0], y = 2, residual y-target=-1; loss is residual². All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Check w direction: Analytic derivative2×residual×2=-4. → Check b direction: Analytic derivative2×residual=-2. → Numerical check: With step 0.1: w losses 0.64, 1.44 give -4; b losses 0.81, 1.21 give -2.

graphics.title: Two separate probes at one parameter vector
graphics.alt: Two separate probes at one parameter vector. w near 1 | b is 0 and x is 2 | First entry -4. b near 0 | w is 1 and x is 2 | Second entry -2. Assemble in order [w, b] | Same original model | Gradient [-4, -2]
source: sections.diagram:Two separate probes at one parameter vector

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: With step 0.1: w losses 0.64, 1.44 give -4; b losses 0.81, 1.21 give -2. Changed condition: Swap the two gradient components in the program output. Expected result: The coordinate-wise numerical check exposes the mismatch. Reason: The w perturbation changes y twice as strongly as the same b perturbation.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A gradient lists the slope for each parameter, in a declared order. Changing w by a small amount changes the prediction twice as much as changing b by the same amount. That explains the different derivative magnitudes. Perturb one coordinate while holding the other fixed, then compare the numerical slope with its analytic counterpart. Limit: The exact agreement occurs for this quadratic toy case; finite differences in larger models involve rounding and step-size limits.

graphics.title: Updating parameters: the case
graphics.alt: Use one explicit gradient update and then recompute the loss. Supplied facts: Model y=2w+b, target 5. Start w=1, b=1; learning rate 0.05. Initial y=3, error y−target=−2, squared loss 4. All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Compute gradient: Gradient for [w, b]=[2×(-2)×2, 2×(-2)]=[-8,-4]. → Update simultaneously: New w=1-0.05×(-8)=1.4; new b=1.2. → Check new loss: New y=4, residual -1, loss 1: lower than4.

graphics.title: Loss before and after rate 0.05 update
graphics.alt: Loss before and after rate 0.05 update. Units: squared error. before: 4. after: 1.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: New y=4, residual -1, loss 1: lower than4. Changed condition: Set learning rate 0.2 from the same starting point. Expected result: New w=2.6, b=1.8, y=7, squared loss 4: no improvement. Reason: The larger update jumps to an equally distant point on the opposite side of the target.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Gradient descent subtracts learning rate times gradient. A negative gradient makes this subtraction increase the parameter. Compute both gradients at the original [w,b] before updating either one. The small step brings the prediction closer to five, reducing squared error. A larger step can cross the target and undo that gain, so the new prediction and loss must be recalculated. Limit: One successful toy update is not evidence of convergence for a real network or generalisation to unseen data.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Freeze hidden step: h=3 for this pair; only v is trainable. → Compute initial gradient: Loss9; gradient 2(3v-3)×3=-18 at v=0. → Update and verify: v becomes1; prediction 3 and loss 0. Next gradient is 0.

graphics.title: One full-data update from v is 1
graphics.alt: One full-data update from v is 1. Forward and loss | Predictions [1, 2] for targets [2, 4] | Errors [-1, -2], MSE 2.5. Gradient | 2 times (-1 times 1 - 2 times 2) / 2 | Gradient -5. Update with rate 0.1 | 1 - 0.1 times -5 | Next v is 1.5

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: v becomes1; prediction 3 and loss 0. Next gradient is 0. Changed condition: Change target from 3 to6 and restart v = 0 with the same rate. Expected result: First gradient=-36; v becomes2; prediction 6 and loss 0. Reason: The hidden value remains3, but the target residual and required output weight double.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Only the output weight v is being fitted in this toy network; the hidden ReLU is fixed. The training input gives hidden value three. Squared-error slope points v from zero towards one, and this specially chosen rate reaches one in a single update. Zero loss on one training pair is exact fitting of that pair, not evidence about other inputs. Limit: A zero loss on one example is memorised fit to that example, not proof of a generally useful image classifier.

graphics.title: Batching and epochs: the case
graphics.alt: Show why an epoch’s example order can matter for single-example updates. Supplied facts: Toy y=wx, rate 0.1, squared loss, start w = 0. Training A=(x = 1, target 2), B=(x = 2, target 0). All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: A then B: A gradient -4 gives w = 0.4; B gradient 3.2 then gives w = 0.08. → Restart and reverse: B at w=0 has gradient 0; A then gives w = 0.4. → Compare full batch: At w = 0 mean gradient=(-4+0)/2=-2; one full-batch update gives w = 0.2.

graphics.title: One pass can contain different numbers of updates
graphics.alt: One pass can contain different numbers of updates. A then B separately | 0 to 0.4 to 1.68 | 2. A and B together | 0 to 1 | 1. B then A separately | 0 to 1.6 to 1.68 | 2
source: sections.diagram:One pass can contain different numbers of updates

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: At w = 0 mean gradient=(-4+0)/2=-2; one full-batch update gives w = 0.2. Changed condition: Use only one full-batch update after reversing record order. Expected result: The updated weight remains 0.2. Reason: The same mean of the two starting gradients is unchanged by their order.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A single-example update changes the weight before the next example’s gradient is calculated. Reversing the example order can therefore change the path. A full-batch update computes both gradients at the same starting weight and averages them before changing that weight. The distinction is when the update occurs, not whether the examples have different labels. Limit: Different order effects do not mean a universally better batching strategy; compare declared schedules and budgets fairly.

graphics.alt: Compare learning rates with identical starting loss and update counts. Supplied facts: Loss J(a)=(a-4)²; gradient 2(a-4); start a =  = 0. Compare two updates at rates0.25 and 0.75. graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Rate0.25: First a = 2, loss 4; second a = 3, loss 1. → Rate0.75: First a = 6, loss 4; second a = 3, loss 1. → Inspect paths: Both end at 3 and loss 1; larger rate crosses the optimum while smaller rate stays below it.

graphics.title: The update factor explains three behaviours
graphics.alt: The update factor explains three behaviours. 0.05 gives 0.75 | Same side and shrinking | Multiplied by 0.5625. 0.3 gives -0.5 | Alternating and shrinking | Multiplied by 0.25. 0.5 gives -1.5 | Alternating and growing | Multiplied by 2.25
source: sections.diagram:The update factor explains three behaviours

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Both end at 3 and loss 1; larger rate crosses the optimum while smaller rate stays below it. Changed condition: Add a rate 1 run from a = 0. Expected result: Its path is 8 then 0, with loss 16 at both steps. Reason: The update alternates across4 without reducing the initial loss.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Keep the starting parameter and update budget identical to compare rates fairly. Rate one-quarter approaches the optimum from below; rate three-quarters crosses it and comes back. Their final losses happen to match after two updates, despite different paths. Rate one repeatedly overshoots by the same distance, so using the correct gradient alone does not ensure improvement. Limit: These quadratic paths explain step size. Real nonconvex networks can have more complicated rate behaviour.

graphics.alt: Plot training and validation loss for checkpoints before opening final cases. Supplied facts: Supplied checkpoint losses: epoch 1 train4, val3; epoch 2 train2, val2; epoch 3 train1, val2.5. Selection: smallest validation loss. All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Read training curve: Training loss falls4→2→1. → Read validation curve: Validation loss falls3→2 then rises to2.5. → Choose checkpoint: Select epoch 2, not epoch 3, under the declared validation criterion.

graphics.title: Checkpoint losses
graphics.alt: Checkpoint losses. epoch 1: training = 4, validation = 3. epoch 2: training = 2, validation = 2. epoch 3: training = 1, validation = 2.5.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Select epoch 2, not epoch 3, under the declared validation criterion. Changed condition: Epoch3 validation loss is instead1.5. Expected result: Select epoch 3 under the unchanged criterion. Reason: Its measured validation loss is now below epoch 2’s2; the training curve alone never settled selection.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: The training curve measures fit to examples used for learning. The validation curve measures a separate set used to choose a checkpoint. The final training loss is smallest here, but its validation loss has risen. Under the supplied selection rule, keep checkpoint two. A later final test must remain outside both learning and checkpoint selection. Limit: A single curve has sampling and run variability; validation-selected checkpoints still require untouched final evidence.

graphics.title: Regularisation and early stopping: the case
graphics.alt: Separate a regularisation penalty from prediction loss and an early-stopping rule. Supplied facts: Toy objective J(a)=(a-3)²+2a²; start a = 0; gradient 6a-6; rate 1/6. Separate validation losses:[5, 3, 3, 4], patience 1, no ties as improvement. All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Regularised update: At 0 gradient -6; update gives a = 1. → Split objective: At 1 prediction term 4, penalty 2, total 6; at 0 total 9. → Early-stop separately: Best validation checkpoint is 2 with loss 3; checkpoint 3 is no improvement, so stop at 3.

graphics.title: Patience two with strict improvement
graphics.alt: Patience two with strict improvement. 0 then 1 then 2 | 4 then 2 then 1.5 | Save each improved state. 3 then 4 | 1.6 then 1.4 | Wait once then reset. 5 then 6 | 1.45 then 1.46 | Two misses so stop at 6

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Best validation checkpoint is 2 with loss 3; checkpoint 3 is no improvement, so stop at 3. Changed condition: Change patience from 1 to2 under the same tie rule. Expected result: Stop at checkpoint 4; still restore checkpoint 2. Reason: Checkpoints 3 and 4 are two consecutive non-improvements; a later stop does not redefine the best checkpoint.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Regularisation adds a parameter penalty to the training objective. Here it discourages large a, so the objective balances prediction error against that penalty. Early stopping is a different decision based on the supplied validation sequence. A tied validation loss is not improvement under this policy; stop when the patience allowance is used and restore the best checkpoint. Limit: Regularisation and early stopping are different tools; neither guarantees better performance in every dataset.

graphics.alt: Reproduce two training traces by saving their distinct initial values. Supplied facts: LossJ(a)=(a-2)²; gradient 2(a-2); rate 0.25; two updates. Restart from a = 0 and separately a = 4. All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Start from 0: Updates: a = 1 then 1.5; final loss 0.25. → Start from 4: Updates: a = 3 then 2.5; final loss 0.25. → Record experiment: Save initial values, rate, objective and update count; the same final loss hides different parameter paths.

graphics.title: Identical units receive identical updates
graphics.alt: Identical units receive identical updates. First ReLU unit | u is 1 and a is 1 | u is 0.8 and a is 0.8. Second ReLU unit | v is 1 and b is 1 | v is 0.8 and b is 0.8

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Save initial values, rate, objective and update count; the same final loss hides different parameter paths. Changed condition: Repeat the a = 0 run with identical arithmetic and settings. Expected result: It again reaches1 then 1.5 in this deterministic toy calculation. Reason: Identical initial state and update rules determine the same arithmetic trace.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Initialisation supplies the parameter values before learning begins. The same update rule can follow different paths from different starts. Here the two paths end on opposite sides of two and have equal squared distance, so equal loss does not imply equal parameters. Save initial values and settings to reproduce this arithmetic, as well as the final result. Limit: A saved seed alone does not reproduce every software or hardware execution; record environment and nondeterminism too.

graphics.title: Debugging shapes and gradients: the case
graphics.alt: Catch a gradient -order bug before the optimiser changes parameters. Supplied facts: Toy y=2a+3c, target 4, start [a, c]=[1, 0]. Loss (y-4)². Program claims gradient [-12,-8] in order [a, c]. All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Compute correct gradient: y = 2, residual -2: gradient [-8,-12], not [-12,-8]. → Check coordinates: Step 0.1: a losses 3.24, 4.84 give -8; c losses 2.89, 5.29 give -12. → Apply correct update: At rate 0.01: new [a, c]=[1.08, 0.12]; y = 2.52, loss 2.1904.

graphics.title: Repair from the first disagreement
graphics.alt: Repair from the first disagreement. Input and dimensions | x length 2 W 3 by 2 b length 3 | Dimensions match. Scores before ReLU | [1, 2, 0] | [1, 2, -1]. Hidden activations | [1, 2, 0] | [1, 2, 0]

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: At rate 0.01: new [a, c]=[1.08, 0.12]; y = 2.52, loss 2.1904. Changed condition: The program changes its declared order to [c, a] and returns [-12,-8]. Expected result: That vector now matches the declared coordinate order. Reason: Gradient values are meaningful only when their parameter names and array positions agree.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Array shape and coordinate meaning both matter. A vector with two entries can have the right length but assign each derivative to the wrong parameter. Label the entries a and c, then perturb one coordinate at a time to check their slopes. Repairing the coordinate mapping is necessary before using the gradient to update the network. Limit: A correct gradient at one point does not establish every batch, shape or activation path is implemented correctly.

graphics.title: Learned representations: the case
graphics.alt: See when a representation preserves a distinction and when it destroys it. Supplied facts: Toy input [left, right]; representation h=[ReLU(left-right), ReLU(right-left)]. A=[5, 2]; B=[2, 5]; target is left-brighter versus right-brighter. All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Encode A: A becomes [3, 0], with left brighter. → Encode B: B becomes [0, 3], with right brighter. → Compare collapsed summary: If the head receives only h1+h2, both become3 and the target distinction is lost.

graphics.title: A representation can preserve direction
graphics.alt: A representation can preserve direction. A: left = 5, right = 2, h1 = 3, h2 = 0. B: left = 2, right = 5, h1 = 0, h2 = 3.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: If the head receives only h1+h2, both become3 and the target distinction is lost. Changed condition: The head keeps both ordered hidden values instead of their sum. Expected result: It can distinguish [3, 0] from [0, 3] in this example. Reason: The representation retains the direction of brightness difference when coordinates stay separate.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A hidden representation decides which distinctions remain available to an output head. These two hidden coordinates preserve whether the left or right side is brighter. Adding them discards that direction and gives both examples the same scalar. A deterministic head cannot assign different labels to identical inputs; retain the distinction or change the task. Limit: This is a hand-chosen representation, not evidence that a trained image model actually learned these units.

graphics.title: Image tensors and channels: the case
graphics.alt: Move colour values between tensor layouts without changing the pixels. Supplied facts: Toy RGB image has 2 rows, 1 column. Top pixel [1, 4, 7]; bottom [2, 5, 8]. HWC means height, width, channel. All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Record HWC shape: Shape is [2, 1, 3]; top green is 4 and bottom green5. → Reorder to CHW: Shape [3, 2, 1]; red plane [[1],[2]], green [[4],[5]], blue [[7],[8]]. → Check same pixel: Bottom green is HWC [1, 0, 1]=5 and CHW [1, 1, 0]=5.

graphics.title: Two RGB pixels before layout conversion
graphics.alt: Two RGB pixels before layout conversion. top pixel: red = 1, green = 4, blue = 7. bottom pixel: red = 2, green = 5, blue = 8.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Bottom green is HWC [1, 0, 1]=5 and CHW [1, 1, 0]=5. Changed condition: Add a batch containing three identical images in NHWC layout. Expected result: Batch shape is [3, 2, 1, 3]. Reason: The new first dimension counts images; it does not add a fourth colour channel.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A tensor is an array with named dimensions. HWC orders height, width and colour; CHW puts colour first. Rearranging the layout changes where values are stored, not the colour measurement itself. Trace a named pixel through both layouts using zero-based indices. Adding a batch dimension counts images and does not add a new colour channel. Limit: Shape consistency does not prove correct colour order or value range; document channel names and preprocessing.

graphics.title: Convolution as a local operation: the case
graphics.alt: Draw the exact patch-by-patch arithmetic of a local image operation. Supplied facts: Image rows [1, 2, 3],[4, 5, 6]; kernel rows [1, 0],[0,-1]. Use unflipped kernel, no padding, stride1, bias0. All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: First patch: 1×1+2×0+4×0+5×(-1)=-4. → Second patch: 2×1+3×0+5×0+6×(-1)=-4. → Feature map: Output shape1×2 and map [[-4,-4]]; the same kernel is reused at each position.

graphics.title: Image used by both local kernel windows
graphics.alt: Image used by both local kernel windows. row0: col0 = 1, col1 = 2, col2 = 3. row1: col0 = 4, col1 = 5, col2 = 6.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Output shape1×2 and map [[-4,-4]]; the same kernel is reused at each position. Changed condition: Add shared bias2 after each patch sum. Expected result: Feature map becomes [[-2,-2]]. Reason: Bias adds2 to each output; it does not change patch products or output shape.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A local kernel combines the values in one small image window with a fixed set of weights. Slide that same kernel to the next valid window and repeat the products. Sharing weights lets the operation look for the same local pattern at different positions. This example declares an unflipped kernel; adding bias changes each window result without changing which pixels were used. Limit: A local filter detects a numerical pattern; one feature map does not establish recognition or learned visual understanding.

graphics.title: Pooling and spatial information: the case
graphics.alt: Pool a small map and show the detail it cannot retain. Supplied facts: Feature map rows [1, 4, 2, 0],[3, 2, 5, 1]. Pool non-overlapping2×2 windows, stride2, no padding. All inputs and outcomes in this worked example are invented classroom data; no real model run is claimed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Left window: Values1, 4, 3, 2: max 4, mean 2.5. → Right window: Values2, 0, 5, 1: max 5, mean 2. → Compare summaries: Max map [[4, 5]], mean map [[2.5, 2]], both shape1×2.

graphics.title: Two adjacent pooling windows
graphics.alt: Two adjacent pooling windows. row0: left0 = 1, left1 = 4, right0 = 2, right1 = 0. row1: left0 = 3, left1 = 2, right0 = 5, right1 = 1.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Max map [[4, 5]], mean map [[2.5, 2]], both shape1×2. Changed condition: Swap1 and 4 within the left window. Expected result: Both pooled maps remain unchanged. Reason: Max and mean ignore the positions of values inside the same window.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Pooling compresses each local window into a summary. Maximum keeps its largest value; mean keeps its average. Neither summary records where each value appeared. Swapping values inside one window leaves both summaries unchanged here, so the pooled output cannot reconstruct the original arrangement. The chosen window, stride and boundary policy determine the output shape. Limit: Pooling is a declared aggregation, not automatic improvement; losing location can harm tasks that need precise positions.

graphics.alt: First update: Gradient2(2a-2)×2=-8; new a =  = 0.5, training loss 1. → Second update: Gradient at 0.5 is-4; new a =  = 0.75, training loss 0.25. → Validation score: At reserved d1, target 1: prediction 0.75, squared error0.0625.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit

graphics.alt: Measure embedding neighbours without turning numerical proximity into factual certainty. Supplied facts: Toy tableP=[0, 1], Q=[3, 1], R=[1, 4]; query [1, 1].
