Supported question: Explain why retrieval success permits the checked 15:00 fallback when drafting fails. What changes if retrieval fails too, and why can a template not fill that evidence gap?

graphics.title: Capstone release review: the case
graphics.alt: Review every mandatory gate. A capstone release needs factual, access and deletion gates to pass. Supplied facts: Factual and access checks pass. Deletion fails because a listed backup remains. All three gates are mandatory.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: List evidence: Record two passes and the specific deletion failure. → Apply decision rule: Block release; a majority of passes is insufficient. → Specify repair: Remove the listed copy and verify it before a fresh review.

graphics.title: Capstone release review — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Capstone release review — evidence trace. Ordinary cases18/20 pass; access all pass; no effects; rollback not tested. | Toy release requires all access tests, no unauthorised effects, at least90% ordinary-case pass and a compatible rollback rehearsal. | 90% ordinary threshold met but rollback evidence missing, so release is not ready. Absence of a failure report is not a passed rehearsal.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Remove the listed copy and verify it before a fresh review. Changed condition: Every listed deletion location passes new verification. Expected result: That gate can pass; review the complete current evidence before approving release. Reason: One repaired gate does not automatically refresh evidence for every other gate.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Release review applies explicit conditions to a specific candidate version. Completed coding is not evidence that all operational obligations are satisfied. Limit: Approval cannot guarantee zero future faults; retain ownership, monitoring and recovery arrangements.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Grounded Learning Service, retain an annotated trace and the changed-case result. Name the contract or evidence that makes the deciding step valid, so another team can review it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Apply the three mandatory release gates to the recorded results. Why do two passes not outweigh the deletion failure, and what evidence must follow its repair?

graphics.title: Engineering demonstration and defense: the case
graphics.alt: Defend one complete service trace. At the demonstration, a challenger asks how a room answer was produced and what the bot cannot do. Supplied facts: Approved card V7 says club V uses room E. All trusted tools are read-only.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Show source path: Connect the question to retrieved card V7. → Support the claim: Room E follows from V7, not merely fluent wording. → Show authority: The service cannot edit rooms or send messages. → Name missing evidence: With no approved card, decline to invent a room.

graphics.title: Engineering demonstration and defense — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Engineering demonstration and defense — evidence trace. Demo succeeds on three cases using mocked storage. Presenter claims real network reliability and production security. | Present requirements, architecture, contracts, permissions, evaluation, resource measurements and recovery. Show one supported case, one legitimate review and one denied operation. State what was mocked and what remains untested. | The demo supports the three fixture behaviours only. Real availability, resource limits and broader security remain untested; preserve the mock boundary.
source: sections.diagram:Engineering demonstration and defense — evidence trace

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: With no approved card, decline to invent a room. Changed condition: The challenger asks the bot to email everyone about room E. Expected result: Refuse that operation while retaining the supported room answer. Reason: Knowing a fact does not grant authority for an external action.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A defence links behaviour to evidence and limitations. Demonstrate both a valid answer path and a meaningful refused request. Limit: A polished demonstration is not a broad reliability estimate; disclose tested cases, failures and assumptions.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Grounded Learning Service, retain an annotated trace and the changed-case result. Name the contract or evidence that makes the deciding step valid, so another team can review it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Locate V7, room E and read-only scope in the demonstration. Which evidence supports the answer, and why must a request to email everyone still be refused?

weeks.title: A question that evidence can answer

graphics.title: A question that evidence can answer: the case
graphics.alt: A question with a measurable answer. A team wants to know whether giving a diagram changes accuracy on six fixed plant-identification tasks. Supplied facts: Candidate questions: "Are diagrams wonderful?" and "Does version B answer more of these six tasks correctly than version A?"

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Narrow the question: Name versions A and B, the six tasks and correct-answer scoring. → Define the comparison: Use the same tasks and labels with and without the diagram. → Bound the conclusion: The study can compare those versions on those tasks, not all diagrams or learners.

graphics.title: A question that evidence can answer — evidence trace
graphics.alt: A question that evidence can answer — evidence trace. Proposal says prove AI is useful; available records are retrieval results for five room queries. | For fictional classroom retrieval, ask whether method B returns more relevant records than lexical baseline A on a reserved judged query set at cutoff3. Define eligible corpus and relevance rules before running. | Narrow to relevant retrieval at a declared cutoff on those queries. The supplied records cannot answer universal usefulness or deployment impact.
source: sections.diagram:A question that evidence can answer — evidence trace

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: The study can compare those versions on those tasks, not all diagrams or learners. Changed condition: Replace the six tasks with six easier tasks only for B. Expected result: The comparison no longer isolates the diagram condition. Reason: Task difficulty now changes alongside the proposed intervention.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: An answerable research question connects a change to an observable outcome and a specified population. Opinion words need an operational definition before measurement. Limit: This fictional study does not establish effects on children or general classroom learning.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Which proposed diagram question has a measurable outcome? Name its versions, six-case denominator and fixed scoring, then explain why giving only B easier tasks spoils the comparison.

graphics.title: Reading a research claim: the case
graphics.alt: Read a claim with its denominator. A fictional paper headline says a prompt is twice as effective. Its table reports four correct cases instead of two. Supplied facts: Baseline: 2/10 correct. New prompt: 4/10 on the same ten cases. Scoring is fixed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Find the measured outcome: The table counts correct answers, not learning or satisfaction. → Calculate both changes: 20%→40% is twice the rate and a 20-percentage-point increase. → Check claim scope: These ten cases support a descriptive comparison, not universal doubling.

graphics.title: Correctness on ten shared cases
graphics.alt: Correctness on ten shared cases. Units: correct answers out of 10. Baseline: 2. New prompt: 4.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: These ten cases support a descriptive comparison, not universal doubling. Changed condition: The headline changes to "every learner improves twice as much". Expected result: That learner claim is unsupported by these answer counts. Reason: The outcome and experimental unit have changed in the wording without new evidence.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A research claim compresses a method and result. Unpack the measured variable, denominator and comparison before accepting the headline. Limit: Small case counts leave substantial uncertainty; no significance or causal effect is supplied.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Calculate the baseline and new rates for 2/10 and 4/10. Explain both twice the rate and the percentage-point change, and say why neither measures every learner’s improvement.

graphics.title: Finding primary research: the case
graphics.alt: Find the source behind a summary. A blog describes a fictional benchmark improvement and links an original study report. Supplied facts: Blog says "90% reliable". Original report records 9/10 correct on one fixed fictional task set and describes its labels.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Follow the primary link: Open the original report rather than treating the blog as the measurement. → Locate methods and results: Identify the ten cases, labels and nine correct results. → Record source details: Keep report version and page or table reference with the exact scoped result.

graphics.title: Finding primary research — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Finding primary research — evidence trace. A blog says experiment had100 cases; original methods say40 and supplementary version says60 after revision. | Record title, authors, version, date, identifier and access location. Distinguish paper, code, data and commentary. Verify that a quoted claim belongs to the cited version. | Track versions and use the correct original record for the claim. The blog is secondary; the two original versions must not be merged silently.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Keep report version and page or table reference with the exact scoped result. Changed condition: The original report is unavailable and only the blog remains. Expected result: Mark the measurement as unverified rather than filling in absent methods. Reason: The summary cannot supply details that have not been inspected.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Primary research exposes the procedure and observations behind a summary. It still needs scrutiny; being original does not make every interpretation correct. Limit: This example names fictional documents; it is a source-tracing exercise, not a real literature citation.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Separate what the blog claims from what the original report records. Which methods and denominator must be inspected, and what status is honest if the original report is unavailable?

graphics.title: Methods results and limitations: the case
graphics.alt: Separate procedure, finding and limit. A fictional report tests two frozen classifiers on five labelled leaf photos from one camera. Supplied facts: A is correct on 3/5; B on 4/5. No outdoor photos appear in the set.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Identify the method: Same five photos, labels and scoring are used for both models. → State the result: A scores 60%; B scores 80% on this fixed set. → State the limit: The set supplies no outdoor-camera performance evidence.

graphics.title: Two models on five shared photos
graphics.alt: Two models on five shared photos. Units: correct photos out of 5. A: 3. B: 4.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: The set supplies no outdoor-camera performance evidence. Changed condition: The conclusion says B is best for outdoor farming. Expected result: Reject that extension without outdoor evidence. Reason: The reported conditions do not include the proposed use population.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Methods tell how evidence was produced; results state observations; limitations describe what those observations cannot settle. Keeping them distinct prevents a result from becoming an oversized claim. Limit: Five observations cannot establish a stable ranking or causal mechanism; source and sampling assumptions remain important.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Place the five-photo procedure, 3/5 versus 4/5 finding and missing outdoor evidence in their proper categories. Why cannot the result establish that B is best for outdoor farming?

graphics.title: Replication and reproduction: the case
graphics.alt: Same records versus new experiment. A team first reruns a supplied analysis, then collects new records with the same protocol. Supplied facts: Original recorded labels: [1,0,1,1]. Analysis counts correct cases. New independent set: [1,1,0,0]. Binary entries mean 1=correct and 0=incorrect.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Reproduce the analysis: Reusing the supplied four records gives 3/4=75%. → Repeat the protocol: The new four-record set gives 2/4=50%. → Compare purposes: The first checks computational reproduction; the second probes repeatability with new observations.

graphics.title: Different four-record datasets
graphics.alt: Different four-record datasets. Units: correct cases out of 4; samples differ. Saved analysis: 3. New sample: 2.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: The first checks computational reproduction; the second probes repeatability with new observations. Changed condition: The rerun of the original records outputs 2/4. Expected result: Investigate code, version, input or scoring differences. Reason: The same fixed records should give the same deterministic count.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Reusing data and collecting new data answer different questions. A different new-sample result can arise without a code error; inspect both protocols and variability. Limit: Four-case samples are illustrative; neither result alone establishes broad reliability.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Calculate the scores from the original and new four-record sets. Which activity reproduces saved analysis, which repeats the protocol, and why does a different rerun of the original data need investigation?

graphics.title: A literature comparison matrix: the case
graphics.alt: A literature matrix that preserves differences. Two fictional studies evaluate related tools under different conditions. Supplied facts: Study S1: 8/10 correct on indoor photos. S2: 16/20 on outdoor photos. Both report 80%.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Record each method: Keep population, task, model version and scoring in separate columns. → Compare rates carefully: Both rates are 80%, with different denominators and conditions. → Name missing comparison: Neither study directly compares both tools on the same photos.

graphics.title: Same rate, different study conditions
graphics.alt: Same rate, different study conditions. Study S1: Correct = 8, Total = 10, Condition = Indoor. Study S2: Correct = 16, Total = 20, Condition = Outdoor.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Neither study directly compares both tools on the same photos. Changed condition: Remove the indoor/outdoor column. Expected result: The matrix conceals an important condition difference. Reason: A reader might now mistake unlike studies for a controlled head-to-head comparison.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A literature matrix helps compare evidence without flattening differences. Equal percentages do not mean equivalent tasks, samples or methods. Limit: These fictional studies illustrate comparison practice; no real literature finding is asserted.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Explain why 8/10 indoors and 16/20 outdoors share a rate but not a controlled comparison. Which condition column must the literature matrix preserve?

graphics.title: Hypotheses and measurable outcomes: the case
graphics.alt: Write a testable hypothesis before scoring. A team predicts that a retrieval rule will reduce unsupported answers on a fixed validation set. Supplied facts: Ten cases are reserved. Unsupported means a factual claim absent from the approved card. Prediction: B has fewer unsupported cases than A.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Name the directional claim: The prediction concerns unsupported cases, not writing elegance. → Define scoring first: Each answer either contains an unsupported claim or does not under the fixed rubric. → Freeze the comparison: Run both versions on the same cases after recording the hypothesis.

graphics.title: Hypotheses and measurable outcomes — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Hypotheses and measurable outcomes — evidence trace. After seeing faster responses, the team changes its primary claim from support improvement to speed improvement. | Toy hypothesis:method B improves supported-answer rate over baseline A on a reserved paired set. Define support rubric and failure treatment; record secondary outcomes separately. | Report the change as exploratory/post-result revision. Preserve the original support hypothesis; do not present speed as the prespecified primary outcome.
source: sections.diagram:Hypotheses and measurable outcomes — evidence trace

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Run both versions on the same cases after recording the hypothesis. Changed condition: B sounds friendlier but has the same unsupported count as A. Expected result: The stated improvement hypothesis is not supported on these cases. Reason: Friendliness is a different outcome from the predefined unsupported-case count.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A hypothesis makes an expected pattern explicit before seeing outcomes. The measured definition must be clear enough for another reviewer to apply. Limit: No power calculation or significance claim is provided; a null descriptive difference is not proof of exact equality.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Name the predicted outcome and how unsupported is scored. If B sounds friendlier but ties A’s unsupported count, does the recorded improvement hypothesis receive support?

graphics.title: Baselines and fair comparisons: the case
graphics.alt: A baseline deserves a fair chance. Two classifiers answer the same eight fixed questions with the same allowed sources. Supplied facts: Simple rule A: 6/8 correct. New model B: 7/8 correct. No test case is used to tune either version.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Declare baseline: A uses a simple documented rule rather than an intentionally weak placeholder. → Measure fairly: A is 75%; B is 87.5% on the same eight cases. → Interpret cautiously: B adds one correct case here; compare resources and failure types too.

graphics.title: Two versions on eight shared cases
graphics.alt: Two versions on eight shared cases. Units: correct answers out of 8. A: 6. B: 7.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: B adds one correct case here; compare resources and failure types too. Changed condition: Give B the answer key before testing. Expected result: The resulting comparison is invalid as unseen evaluation. Reason: B would receive privileged information that A did not receive.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A baseline anchors the claim of improvement. Fair comparison keeps information access, cases and scoring aligned while allowing the declared method difference. Limit: Eight cases do not establish a stable advantage or statistical significance.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Calculate 6/8 and 7/8 correctness and name the one-case gain. Why is giving B the answer key incompatible with an unseen comparison to the simple baseline?

graphics.title: Experimental units and independence: the case
graphics.alt: Photos are not always independent plants. A dataset has twelve photos: three views of each of four plants. The intended use is identifying new plants. Supplied facts: Plant IDs P1–P4 each have three views. All views of a plant must stay in one split.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Identify the unit: Four plants, not twelve independent plants, generated the observations. → Group before splitting: Assign whole plant IDs to training or evaluation. → Trace a valid split: Train on P1,P2 and evaluate on P3,P4: six photos per split.

graphics.title: Keep all views of a plant together
graphics.alt: Keep all views of a plant together. Train: 6 photos: Plant with 3 views = P1, Plant with 3 views = P2. Evaluate: 6 photos: Plant with 3 views = P3, Plant with 3 views = P4.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Train on P1,P2 and evaluate on P3,P4: six photos per split. Changed condition: Put one P1 view into evaluation while other P1 views train. Expected result: Flag object-level leakage for this new-plant target. Reason: Evaluation now includes a plant already represented during training.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Repeated views from one object share information. Counting them as independent units or scattering them across splits can exaggerate evidence for new-object performance. Limit: Four plants offer little population coverage; even a group-correct split may be too small for broad conclusions.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Count independent plants and photo views. Construct the stated group-correct split, then explain why placing a P1 view in evaluation creates leakage for the new-plant goal.

graphics.title: Confounders and controls: the case
graphics.alt: Separate background from class. Training data show every healthy leaf on white paper and every spotted leaf on blue paper. Supplied facts: Goal is leaf condition, not paper colour. A proposed check uses both paper colours for each condition.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Identify coupled variables: Condition and background change together in the original collection. → Cross the conditions: Collect healthy-white, healthy-blue, spotted-white and spotted-blue cases. → Inspect the shortcut: Compare predictions when the same leaf’s background changes under a controlled test.

graphics.title: Cross class with paper background
graphics.alt: Cross class with paper background. Healthy: White paper = Collect, Blue paper = Collect. Spotted: White paper = Collect, Blue paper = Collect.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Compare predictions when the same leaf’s background changes under a controlled test. Changed condition: New cases still use only healthy-white and spotted-blue. Expected result: The collection does not resolve the background confounding. Reason: The same two variables remain coupled instead of being varied separately.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A confounder can provide an alternative explanation for a result. Crossing conditions makes the intended feature and the nuisance feature less entangled. Limit: A changed-background test can diagnose sensitivity; it does not prove the model’s complete internal reasoning.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Draw the four condition/background combinations. Which variables were coupled before, and why would collecting only healthy-white and spotted-blue again leave the confounding unresolved?

graphics.title: Sampling variability: the case
graphics.alt: Two small samples can differ. A fixed classifier is scored on two distinct four-case samples from a declared collection. Supplied facts: Sample A has 3 correct of 4; sample B has 2 correct of 4. The model and rubric are unchanged.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Keep model fixed: No training or threshold change occurs between samples. → Compute observed rates: A is 75%; B is 50%, differing by 25 percentage points. → Consider sampling: Different included cases can change a small-sample rate.

graphics.title: Two distinct samples, fixed model
graphics.alt: Two distinct samples, fixed model. Units: correct cases out of 4 in each sample. Sample A: 3. Sample B: 2.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Different included cases can change a small-sample rate. Changed condition: Evaluate the exact same fixed four cases twice with deterministic predictions. Expected result: The counts should agree unless some condition, data or scoring changed. Reason: The sampling explanation no longer applies when the records are identical.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Sampling variability means a statistic can vary because different units were observed. Do not automatically attribute every rate change to a model improvement or deterioration. Limit: These two samples do not supply a probability model or confidence interval; none is invented.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Calculate the two four-case rates and their difference. Explain how changed included cases can affect a fixed model, and why identical deterministic records should not differ on a rerun.

graphics.title: Uncertainty intervals: the case
graphics.alt: Read a supplied uncertainty interval. A fictional study supplies an interval for a mean time difference under its stated sampling model. Supplied facts: Estimated difference B−A is -0.8 seconds; supplied 95% confidence interval is [-1.4,-0.2] seconds. Assume the study’s interval method is appropriate.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Locate the estimate: -0.8 lies between the interval endpoints. → Interpret the sign: Negative B−A means B took less time under this measurement convention. → Respect coverage meaning: 95% describes the method’s long-run coverage, not a 95% probability for this fixed parameter.

graphics.title: Supplied interval for B minus A time
graphics.alt: Supplied interval for B minus A time. Original supplied interval: Lower endpoint (s) = -1.4, Estimate (s) = -0.8, Upper endpoint (s) = -0.2. Changed supplied interval: Lower endpoint (s) = -1.4, Estimate (s) = not specified, Upper endpoint (s) = 0.3.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: 95% describes the method’s long-run coverage, not a 95% probability for this fixed parameter. Changed condition: Use a supplied interval [-1.4,0.3] instead. Expected result: It includes zero and positive differences, so both no difference and slower B remain compatible with that interval. Reason: The new upper endpoint crosses zero.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: An uncertainty interval conveys precision under assumptions. Its endpoints, units, comparison direction and method all matter; the interval is supplied here, not calculated from unavailable raw data. Limit: An interval does not establish practical value or causality, and invalid sampling assumptions can invalidate its interpretation.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Locate -0.8 and zero relative to the supplied interval [-1.4,-0.2]. Interpret the sign and confidence-method meaning, then describe what changes with interval [-1.4,0.3].

graphics.title: Effect size and practical importance: the case
graphics.alt: An improvement with a practical threshold. A team compares error rates against a predeclared practical threshold. Supplied facts: A makes 20 errors in 1000 tasks; B makes 15. Practical improvement requires at least 10 fewer errors per 1000.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Compute rates: A is 2%; B is 1.5%. → Compute effect size: B has 5 fewer errors per 1000, a 0.5-percentage-point reduction. → Apply practical threshold: Five is less than ten, so the observed change misses this threshold.

graphics.title: Errors on 1000 tasks
graphics.alt: Errors on 1000 tasks. Units: errors per 1000 tasks. A: 20. B: 15.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Five is less than ten, so the observed change misses this threshold. Changed condition: B makes 8 errors in 1000. Expected result: The reduction becomes 12 per 1000 and meets the stated practical threshold. Reason: Twenty minus eight exceeds the required ten fewer errors.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Effect size describes how much the outcome changes. Practical importance depends on the real decision criterion; relative changes can sound large while absolute changes remain small. Limit: No uncertainty or statistical significance is supplied; these counts alone cannot establish a general effect.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Calculate the absolute error-rate reduction from 20/1000 to 15/1000. Does it meet the ten-fewer-errors threshold, and what changes when B has eight errors?

graphics.title: Statistical tests and assumptions: the case
graphics.alt: A small exact paired sign-flip test. Compare three independent task pairs under a null that permits each difference’s sign to flip independently with equal probability. Supplied facts: A times [5,8,4] seconds; B [4,6,3]. Differences B−A are [-1,-2,-1]. Use a two-sided statistic: absolute sum of differences. Assume the stated sign-symmetry null is appropriate.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Preserve paired differences: Differences are -1,-2,-1; their sum is -4 and mean is -4/3 seconds. → Enumerate null sign flips: Eight equally likely flips give sums -4,-2,0,2,4 with counts 1,2,2,2,1. → Count equally extreme sums: Only -4 and 4 have absolute sum at least 4: exact two-sided p=2/8=0.25.

graphics.title: Three independent paired task times
graphics.alt: Three independent paired task times. Task 1: A seconds = 5, B seconds = 4, B−A seconds = -1. Task 2: A seconds = 8, B seconds = 6, B−A seconds = -2. Task 3: A seconds = 4, B seconds = 3, B−A seconds = -1.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Only -4 and 4 have absolute sum at least 4: exact two-sided p=2/8=0.25. Changed condition: Break the task pairing and use unrelated A and B measurements. Expected result: This paired sign-flip calculation is no longer justified by the stated design. Reason: Its differences must come from the same task, with the declared independent sign-symmetry assumptions.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A test compares an observed statistic with outcomes under a specified null model. Here the sign-flip assumptions make eight arrangements equally likely. At a predeclared 0.05 threshold, p=0.25 does not reject the null; it does not prove no difference. Limit: Three pairs provide coarse evidence. The p-value is not the probability that the null is true; invalid independence or symmetry assumptions invalidate this test.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, save paired differences, the null assumptions, all eight sign arrangements and the decision rule. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Calculate each paired difference and the observed sum. Count null arrangements with absolute sum at least four, compute p, and explain the decision at threshold 0.05.

graphics.title: Multiple comparisons: the case
graphics.alt: Six declared prompt comparisons. A team performs six valid hypothesis tests and applies a predeclared Bonferroni familywise threshold. Supplied facts: Familywise alpha=0.05. Supplied unadjusted p-values are 0.004,0.012,0.02,0.08,0.4,0.9. These values are stipulated, not calculated from invented data.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Count the planned tests: There are six tests in the declared family. → Compute corrected threshold: 0.05/6 is about 0.00833 for each test. → Apply all six decisions: Only 0.004 is below 0.00833; the other five do not reject under this rule.

graphics.title: Supplied p-values and six-test decisions
graphics.alt: Supplied p-values and six-test decisions. Test 1: Supplied p = 0.004, At cutoff 0.00833 = Reject. Test 2: Supplied p = 0.012, At cutoff 0.00833 = Do not reject. Test 3: Supplied p = 0.02, At cutoff 0.00833 = Do not reject. Test 4: Supplied p = 0.08, At cutoff 0.00833 = Do not reject. Test 5: Supplied p = 0.4, At cutoff 0.00833 = Do not reject. Test 6: Supplied p = 0.9, At cutoff 0.00833 = Do not reject.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Only 0.004 is below 0.00833; the other five do not reject under this rule. Changed condition: The declared family has ten tests instead of six; keep the listed values unchanged. Expected result: The cutoff becomes 0.005, and only 0.004 among the listed values still rejects. Reason: The error allowance is divided among ten tests; all ten results must be reported, including the four not supplied here.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Searching many comparisons provides more chances for false positives. Bonferroni divides the error allowance across the declared family; valid individual p-values are required. A rejected null is not automatically a large or useful improvement. Limit: No effect size or real data is supplied. Bonferroni can be conservative and cannot repair invalid p-values or undisclosed outcome-driven test selection.

graphics.title: Ablation studies: the case
graphics.alt: Remove one component at a time. A retrieval pipeline has search plus a relevance filter. A team tests the filter’s contribution. Supplied facts: Full pipeline: 8/10 correct. Filter removed: 6/10 on the same cases, with all other settings fixed.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Name the component: The relevance filter is the single declared change. → Run the ablation: Remove only the filter and preserve cases and scoring. → Compare outcomes: Correctness falls from 80% to 60%, two cases in this set.

graphics.title: Relevance-filter ablation
graphics.alt: Relevance-filter ablation. Units: correct answers out of 10 shared cases. Full pipeline: 8. Filter removed: 6.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Correctness falls from 80% to 60%, two cases in this set. Changed condition: Remove the filter and also change the model version. Expected result: The comparison no longer isolates the filter. Reason: Two simultaneous changes provide alternative explanations.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: An ablation probes a component by removing or changing it while holding the rest fixed. It supports a scoped comparison, not a claim that the component always helps. Limit: Interactions and small-sample variability remain; this illustrative difference is not a universal causal estimate.

graphics.title: Sensitivity analysis: the case
graphics.alt: A decision sensitive to the cutoff. A toy score rule predicts positive when score is at least the chosen cutoff. Supplied facts: Scores are 0.4,0.6,0.8. Cutoff 0.5 marks the last two positive; cutoff 0.7 marks only 0.8 positive.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Hold scores fixed: Keep the same three supplied scores. → Apply cutoff 0.5: 0.6 and 0.8 meet the boundary. → Apply cutoff 0.7: Only 0.8 meets the new boundary.

graphics.title: Score decisions under inclusive cutoffs
graphics.alt: Score decisions under inclusive cutoffs. Cutoff 0.5: Score 0.4 = No, Score 0.6 = Yes, Score 0.8 = Yes. Cutoff 0.7: Score 0.4 = No, Score 0.6 = No, Score 0.8 = Yes. Cutoff 0.6: Score 0.4 = No, Score 0.6 = Yes, Score 0.8 = Yes.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Only 0.8 meets the new boundary. Changed condition: Set the cutoff to exactly 0.6. Expected result: 0.6 and 0.8 are positive because the rule includes equality. Reason: The declared at-least boundary includes the threshold value.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Sensitivity analysis checks how conclusions change under plausible choices. Changing a cutoff changes the decision rule, not the recorded scores or their accuracy. Limit: Without reference labels, these counts do not identify the best cutoff or establish correctness.

graphics.title: Dataset and benchmark limitations: the case
graphics.alt: A benchmark can miss the intended setting. A plant model is evaluated on clean indoor photos but proposed for shaded outdoor photos. Supplied facts: Indoor benchmark: 9/10 correct. No outdoor cases are present. The same model is intended for both.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Name measured setting: All ten benchmark images are clean indoor photos. → Report the result: The observed indoor score is 90%. → Name missing evidence: Outdoor shade performance remains unmeasured.

graphics.title: Benchmark conditions
graphics.alt: Benchmark conditions. Indoor benchmark: Correct = 9, Total = 10. Added outdoor slice: Correct = 2, Total = 4.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Outdoor shade performance remains unmeasured. Changed condition: Add four reserved outdoor cases, of which two are correct. Expected result: Report the outdoor slice as 2/4=50%, separately from indoor results. Reason: The new records finally measure the missing condition, with a small denominator.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A benchmark represents particular tasks and collection conditions. High performance on it cannot automatically establish fitness for a different deployment setting. Limit: Neither slice estimates all future photos; inspect sampling, labels and grouping.

graphics.title: Research ethics and consent: the case
graphics.alt: Consent is specific, not universal. A fictional study asks adults to submit anonymous drawings for one pattern-recognition investigation. Supplied facts: Consent covers this study only. It excludes public posting of originals and unrelated face-recognition research.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: State the purpose: Explain the drawing task and planned use before participation. → Respect exclusions: Do not publish originals or transfer them to the unrelated project. → Keep the agreement: Record permitted uses and the approved withdrawal procedure.

graphics.title: Research ethics and consent — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Research ethics and consent — evidence trace. Proposal automatically copies student essays into a study because they were submitted for grading. | Use fictional records for this course. For the supplied classroom policy, a real study needs responsible review, plain-language purpose, opt-in consent and withdrawal handling before collection. Do not implement real recruitment in this exercise. | The grading purpose does not establish research permission under the policy. Redesign around fictional data or obtain required review and voluntary permission before collection.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Record permitted uses and the approved withdrawal procedure. Changed condition: A new project requests the same drawings for an excluded purpose. Expected result: Do not reuse them under the existing consent; seek the required new authorisation. Reason: The new purpose falls outside the stated agreement.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Research ethics includes what people agree to, how they can decline and how risks are addressed. A contribution does not grant unlimited reuse. Limit: This fictional adult scenario is not approval for research with children; real oversight and applicable rules are separate requirements.

graphics.title: Privacy and data governance: the case
graphics.alt: Govern data by purpose and access. A fictional project needs task scores and random participant codes, but not names. Supplied facts: The analysis table holds codes and scores. A separate restricted key links codes to names only for authorised withdrawal handling.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Separate tables: Keep analysis records apart from the identity key. → Limit access: Analysts receive scores and codes, not the name linkage. → Define retention: Apply the approved deletion schedule to both stores and listed copies.

graphics.title: Keep analysis records separate from the identity key
graphics.alt: Analysts receive random participant codes and scores. A separate restricted key links codes to names only for authorised withdrawal handling. Keeping the key restricted reduces exposure; it does not guarantee anonymity.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Apply the approved deletion schedule to both stores and listed copies. Changed condition: Publish the identity key with the analysis table. Expected result: The records become directly linkable to names and breach this access design. Reason: Separation only helps while the linkage key remains restricted.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Pseudonymous codes reduce routine exposure but are not the same as irreversible anonymity. Governance specifies purpose, readers, locations and retention. Limit: Small groups or unusual records may still be identifiable without names; evaluate re-identification risk.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project

Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Point to the analysis table and the restricted identity key. Why are the codes pseudonymous rather than guaranteed anonymous, and what changes if the key is published?

graphics.title: Predefining an analysis plan: the case
graphics.alt: Freeze decisions before the result. A team records its outcome, exclusions and analysis before evaluating a reserved set. Supplied facts: Plan: compare correct counts on 12 cases; exclude only unreadable files identified before scoring; report all version results.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Write the rule first: Record the outcome and justified unreadable-file exclusion. → Protect the reserved set: Do not choose exclusions from which cases each model fails. → Report deviations: If the plan changes, mark the change and give its reason.

graphics.title: Predefining an analysis plan — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Predefining an analysis plan — evidence trace. Plan includes all20 cases. After results, the team removes four failed cases because they make the graph look worse. | Declare primary metric, eligible cases, missing handling, baseline, test assumptions and reporting. Timestamp/version the plan; label later choices exploratory. | The exclusion is outcome-informed and violates the plan. Report original16/20 if16 passed, and label any revised analysis with reasons rather than hiding failures.
source: sections.diagram:Predefining an analysis plan — evidence trace

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: If the plan changes, mark the change and give its reason. Changed condition: Exclude two readable cases because the new model fails them. Expected result: That outcome-driven exclusion violates the recorded rule. Reason: Model failure is not the predeclared unreadable-file criterion.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: An analysis plan limits flexibility after outcomes are known. Necessary changes can be transparent, but they should not be silently presented as the original plan. Limit: A plan cannot correct poor sampling or guarantee valid assumptions; it makes decisions auditable.

graphics.title: Pilot experiments: the case
graphics.alt: A pilot tests the procedure. A pilot checks whether the team can score answers consistently before running the main study. Supplied facts: Two reviewers score four practice answers. They agree on three and disagree on one; these answers are excluded from final evaluation.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Try the workflow: Both reviewers apply the draft rubric to four practice answers. → Measure agreement: Agreement is 3/4=75% on this pilot. → Repair the rubric: Discuss the disagreement and clarify the scoring rule before the main run.

graphics.title: Reviewer agreement on four pilot answers
graphics.alt: Reviewer agreement on four pilot answers. Units: pilot answers out of 4. Agree: 3. Disagree: 1.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Discuss the disagreement and clarify the scoring rule before the main run. Changed condition: Add the corrected pilot answers into final evaluation. Expected result: Declare them previously exposed rather than untouched final evidence. Reason: Rubric development already used those answers.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A pilot can reveal missing instructions, practical delays or ambiguous scoring. It is preparation, not an untouched final estimate after the team uses it to revise methods. Limit: Four pilot answers do not establish long-run reviewer reliability or a stable performance effect.

graphics.title: Power and resource tradeoffs: the case
graphics.alt: A simulated detection-and-resource trade-off. A fictional simulation repeats a study under the same assumed alternative effect, using two independent-unit sample sizes. Supplied facts: There are 100 simulation trials per design. At n=20, 60 detect the specified effect; at n=40, 80 detect it. Each independent unit costs 2 resource units. Same test and effect assumptions are used.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Estimate simulated detection: Observed detection fractions are 60/100=60% and 80/100=80%. → Calculate design cost: n=20 costs 40 resource units; n=40 costs 80 units. → Compare the trade-off: Doubling cost adds 20 percentage points of simulated detection under these assumptions.

graphics.title: Stipulated simulation and resource records
graphics.alt: Stipulated simulation and resource records. Smaller design: Independent units = 20, Detections = 60, Trials = 100, Cost units = 40. Larger design: Independent units = 40, Detections = 80, Trials = 100, Cost units = 80.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Doubling cost adds 20 percentage points of simulated detection under these assumptions. Changed condition: Change the assumed effect or variability but keep the sample sizes. Expected result: The detection fractions need new simulation; the resource costs stay 40 and 80. Reason: Power depends on the data-generating assumptions, while this stated unit-cost calculation does not.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Power is the probability of detecting a specified effect under a specified model and decision rule. Repeated simulation can estimate it; the estimate depends on effect size, variability, design and test assumptions, not sample size alone. Limit: Only 100 trials per design produce noisy estimates. They are fictional stipulated results, not executed simulation or evidence about pupils.

What additional detection is observed for the extra forty units, and does that establish power for an actual classroom study?

graphics.title: Reproducible environment and records: the case
graphics.alt: A reproducible calculation record. A teammate must rerun a three-value mean without guessing the input or software version. Supplied facts: Data file contains 2,4,6. Recorded script sums values and divides by count; environment and file hash are saved.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Identify exact input: Use the three recorded values, not a similarly named edited file. → Trace calculation: Sum is 12; count is 3; mean is 4. → Save provenance: Retain script version, environment description and data hash with the output.

graphics.title: Recorded mean calculation
graphics.alt: Recorded mean calculation. Original data: Value 1 = 2, Value 2 = 4, Value 3 = 6, Mean = 4. Changed data: Value 1 = 2, Value 2 = 4, Value 3 = 9, Mean = 5.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Retain script version, environment description and data hash with the output. Changed condition: The data file changes to 2,4,9. Expected result: The mean becomes 15/3=5, and the saved input hash must change. Reason: The calculation is the same but its input records differ.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Reproducibility needs the materials and decisions that produced a result. A screenshot of 4 does not specify which data or calculation generated it. Limit: Environment records support rerunning; they do not certify correct sampling, labels or scientific interpretation.

graphics.title: Running the primary experiment: the case
graphics.alt: Run the frozen experiment. A research team freezes versions A and B, labels and scoring before a six-case primary run. Supplied facts: A scores [1,0,1,1,0,1]; B scores [1,1,1,0,1,1]. Both answer the same six cases. Binary entries mean 1=correct and 0=incorrect.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Keep versions fixed: No case result may trigger tuning during this run. → Compute results: A totals 4/6; B totals 5/6. → Keep case-level records: Cases two and five favour B; case four favours A.

graphics.title: Paired primary case outcomes
graphics.alt: Paired primary case outcomes. Version A: Case 1 = 1, Case 2 = 0, Case 3 = 1, Case 4 = 1, Case 5 = 0, Case 6 = 1. Version B: Case 1 = 1, Case 2 = 1, Case 3 = 1, Case 4 = 0, Case 5 = 1, Case 6 = 1.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Cases two and five favour B; case four favours A. Changed condition: Tune B after inspecting its case-four failure, then rescore the same set. Expected result: Label the rerun as development on exposed cases, not untouched primary evaluation. Reason: The evaluation outcomes have now influenced the version.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Running the primary experiment means following the declared protocol and retaining raw outcomes. Overall scores alone hide different failure patterns. Limit: Six illustrative cases do not establish a population advantage or statistical significance.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project

graphics.title: Inspecting failures and anomalies: the case
graphics.alt: Inspect an anomaly without erasing it. A timing study records four runs and notices one unusually long duration. Supplied facts: Durations are 2,2,2,10 seconds. Logs show a source timeout on the fourth run. The plan includes timeouts in reporting.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Keep the raw record: The fourth duration remains 10 seconds. → Compute summaries: Mean is 16/4=4 seconds; median is 2 seconds. → Investigate the event: Report the timeout evidence and distinguish it from an untested explanation.

graphics.title: All four recorded durations
graphics.alt: All four recorded durations. Units: seconds; run 4 includes timeout. Run 1: 2. Run 2: 2. Run 3: 2. Run 4: 10.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Report the timeout evidence and distinguish it from an untested explanation. Changed condition: Delete the 10-second record only because it looks bad. Expected result: The mean becomes 2 seconds but the selective report violates this plan. Reason: Observed inconvenient outcomes are not an approved exclusion reason.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: An anomaly invites investigation, not automatic deletion. A slow failure may be part of real service behaviour; the predefined rule determines inclusion. Limit: A logged timeout does not identify every underlying cause; report conditions and test explanations.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Calculate mean and median for 2,2,2,10. What does the timeout log establish, and why is deleting that inconvenient record incompatible with the stated plan?

graphics.title: Robustness across conditions: the case
graphics.alt: Check robustness across conditions. A fixed classifier is tested separately on indoor and shaded outdoor cases. Supplied facts: Indoor 7/8 correct; outdoor 3/8 correct. The rubric and frozen model are unchanged.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Name both slices: Each condition has eight labelled cases. → Compute rates: Indoor is 87.5%; outdoor is 37.5%. → Bound robustness: The large observed gap motivates investigation rather than claiming condition independence.

graphics.title: Fixed model across conditions
graphics.alt: Fixed model across conditions. Units: correct cases out of 8 per condition. Indoor: 7. Shaded outdoor: 3.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: The large observed gap motivates investigation rather than claiming condition independence. Changed condition: Report only the combined 10/16=62.5%. Expected result: The arithmetic is correct, but the condition gap becomes hidden. Reason: Combining records discards the slice distinction relevant to the deployment goal.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Robustness asks whether behaviour survives relevant changes in conditions. A total score can hide a weak slice; keep the scenario and denominator visible. Limit: Eight cases per slice do not establish stable population rates or the reason for the difference.

Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. graphics.title: Negative results and claim revision: the case
graphics.alt: A negative result changes the claim. A proposed prompt improvement ties the baseline on a fixed eight-case evaluation. Supplied facts: A and B each score 6/8. Before running, the team predicted B would score higher.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Recall the prediction: The claim was a higher correct count for B. → State the finding: Both versions score 75%; no observed count advantage appears here. → Revise cautiously: Report the unsupported prediction and a justified next test.

graphics.title: No observed count advantage
graphics.alt: No observed count advantage. Units: correct cases out of 8 shared cases. A: 6. B: 6.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Report the unsupported prediction and a justified next test. Changed condition: B wins on one new task after the team chooses it because A fails. Expected result: Treat that selected demonstration as exploratory, not a replacement for the original result. Reason: Case selection now depends on outcomes.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A negative result can be informative when methods and limits are clear. A tie does not prove the methods are equivalent under all conditions or that the experiment was worthless. Limit: A tie on eight cases is not an equivalence test; uncertainty and practical thresholds remain unspecified.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Does a 6/8 tie support the prediction that B scores higher? Explain why one newly selected favourable demonstration does not replace the original result or prove equivalence.

graphics.title: Figures that preserve evidence: the case
graphics.alt: Draw bars that preserve the comparison. A report plots correct counts for two versions on the same ten cases. Supplied facts: A has 6/10 correct; B has 8/10. The count axis should start at zero and identify the ten-case denominator.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Draw honest bars: Use heights 6 and 8 on a zero-based correct-count axis. → Label the scale: State counts out of ten, not an unspecified quality score. → Keep context nearby: Note the fixed tasks and absence of a significance test.

graphics.title: Zero-based correct counts
graphics.alt: Zero-based correct counts. Units: correct cases out of 10. A: 6. B: 8.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Note the fixed tasks and absence of a significance test. Changed condition: Start the axis at 5 without making the truncation obvious. Expected result: The bars exaggerate the visual contrast and require correction or clear disclosure. Reason: Visible heights no longer correspond to the full count scale.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Figures make evidence easier to inspect when labels and scales preserve meaning. A dramatic-looking visual cannot supply missing uncertainty or representativeness. Limit: A well-labelled chart still cannot establish a causal or population claim from ten cases.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Draw count bars for 6/10 and 8/10 using the stated axis. Why must the denominator and fixed task context remain visible, and what distortion arises from an undisclosed axis start at five?

graphics.title: Writing the methods section: the case
graphics.alt: Methods that another team can repeat. A paper describes a toy string-classification experiment using a stated length rule. Supplied facts: Inputs: "oak", "pine", "willow". Rule: length at least 4→long, otherwise short. No whitespace trimming occurs.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Record exact inputs: Preserve the three strings and no-trimming policy. → State procedure: Apply the inclusive length boundary at four characters. → Show resulting labels: Oak is short; pine and willow are long.

graphics.title: Writing the methods section — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Writing the methods section — evidence trace. Methods says used AI on data and got good scores; code and split are absent. | Report question, units, sampling, permissions, data roles, baseline, procedure, metrics, uncertainty assumptions, missing/exclusion handling and versions. Distinguish prespecified and later changes. | It omits model/procedure version, data identity, units/splits, baseline, metric and scoring. Reproduction and validity cannot be assessed from the description.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Oak is short; pine and willow are long. Changed condition: Change the rule to length greater than 4. Expected result: Pine becomes short; willow stays long and oak stays short. Reason: The equality case distinguishes the two procedures.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A methods section specifies inputs, processing, boundaries, versions and scoring. Precise procedures allow a reader to repeat the computation instead of inferring it from the final labels. Limit: Repeating this deterministic toy rule does not validate a learned model or establish ecological categories.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project

graphics.title: Writing results and limitations: the case
graphics.alt: Write results without enlarging them. A fictional study evaluates answer support on twelve fixed questions from one approved collection. Supplied facts: A supports 9/12 answers; B supports 10/12. No user learning outcomes are recorded.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Report the observation: A is 75%; B is about 83.3%, a one-case improvement. → Link to the method: Name the collection, rubric and twelve-case denominator. → State limits: Do not infer that children learn more from this answer-support measure.

graphics.title: Supported answers in one collection
graphics.alt: Supported answers in one collection. Units: supported answers out of 12. A: 9. B: 10.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Do not infer that children learn more from this answer-support measure. Changed condition: Write "B makes every student smarter". Expected result: Remove that sentence as unsupported by the study. Reason: The measured unit was answers, not student understanding or intelligence.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Results describe what was measured; limitations prevent substitution of a different outcome or population. A small descriptive improvement needs its scope attached. Limit: No significance or stable population effect is established; broader task and learner evidence would require another study.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. graphics.title: Peer review and response: the case
graphics.alt: Respond to a reviewer with evidence. A reviewer asks why four photos of one plant were treated as four independent plants. Supplied facts: The original table contains four views of P1 and four views of P2: eight photos from two plants.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Identify the concern: The reviewer questions the unit of analysis. → Check the records: Plant identifiers confirm two plants, not eight independent plants. → Revise transparently: Correct the description and revise any analysis that assumed independence.

graphics.title: Peer review and response — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Peer review and response — evidence trace. Reviewer asks for a fitted-line baseline; author responds that the neural network is advanced, without a comparison. | For each comment record concern, response, change location and new evidence if needed. If no new evidence exists, narrow the claim instead of promising an unperformed test. | The response lacks evidence. Add a fair comparison under the plan or narrow the claim to the existing baseline; record any new analysis as such.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Correct the description and revise any analysis that assumed independence. Changed condition: The team only changes "photos" to "plants" without revisiting analysis. Expected result: The substantive independence issue remains unresolved. Reason: Renaming records does not change their shared source objects.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Peer review should connect a criticism to the actual records and a concrete correction or reasoned response. Polite language alone cannot repair a methodological error. Limit: Two plants provide limited coverage; grouping correctly does not create more independent evidence.

graphics.title: Independent reproduction check: the case
graphics.alt: An independent rerun with a disagreement. A second team follows the saved protocol on the same fixed data and obtains a different score. Supplied facts: Original correct count is 5/6. Rerun is 4/6. Case Q3 is the only scoring disagreement. No new model outputs are generated.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Compare exact artefacts: Verify data and rubric versions before changing the result. → Locate disagreement: The score difference is concentrated in Q3. → Resolve by the rubric: Inspect Q3’s saved answer and rule; document whichever scoring decision is justified.

graphics.title: Independent reproduction check — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Independent reproduction check — evidence trace. Operator gets different MSE because the supplied script averages absolute errors while paper names squared error. | Provide manifest, fixture data, code, environment and expected metric definition. Record assistance and mismatches; reproduction is not new-data replication. | Metric contract mismatch explains a candidate discrepancy. Correct/report script and rerun; preserve original artifact versions and results.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Inspect Q3’s saved answer and rule; document whichever scoring decision is justified. Changed condition: Q3’s saved file is missing from the archive. Expected result: Mark exact reproduction incomplete until the required artefact is recovered or the limitation disclosed. Reason: A missing record prevents checking the contested decision.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: An independent reproduction check can uncover interpretation or implementation differences. Do not average incompatible scores or simply choose the higher one. Limit: This check concerns saved outputs and scoring, not new-sample replication or future model behaviour.

graphics.title: Final project manuscript: the case
graphics.alt: Build a manuscript from claim to record. A capstone manuscript compares two frozen pattern classifiers on ten reserved cases. Supplied facts: A is correct on 7/10; B on 8/10. All cases are indoor, from five plants with two views each.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: State bounded claim: B adds one correct photo on this indoor set. → Describe dependence: Ten photos come from five plants; report the grouping. → Present results: Show 70% and 80% with counts and case-level outcomes. → Preserve limitations: Do not claim outdoor robustness or ten independent plants.

graphics.title: Indoor capstone photo outcomes
graphics.alt: Indoor capstone photo outcomes. Units: correct photos out of 10; five plants. A: 7. B: 8.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Do not claim outdoor robustness or ten independent plants. Changed condition: The abstract calls the study a test on ten independent plants. Expected result: Correct it to five plants with two views each. Reason: The source-object count, not the photo count, defines the independent plants.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A final manuscript aligns question, procedure, evidence and scope. Every figure and conclusion should point back to the records that support it. Limit: No population superiority or significance claim is supplied; dependence and sample coverage need explicit treatment.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For the Reproducible AI Research Study, retain an annotated worked trace and the changed-case reasoning. Connect the claim to its records, units and assumptions so another investigator can challenge or reproduce it. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Connect the manuscript’s 7/10 and 8/10 scores to the five-plant grouping. Which abstract claim must be corrected if it says ten independent plants?

graphics.title: Presentation and challenge session: the case
graphics.alt: Answer a challenge without inventing evidence. At the presentation, a reviewer asks whether the model works on a different camera. Supplied facts: The project tested twelve photos from camera A only. Ten were correct; no camera B records exist.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: State measured result: Report 10/12 correct on camera A. → Address the challenge: Say camera B performance is not measured. → Propose a valid next test: Use reserved camera-B cases with labels, grouping and a fixed scoring rule.

graphics.title: Presentation and challenge session — evidence trace
graphics.alt: Presentation and challenge session — evidence trace. A presenter shows one perfect output after a20-case study with14 passes. | Use a short sequence:question, design, primary result, failure, limitation, next question. Answer unfamiliar challenges by locating evidence or stating it is missing. | The demonstration is one example; study rate70%. Present aggregate and failures and do not call the best output representative without evidence.
source: sections.diagram:Presentation and challenge session — evidence trace

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Use reserved camera-B cases with labels, grouping and a fixed scoring rule. Changed condition: The reviewer shows one camera-B success. Expected result: That is one demonstration, not an estimate of broad camera-B reliability. Reason: One selected observation does not represent the full proposed condition.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A challenge session tests whether the team knows its evidence boundary. An honest unknown plus a specific future test is stronger than an unsupported confident promise. Limit: The original result and proposed study still need sampling and uncertainty discussion.

Supported question: Answer the camera-B challenge using only the twelve camera-A records. Why is one displayed camera-B success a demonstration rather than broad evidence of camera-B reliability?

graphics.title: Research defense and next questions: the case
graphics.alt: Defend the next research question. A research defence identifies a observed weakness and a testable follow-up. Supplied facts: A frozen model is correct on 8/10 clear images and 4/10 shaded images. Source objects are grouped within each condition.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: State slice outcomes: Clear is 80%; shaded is 40%. → Limit the interpretation: Shade sensitivity is plausible, but camera or object differences may also matter. → Design follow-up: Photograph the same held-out objects under both light conditions using one camera and fixed scoring.

graphics.title: Defence: different condition slices
graphics.alt: Defence: different condition slices. Units: correct cases out of 10 per slice. Clear: 8. Shaded: 4.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Photograph the same held-out objects under both light conditions using one camera and fixed scoring. Changed condition: Change cameras as well as lighting in the follow-up. Expected result: The design again entangles two conditions. Reason: A camera difference provides another explanation for any performance gap.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A defence should explain results, uncertainty and what would discriminate between explanations next. A controlled paired follow-up is more informative than simply collecting extra easy images. Limit: Even a paired follow-up needs adequate independent objects and justified analysis; no causal conclusion is claimed yet.

How does the same-object, one-camera follow-up help, and why does changing cameras again reintroduce confounding?

weeks.title: From a paper algorithm to Python

graphics.title: From a paper algorithm to Python: the case
graphics.alt: Convert a seed-count algorithm. The paper plan counts seeds in identical trays, then adds a labelled spare tray. Supplied facts: Python 3: trays=4; per_tray=6; spare=2; total=trays*per_tray+spare; print(total). All quantities count seeds.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Name the inputs: Four trays hold six seeds each; two extra seeds are separate. → Translate the plan: Multiply tray count by seeds per tray, then add the spare count. → Trace the assignment: 4*6+2 is 26; total stores 26 and print displays it.

graphics.title: A calculation from paper to output
graphics.alt: A calculation from paper to output. Record pack count | packs = 4 | Name holds 4. Multiply two quantities | total = packs * per_pack | Name holds product. Show the answer | print(total) | Displays the value
source: sections.diagram:A calculation from paper to output

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: 4*6+2 is 26; total stores 26 and print displays it. Changed condition: Change spare to 5 while keeping both tray inputs fixed. Expected result: The printed total becomes 29. Reason: 4*6 remains 24; adding five gives 29.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Python follows the arithmetic instructions. This translation automates a declared counting rule; it does not train a model from examples. Limit: The calculation assumes identical tray sizes and measured counts; it cannot detect a miscounted tray.

Why does the spare count get added once, and what prints when spare is five?

graphics.title: Values variables and types: the case
graphics.alt: A number and its printed-looking text. A program stores a numeric badge count and a string that looks like that count. Supplied facts: Python 3: count=8; tag="8"; print(count+2); print(tag+"2").

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Inspect types: count is an integer; tag is a string. → Apply addition: Integer addition gives 10; string concatenation gives the text 82. → Predict a mixed operation: count+tag raises TypeError rather than silently converting tag.

graphics.title: A saved value is not a live link
graphics.alt: A saved value is not a live link. count = 8 | 8 | Not assigned. saved = count | 8 | 8. count = count + 2 | 10 | 8
source: sections.diagram:A saved value is not a live link

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: count+tag raises TypeError rather than silently converting tag. Changed condition: Change count to 10, leaving tag unchanged. Expected result: The two valid outputs become 12 and 82. Reason: Only the integer variable changes; the string still contains the character 8.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Values carry types, not merely appearances. The plus operator performs numeric addition for these integers and concatenation for these strings; the mixed operation is invalid here. Limit: These examples use built-in integers and strings; operator behaviour depends on types and is not proof of general model reasoning.
