Supported question: Predict both print outputs and explain why they differ. Does count+tag work, and what happens to each valid output after count becomes ten?

graphics.title: Expressions and operator order: the case
graphics.alt: Parentheses change an expression. A toy shelf calculator compares adding a fixed cost after multiplication with multiplying an entire group. Supplied facts: Python 3: print(3+2*5); print((3+2)*5). Inputs are dimensionless for this arithmetic exercise.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Use precedence: In 3+2*5, multiplication happens first. → Compute first result: 2*5 is 10; adding 3 gives 13. → Compute grouped result: Parentheses give 3+2=5 first; multiplying by 5 gives 25.

graphics.title: Two expressions with different meanings
graphics.alt: Two expressions with different meanings. 3 * 8 + 2 | 3 * 8 is 24 | 24 + 2 is 26. 3 * (8 + 2) | 8 + 2 is 10 | 3 * 10 is 30. (3 * 8) + 2 | 3 * 8 is 24 | 24 + 2 is 26

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Parentheses give 3+2=5 first; multiplying by 5 gives 25. Changed condition: Replace the final multiplier 5 with 4 in both expressions. Expected result: The first result is 11; the grouped result is 20. Reason: 3+2*4=3+8; (3+2)*4=5*4.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Parentheses explicitly group an operation. Without them, Python multiplication takes priority over addition; the same numerals can therefore describe different procedures. Limit: Arithmetic correctness does not decide which expression matches a real problem; the written model must define the intended quantities.

Use actual Python 3 results to check the prediction after reasoning first. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Trace the operation order in both expressions. Identify which picture step changes with parentheses and predict both results when the multiplier becomes four.

graphics.title: Boolean conditions: the case
graphics.alt: Two conditions for entry. A toy club accepts integer ages from 12 through 15 inclusive. Supplied facts: Python 3: age=15; allowed=(age>=12) and (age<=15); print(allowed). No type validation is implemented here.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Check lower boundary: 15>=12 is True. → Check upper boundary: 15<=15 is also True. → Combine with and: Both comparisons are True, so allowed is True.

graphics.title: Two requirements must both hold
graphics.alt: Two requirements must both hold. 12 min, quiet False | 12 <= 12 is True | True and False is False. 12 min, quiet True | 12 <= 12 is True | True and True is True. 15 min, quiet True | 15 <= 12 is False | False and True is False

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Both comparisons are True, so allowed is True. Changed condition: Change age to 16. Expected result: The result becomes False. Reason: The lower condition remains True, but the upper condition fails.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A Boolean condition represents a yes-or-no result. And requires both conditions; checking only one boundary would accept values outside the intended interval. Limit: This condition checks a declared numeric interval, not identity or authorisation; unexpected input types need separate handling.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For Python readiness before the Responsible Plant Classifier, retain a trace of the values, the predicted outputs and the changed-case explanation. Use actual Python 3 results to check the prediction after reasoning first. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Give both comparison results for ages 11, 15 and 16. Which comparison rejects each outside value, and why does and matter?

graphics.title: Branching and boundary tests: the case
graphics.alt: Check invalid values before branching. A toy shelf label uses fewer than five books as "small", otherwise "large", but negative counts are invalid. Supplied facts: Python 3: if count<0: label="invalid"; elif count<5: label="small"; else: label="large". Read as indented branches.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Check validity: For count=-2, the first condition selects invalid. → Check small boundary: For count=4, validity passes and count<5 selects small. → Handle equality: For count=5, both earlier conditions fail, so large is selected.

graphics.title: Check invalid values before the size rule
graphics.alt: First ask count less than zero: yes selects invalid. Otherwise ask count less than five: yes selects small; no selects large. Separate input traces are minus two invalid, four small, five large.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: For count=5, both earlier conditions fail, so large is selected. Changed condition: Remove the first negative-count branch. Expected result: A count of -2 would incorrectly receive small. Reason: Negative two is less than five, but it is not a permitted measured count.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: An if/elif/else chain selects the first matching branch. Putting invalid handling first prevents a negative count from being mislabelled as a small valid collection. Limit: The toy procedure assumes numeric counts; validate types and define missing-value behaviour before using it in a real service.

graphics.alt: For Python readiness before the Responsible Plant Classifier, retain a trace of the values, the predicted outputs and the changed-case explanation. Use actual Python 3 results to check the prediction after reasoning first. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Trace -2, 4 and 5 through the branches. Explain why the negative check comes first and what label -2 gets if it is removed.

graphics.title: Loops and trace tables: the case
graphics.alt: Accumulate a short range. A running total adds the integers visited by range(1,5). Supplied facts: Python 3: total=0; for value in range(1,5): total+=value; print(total). The print is after the loop.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Visit the range: Values are 1,2,3,4; the stop value 5 is excluded. → Trace running total: Totals after each addition are 1,3,6,10. → Print after the loop: The final displayed value is 10.

graphics.title: Running total after each visited value
graphics.alt: Running total after each visited value. Visit 1: Current value = 1, Running total = 1. Visit 2: Current value = 2, Running total = 3. Visit 3: Current value = 3, Running total = 6. Visit 4: Current value = 4, Running total = 10.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: The final displayed value is 10. Changed condition: Replace range(1,5) with range(1,1). Expected result: No values are visited and the final output is 0. Reason: The accumulator starts at zero and an empty loop never changes it.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A loop repeats an operation for each visited value. A trace table distinguishes the current value from the accumulator; the range stop is not included. Limit: This bounded loop does not train an AI model; other loop conditions may require separate termination checks.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For Python readiness before the Responsible Plant Classifier, retain a trace of the values, the predicted outputs and the changed-case explanation. Use actual Python 3 results to check the prediction after reasoning first. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: List the four visited values and their running totals. Explain why 5 is absent and what prints for range(1,1).

graphics.title: Lists and indexing: the case
graphics.alt: Indexes are positions, not values. A list of shelf counts is read by position. Supplied facts: Python 3: counts=[6,1,8]; print(counts[0]); print(counts[-1]); print(len(counts)).

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Draw positions: Indexes 0,1,2 contain 6,1,8 respectively. → Read two positions: Index 0 returns 6; index -1 returns the final value 8. → Check length boundary: Length is 3, but index 3 is beyond the final valid positive index 2.

graphics.title: Zero-based list positions
graphics.alt: Zero-based list positions. Stored counts: Index 0 = 6, Index 1 = 1, Index 2 = 8.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Length is 3, but index 3 is beyond the final valid positive index 2. Changed condition: Replace the second print with print(counts[3]). Expected result: The first print shows 6, then IndexError stops the script before the length print. Reason: The attempted position does not exist.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: List positions begin at zero. A negative index counts from the end; the list length counts entries and is not itself a valid positive index for the final entry. Limit: A valid position does not establish that the stored count is accurate; empty lists also have no final element to read.

Use actual Python 3 results to check the prediction after reasoning first. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Label the three index positions. graphics.title: Functions and arguments: the case
graphics.alt: Match arguments to parameters. A function prints the difference between capacity and reserved spaces. Supplied facts: Python 3: def show_free(capacity,reserved): print(capacity-reserved). Calls: show_free(11,3); show_free(3,11).

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Define without calling: The definition creates the function but prints nothing yet. → Match first arguments: capacity=11 and reserved=3 give a printed 8. → Trace reversed call: capacity=3 and reserved=11 give -8 under the same arithmetic.

graphics.title: Arguments matched in order
graphics.alt: Arguments matched in order. show_remaining(12, 4) | capacity 12; used 4 | 8. show_remaining(10, 7) | capacity 10; used 7 | 3

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: capacity=3 and reserved=11 give -8 under the same arithmetic. Changed condition: Remove both calls and leave the definition only. Expected result: No output is printed. Reason: The body runs only when the function is called.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Positional arguments match parameter names in order. A function definition is not an execution of its body; separate calls supply separate input values. Limit: The arithmetic permits negative results; a real capacity contract may reject reserved>capacity instead of treating it as free space.

Use actual Python 3 results to check the prediction after reasoning first. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Match every argument to a parameter for the two calls. Why do outputs differ, and what prints when both calls are removed?

graphics.title: Return values and local state: the case
graphics.alt: Return values survive their calls. A function returns a local calculation that the caller stores. Supplied facts: Python 3: def extra(a,b): result=a+b; return result. Then first=extra(2,5); second=extra(4,1); print(first,second).

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Trace first call: Its local result is 7; return assigns 7 to first. → Trace second call: Its new local result is 5; return assigns 5 to second. → Read caller values: The final print displays 7 5; the second call does not overwrite first.

graphics.title: Two calls return two values
graphics.alt: Two calls return two values. remaining(12, 4) | spaces becomes 8 | first receives 8. remaining(10, 7) | spaces becomes 3 | second receives 3

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: The final print displays 7 5; the second call does not overwrite first. Changed condition: Add print(result) after the calls in a fresh script with no global result. Expected result: NameError occurs because that local name is not defined in the caller. Reason: A returned value and the function’s internal name are different things.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Returning passes a value back to the caller. Local names belong to a function call; storing the returned value creates a separate caller binding. Limit: The example uses immutable integers; shared mutable objects require additional reasoning about references.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For Python readiness before the Responsible Plant Classifier, retain a trace of the values, the predicted outputs and the changed-case explanation. Use actual Python 3 results to check the prediction after reasoning first. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Trace the two returned values and explain why first stays seven. What happens if the caller tries to print result directly?

graphics.title: Dictionaries and records: the case
graphics.alt: A zero field is still present. A dictionary record describes a shelf. The program distinguishes missing data from an actual zero. Supplied facts: Python 3: shelf={"count":0,"name":"Atlas"}; print(shelf["count"]); print(shelf.get("price")); print("count" in shelf).

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Read a stored field: count exists with numeric value 0. → Read an absent field: get("price") returns None because price is missing and no default was supplied. → Test key membership: "count" in shelf is True even though its value is zero.

graphics.title: Follow the evidence
graphics.alt: Follow the evidence. Read used | 4 | 12 - 4 = 8. Update used | 6 | 12 - 6 = 6

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: "count" in shelf is True even though its value is zero. Changed condition: Add the field price with value 0. Expected result: The price lookup now returns 0 instead of None. Reason: A recorded zero is a present value, whereas the earlier lookup had no field.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Dictionary keys name fields. Presence is different from truthiness of a value; a measured zero should not be discarded as if the field were absent. Limit: None is also a possible explicitly stored value; real record contracts must define how missing and null values are represented.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For Python readiness before the Responsible Plant Classifier, retain a trace of the values, the predicted outputs and the changed-case explanation. Use actual Python 3 results to check the prediction after reasoning first. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Predict all three original outputs. Explain the difference between count=0 and missing price, then predict the lookup after price=0 is added.

graphics.title: Reading structured data: the case
graphics.alt: Read rows with a missing-field policy. A toy table is represented as a list of dictionaries; count only rows with a recorded count. Supplied facts: Python 3 records: [{"count":2},{"count":0},{}]. Policy: include existing numeric counts, including zero; skip an absent field.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Inspect three rows: Two rows contain count; the third does not. → Accumulate values: The included values sum to 2+0=2, with denominator 2. → Report coverage and mean: Mean is 1; measured coverage is 2 of 3 rows.

graphics.title: Included values and absent field
graphics.alt: Included values and absent field. Row 1: Count value = 2, Include in mean? = Yes. Row 2: Count value = 0, Include in mean? = Yes. Row 3: Count value = Absent, Include in mean? = No.

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Mean is 1; measured coverage is 2 of 3 rows. Changed condition: Add {"count":4} as a fourth row. Expected result: Sum becomes 6, denominator 3, mean 2; coverage is 3 of 4. Reason: Only the added recorded value contributes; the existing absent field remains skipped.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: Structured data need a row policy before aggregation. Treating missing as zero changes the statistic and can conceal incomplete coverage; real zero remains an observation. Limit: This worked row policy is explicit; file parsing, malformed values and data provenance require additional checks.

graphics.title: Make the idea visible in your project
graphics.alt: For Python readiness before the Responsible Plant Classifier, retain a trace of the values, the predicted outputs and the changed-case explanation. Use actual Python 3 results to check the prediction after reasoning first. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Circle the included rows, calculate the sum and mean, and state coverage. Repeat after adding the fourth row with count four.

graphics.title: Testing and debugging functions: the case
graphics.alt: Use a test that catches the boundary bug. A function should classify an integer as tiny exactly when it is less than three. Supplied facts: Python 3 intended function: return x<3. Test cases: (2,True),(3,False),(4,False). Candidate bug: return x<=3.

graphics.title: Follow the deciding steps
graphics.alt: Record contract: Strict less-than excludes the value 3. → Run boundary cases: The intended outputs are True, False, False for 2,3,4. → Locate the bug: Using <= passes 2 but fails the test at 3 before the later test.

graphics.title: Follow the evidence
graphics.alt: Follow the evidence. Ordinary case | 8 and 3 | Expect 5. Full case | 8 and 8 | Expect 0. Unused case | 8 and 0 | Expect 8

graphics.title: Change one thing. Trace what follows.
graphics.alt: Original case: Using <= passes 2 but fails the test at 3 before the later test. Changed condition: Remove the test at 3 and keep only 2 and 4. Expected result: The buggy <= function passes those remaining tests. Reason: Both procedures agree away from the equality boundary.

graphics.title: Connect the explanation to its limit
graphics.alt: A revealing test distinguishes a correct implementation from a plausible mistake. Checking only values far from the boundary would miss this inclusive-versus-strict bug. Limit: Passing these cases does not prove correctness for every type or input; the contract and coverage determine what was actually checked.

graphics.alt: For Python readiness before the Responsible Plant Classifier, retain a trace of the values, the predicted outputs and the changed-case explanation. Use actual Python 3 results to check the prediction after reasoning first. Draw your input, deciding step, result and limit. Supported question: Predict the three correct outputs. Which test first catches <=, and why do tests at only two and four miss the bug?
